Most embarrasing of all to government was win of Ramraja Prasad Singh a Supreme Court lawyer who was the only candidate to directly advocate an immediate return to "the golden era of parliamentary rule"-and thus implicitly the abolition of the Panchayat system. His victory in the election while no immediate threat to the regime was a moral defeat and a clear indication of the overwhelming support for parliamentary democracy among the educated elite in the country. Sense of uncertainty and agitation in the government was indicated by the series of events that followed: the reluctance of the Presiding Officer of the Rastriya Panchayat to swear in Ramraja Prasad Singh along with the other newly-elected members; his arrest in the lobby of the legislature in a highly provocative manner by plainclothes men; his trial and conviction by a special tribunal; his release from prison under royal amnesty and finally his swearing in by royal command as a member of the Rastriya Panchayat. Even after release he continued to advocate a return to parliamentary democracy at a series of public meetings in various parts of the country. He was finally rearrested in October and then expelled from the Rastriya Panchayat allegedly for having violated the legislature's code of conduct. Likewise other three MPs of graduate constituency also expressed their liberal thoughts in Rastriya Panchayat for which they were also taken into custody and imprisoned for nearly more than a year and a half. Even after they got out of jail they were deliberately restricted from taking part in the 2033 General Elections because of being charged under the Security Act.

events.title: Communist Leaders Released From Jail
events.detail: As per the instruction of leader Adhikari, a public statement pledging support to the Constructive Leadership of the King was issued and several leaders of the then Nepal Communist Party under custody in Sunsari and Morang districts were freed. Manmohan Adhikari, Sambhu Ram Shrestha and Mohan Bikram Singh were released from jail. Both Manmohan and Mohan Bikram sided with the more radical Communist Party led by Tulsi Lal Amatya.

events.title: BP Koirala Helps in Bangladesh Liberation
events.detail: After returning from Europe trip BP had started collecting arms preparing for the arm revolt against the King. Over time he had colected about a truck of weapon using all the money he had. When the Bangladesh Liberation War started Sheikh Mujib's group reached out to him for weapon throguh Jay Prakash Narayan. For a noble cause BP gave the arms to Mukti Bahini in an assurance that they would pay good amount for the weapons. Later after Bangladesh was liberated Mujib became so dependent upon Indira Gandhi he didn't even thank Jay Prakash Narayan and BP publicly. He only used to send private note of thanks. This diminished BP's respect for Mujib while BP helped wholeheartedly for their cause taking all short of risks he neither thanked him publicly nor gave money for the weapons. This incident made BP and Nepali Congress broke and prompted them to hijack the plane for money.

events.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
events.detail: Tensions began as early as 1948 when Pakistan declared Urdu as the sole national language ignoring Bengali which was spoken by the majority of the population. Revenue generated from East Pakistan’s lucrative jute exports was systematically used to fund development and industrialization in West Pakistan. The breaking point came after the December 1970 democratic elections. The East Pakistani Awami League party led by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman won a clear majority. West Pakistani military and political leaders refused to hand over power. On March 25 1971 the Pakistani military launched Operation Searchlight a brutal crackdown designed to crush the Bengali nationalist movement. In response to the assault the independence of Bangladesh was declared on March 26 1971 and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was arrested. The resistance was spearheaded by the Mukti Bahini (Freedom Fighters) a guerrilla army made up of Bengali soldiers who defected from the Pakistani military paramilitary forces students and peasants. The extreme violence forced over 10 million Bengali refugees to flee across the border into neighboring Indian states creating a massive humanitarian crisis. The war transformed from an internal revolution into a conventional international conflict on December 3 1971 when Pakistan launched pre-emptive airstrikes against airfields in western India. At the end of India-Pakistan War Bangladesh got liberated. Nepal was one of the first nations to recognise Bangladesh on January 16 1972. In retaliation Pakistan broke off relations with Nepal temporarily. Bilateral relations improved considerably when the 1975 military coup in Bangladesh brought to power a government that distanced the country from India with both nations seeking to counter the influence of their largest neighbour. In April 1976 both nations signed bilateral agreements to develop trade transit and civil aviation.

events.title: Kirti Nidhi Bista
events.detail: 2nd Term

events.title: National Education System Plan 2028 (NESP)
events.detail: Objectives: The NESP had two political goals – "to produce citizens who with full faith in the country and the Crown will conduct themselves in accordance with the Panchayat System and to meet the manpower requirements of the development through the spread of scientific and technical education" and to strengthen the ‘national integration’ with a focus on unity around a common language (Nepali) and a common religion and culture (Hinduism). Nationalization of Schools: Most community schools were brought under government control reducing local autonomy and integrating schools into a centralized state structure. Teachers became increasingly state employees and subject to centralized recruitment deployment and administrative oversight reducing independent community influence over schools. Nepali Language: Post revolution education system became highly decentralized with community led efforts. NESP transformed education system through highly centralized and state-controlled textbooks curriculum examinations and teacher management. Nepali was strictly enforced a the medium of instruction. NESP institutionalized and intensified an earlier tendency already visible in the 1956 Nepal National Education Planning Commission (NNEPC) recommendations. Mahendramala: Nepali language primers for all school grades were named Mahendramala. It had stories of potraying Nepali as brave sensationalizing fights of Nalapani and World Wars. It also included the biographies of kings "national bir purusharu patriots and martyrs" as well as lessons on rajbhakti. Without doubt the theme of rajbhakti - service to the monarchy - served to help legitimate the assumption of autocratic power by the king. The book also contained many rastra geets and kakshyagat geets to develop loalty towards nation and the crown concurrently. School Rituals: All the schools were told to keep a portrait of His Majesty the King in their premises. In April 1961 students in all educational institutions were required to recite the national anthem at the beginning of each school day and at the beginning and end of all school functions. Gradually the national anthem and rastra geets displaced the Saraswati Bandana with which children used to begin school in 1950s. Schools also regularly observed royal occasions such as the King's birthday coronations and other state ceremonies through assemblies songs competitions and cultural activities as part of broader efforts to cultivate nationalism and loyalty to the monarchy. National Development Service (NDS): Under NDS all MA level students at Tribhuvan University were required to do nearly a year-long service in some rural location of Nepal. It required students to spend a year in the villages after two semesters in the university. This program lasted between 1974 and 1980 and is considered to be one of the most successful programs executed under the Panchayat System. Completion of a year's service and final written report counted for one of the nine papers required to earn the degree. The initial plan was to field NDS volunteers in 4 sectors: health education agriculture and construction (engineering). During its short life however only the education corps was mobilized. Service began with training and orientation followed by a mandatory 10 months in a rural community. It ended by return to campus and submission of the final report. Assignment to remote areas was given priority. Most students were sent out to teach and were typically posted together in groups of two or three. Their work was overseen by the local school headmaster and the district education officer and by a supervisor who occasionally visited them from Kathmandu. The program's operating expenses were funded entirely by the government and were increased annually. The only outside help came from a few U.N. agencies and the Canadian IDRC who together provided minor logistics support consulting services some publications costs a few vehicles and some field supplies for the. The program was formally inaugurated in July 1974 and 212 students were sent out. Between 1972 and 1979 (when the program was suddenly closed) nearly 3000 students were involved. Altogether 72 of Nepal's 75 districts received NDS volunteers. Politics of NDS: There is a political side to the start and sudden end of the program too. Initially one of the objective for this program was to scatter politically active Master's students out of Kathmandu and break-up organizational structure of student unions. The student unions were banned in Nepal after the introduction of New Education. The program was suddenly terminated in 1979 just before the referendum largly due to the fear of the NDS students acting as agents for the multi-party democratic option in the rural Nepal. Educational Downgrade: During the education boom of 1950s and 60s liberal arts was growing at 61.3% whereas the rate of growth in the other subjects was much less. Most of the student participating in student politics were from the liberal arts background which was alarming for the Panchayat regime. Concurrently as college graduates were increasing due to lack of opportunities unemployment also increased. To counter this the New Education focused to shift graduate education towards science and produce less graduates. Firstly all schools were nationalized and then 'levels' of many schools were downgraded. For instance secondary schools were downgraded to primary school and some schools were merged as well. This made it difficult for students in rural areas to go to secondary or higher secondary schools as there were very few of them and far from home. Many arts and humanies college were closed with the onset of New Education and government took policy to produce manpower just enough to meet country's demand. Government took a tacit policy to pass no more than one-fourth students and most students made fail were from backwarded community.

events.title: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation
events.detail: The Sino-Soviet split had turned China and the USSR into bitter adversaries. Pakistan was highly friendly with China. Moscow feared that a Pakistani victory in East Pakistan backed by Beijing would expand Chinese influence right onto India's borders. USSR and India saw anti-Soviet and anti-India bloc (US-China-Pakistan) forming. In August 1971 the Soviets and Indians signed the Treaty of Peace Friendship and Cooperation which acted as a deterrent against intervention from outside powers. The Bangladesh Liberation became perfect battleground to practice this alliance. Moscow used its United Nations Security Council veto to block resolutions that would have condemned India's intervention and forced a ceasefire before East Pakistan could be liberated. When the US sent a naval fleet into the Bay of Bengal the Soviet Union countered by deploying a nuclear-armed flotilla of its own. The Soviet fleet shadowed the Americans effectively neutralizing the threat of a US attack on India or Bangladesh. Despite its wartime stance the US pivoted quickly after the war becoming the largest foreign aid contributor to the newly established nation of Bangladesh by 1973.

events.title: India-Nepal Treaty of Trade and Transit
events.detail: PM Minister Kirtinidhi Bista's anti-Indian posturings during his first term of office (1969-70) and King Mahendra's open and public demand in 1970 for "justice" for Nepal in accordance with the principles of international law as these apply to landlocked countries had both been intended to pressure New Delhi into granting concessions in the 1960 trade treaty which was due to expire in 1970. Anti-Indian demonstrations were actively sponsored by the government in Kathmandu and several other urban centers. To counter the regime's efforts to whip up anti-India feeling at the popular level New Delhi unilaterally declared its intention to continue the supply of essential commodities to Nepal until a new trade treaty was signed. Nepal's efforts to exert various kinds of pressure on India ended with the February 1971 elections in India which returned Mrs. Gandhi's Congress Party to office with an overwhelming majority. Many Nepali had begun to hold their own government responsible. By mid-1971 the economy and trade of Nepal had been so badly affected that the government was compelled to sign the treaty with India-essentially on New Delhi's terms. Nepal had demanded: (1) separate treaties covering trade and transit; (2) a trade route to East Pakistan through India; (3) removal of qualitative and quantitative restrictions on Nepal's imports from third countries and its exports to India; (4) simplification of customs procedures; (5) additional warehouse space at Calcutta port under Nepali supervision; (6) the right to operate barges in Calcutta port and to utilize sealed truck containers in transporting goods between Calcutta and Nepal; and (7) equal treatment for ships under Nepali flags in Indian ports as that given to Indian ships. In the end however the Indians either refused to accept or made only minor changes in the existing system with respect to the first four Nepali conditions: indeed in some cases the terms were more restrictive on Nepal than those in the 1960 treaty. The only gains were India's acceptance of points five and six of Nepal's demands but these New Delhi had been prepared to concede from the beginning of negotiations in mid-1960s. The stricter Indian controls over Nepal's imports and exports was the price Kathmandu had to pay for its deliberate policy of exploiting certain loopholes in the 1960 Treaty for short-term if lucrative advantages for a small group of influential Nepalis and some Indian commercial interests. Particularly irksome to New Delhi was the extensive use made by overseas exporters in Nepal of the international gift parcel system to import luxury items from abroad and then re-export these-often illegally-to India.

events.title: UN General Assembly Voted to Recognize Mao's China as PRC
events.detail: In 1945 as one of the main victorious Allies of WWII the ROC was granted a permanent veto-wielding seat on the newly formed UN. Even after Chiang Kai-shek’s ROC government fled mainland China and relocated to the island of Taiwan it continued to hold the UN seat for China. Backed heavily by the United States during the peak of the anti-communist Cold War the international community continued to recognize the ROC as the sole legitimate government of all China. Meanwhile Mao had declared the establishment of the PRC in Beijing. Seeking to exploit the growing ideological rift between the Soviet Union and communist China the U.S. began opening diplomatic backchannels with Beijing. This signaled to the rest of the world that Western opposition to the PRC was softening. Seeking to exploit the growing ideological rift between the Soviet Union and communist China the U.S. began opening diplomatic backchannels through Henry Kissinger in 1969 with Beijing. On October 25 1971 the UN General Assembly voted on Resolution 2758. The resolution did not admit a "new country"; instead it voted on which delegation legally represented the existing seat of "China." It formally recognized the PRC as "the only legitimate representative of China to the United Nations" expelling the "representatives of Chiang Kai-shek" from the UN and all its affiliated organizations.

events.title: India-Pakistan War of 1971
events.detail: India provided sanctuary funding and training to the Mukti Bahini straining relations with Pakistan to the breaking point. On December 3 1971 Pakistan launched Operation Chengiz Khan—pre-emptive airstrikes against 11 Indian airfields in the west. Pakistan hoped to replicate Israel’s success in the 1967 Six-Day War. The strikes failed to cause major damage and Indian Prime Minister Indira Gandhi formally declared war that evening. In the Esat the Indian Army coordinated with the Mukti Bahini launched a lightning multi-pronged blitzkrieg and in the west India fought defensive battles to hold its ground in Kashmir Punjab and Rajasthan famously defeating a massive Pakistani tank assault. The Indian Navy launched Operation Trident striking the Karachi port and effectively cutting off sea lanes trapping Pakistani forces in the east. Within two weeks Indian forces completely surrounded Dhaka. On December 16 1971 Pakistani General A.A.K. Niazi signed the instrument of surrender. Over 93000 Pakistani soldiers and civilians surrendered to the Indian Army marking the largest surrender of personnel since World War II. The war drew in global superpowers. The US (siding with Pakistan) sent the USS Enterprise aircraft carrier into the Bay of Bengal as a show of force while the Soviet Union deployed nuclear-armed submarines to block US intervention and protect India. The war permanently reshaped the map of South Asia. East Pakistan became the independent nation of Bangladesh. In 1972 India and Pakistan signed the Simla Agreement releasing the 93000 prisoners of war and converting the old 1949 UN ceasefire line into the modern Line of Control (LoC). Thousands of Bengali refugees crossed through India to seek safety in Nepal as well. The repatriation of the refugees still remains a long-standing diplomatic headache for Kathmandu.

events.title: Central Nucleus Formed
events.detail: The CPN leaders released from jail started gathering leftwing elements from the Amatya-led Communist Party of Nepal and formed a Central Nucleus with an aim to reorganize the party and reunite with the CPN (Pushpa Lal) faction. Leaders like Manmohan Singh, Mohan Bikram SIngh, Nirmal Lama, and Sambhuram Shrestha took this initiative. However, such a merger never took off, partly due to Pushpa Lal's hesitation to merge his own faction into another party and partly due to Pushpa Lal's wish to collaborate with the Nepali Congress against the royal regime (which Mohan Bikram did not accept). This failure gave rise to further parties CPN (Manmohan) and Mohan Bikram Led CPN (Fourth Convention).

events.title: Nepal And Bangladesh Issue
events.detail: Emergence of Bangladesh as an independent state in the face of Peking's determined-if only vocal opposition is indicative of China's inability to directly challenge India's status as the hegemonic power in South Asia. Newly independent state of Bangladesh and the admittance of Bhutan to the United Nations were of considerable significance to Nepal. The emergence of Bangladesh as a result of India's determined armed support to the principle of self determination resurgence of participatory democracy in India Bangladesh and the new civil regime in Pakistan under President Bhutto had put pressure in Nepal's Panchayat regime. Even the Bhutan monarch has accepted the principle of popular legitimacy by voluntarily agreeing to abdicate if two-thirds of that country's national legislature should so request-an example of self-abnegation all of which acted as a pressure to Nepal to move towards democracy.

events.title: Dhalkebar–Pathlaiya Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: After initial request from King Mahendra was rejected by India he sought help of USSR for the construction of the highway. Accordingly Soviet Union began constructing the 109-km Dhalkebar–Pathlaiya section in 1967 which they completed in 1972.

events.title: Nepal Telecommunications Corporation Established
events.detail: In 1972 Nepal Telecom was formally established as a wholly government-owned corporation under the Communications Corporation Act operating as Nepal Telecommunications Corporation. Starting in the late 1960s and 1970s, the World Bank's ⁠International Development Association (IDA) provided concessional credits (such as a $1.7 million credit). In 2004 it was renamed Nepal Doorsanchar Company Limited (NDCL) under the Companies Act (1997). In 2003 Nepal Telecom introduced nationwide GSM services.

events.title: Sunkoshi Hydropower Station Built
events.detail: Sunkoshi Hydropower is a run-of-river hydro-electric plant located in Sindhupalchok District of Nepal built entirely by Chinese Aid. The flow from Sunkoshi River is used to generate 10.05 MW electricity.

events.title: Nepal Divided Into Four Development Regions
events.detail: King Birendra in assistance with geologist Dr. Hark Gurung brought forth the concept of regional development for the harmonious developments of all parts of the country. Subsequently, he divided Nepal into 4 Development Regions in 1972: Eastern, Central, Western and Far Western. The Far-Western region was split into Mid-Western and Far-Western, creating a total of 5 development regions in 1980. These regions were created so the national budget could be split equitably. Each region received its own dedicated planning offices (under the National Planning Commission) to build roads, hospitals, and agricultural networks. Geographically, their vertical division was designed so that the food grown in the fertile Terai could easily be traded straight up into the timber-rich Hills and livestock-rich Mountains within the same administrative boundary.

events.title: Birendra Bir Bikram Shah
events.detail: Died during royal massacre at the age of 55

events.title: Rajeshwar Devkota Resigned
events.detail: Kritinidhi Bista's resignation after the dispute with India became an enouraging event for the opposition faction of Surya Bahadur Thapa. However King Mahendra didn't appoint a new PM instead Bista was reappointed after the India issue cooled down. Surya Bahadur Thapa faction soon got another chance to drag Bista. Election of all reformist candidates in Rastriya Panchayat election from Graduate Constituency was moral defeat of Kritinidhi Bista. Thapa used this opportunity to strengthen his side by tabling a motion of no confidence against the Bista's close ally Rastriya Panchayat Chairman Rajeshwar Devkota. Faced with dwindling support Devkota voluntaraily resigned. This gave signal to Bista and the King that Bista has lost confidence in the house.

events.title: Series of Political Murder
events.detail: Yogendra Man Sherchan: Shortly after being released from an eight-year imprisonment Sherchan was actively working to revive democracy when a government jeep fatally struck him outside his residence at 10:00 PM on Mar 17 1972. Although the driver was arrested to deflect blame the regime avoided conducting a judicial investigation into the state-engineered political murder. He was a freedom fighter and minister of BP cabinet. Ramailo Jhoda (Wetland) Kanda: The administration had a biased view that Jhoda (squatters settlement in Morang) was a gathering ground of revolutionaries rebels and diehard opponents of the Panchayat. Government engineered a violent assault to suppress Diwan Singh Rai leadership among squatter farmers. On August 17 1972 when he was in the house of his fellow fighter Ram Prasad in Kakum Jhoda of Morang a violent gang surrounded the house and made an assault on Rai with spears knives and spades. He was an ex-soldier freedom fighter and minister of BP cabinet. The assassination was never investigated. Keshav Koirala: Keshav Koirala was a democratic activist and freedom fighter born in Okhaldhunga who made Mahottari his base for the anti-panchayat struggle. He was killed in Matihani Mahottari district on August 14 1973. There had been contradictory information as to whether he was shot dead under custody after being arrested by the police for attempting to detonate a symbolic bomb at the Matihani or he had died during an exchange of firing.

events.title: Siddhartha Highway Completed
events.detail: The 181 km Siddhartha Highway (Sunauli-Bhairahawa-Butwal-Palpa-Syangja-Pokhara Road) was heavily funded and executed through Indian aid as a strategic bilateral infrastructure project. Work began in 1964 and the highway was officially completed and opened in 1972.

events.title: NC Begins Its Third Armed Struggle
events.detail: After series of political murder were taking place it became very eminent to start the long awaited armed struggle. Preparation: Girija Prasad Koirala was given the responsibility of directly managing the struggle. He initially set up camps in Farvesgunj and later in Purnia. In Farvesgunj he opened a Mukti Sena camp under the leadership of Yagya Bahadur Thapa and a political camp under his own leadership. In the Mukti Sena camp soldiers were gathered trained and sent to related places. Former Nepali Army Indian Army and British Army were recruited in the Mukti Sena. However due to lack of financial support from Subarna Shamsher the armed struggle had not started. Hariharpur Incident: On Aug 25 1972 the armed struggle began with an attack on the Haripur outpost in Saptari. One policeman was killed and the outpost was captured. The attackers returned to India. After the Nepal government strongly objected to this India ordered the arrest of the attackers. Some cadres were also arrested. They were released by Girija. BP got angry with Girija for carrying out this attack without consulting him. Acting President Subarna also disagreed with that. Murder of Saroj Prasad Koirala: Saroj Prasad Koirala a prominent leader of the NC was assassinated on 18 October 1973 while traveling by train near Madhubani India after being shot three times with a silenced pistol. The killing widely believed to have been orchestrated by the Janakpur Zonal Commissioner using hired criminals shocked the political establishment and was widely condemned by supporters of democracy and human rights. The assassination was never investigated. Koirala was a cousin of BP Koirala. Missed Target And Bomb at Police Barrack Phusre: On 15 December 1973 an armed clash took place between activists led by Ganga Bahadur and police forces in Malangawa Sarlahi resulting in the deaths of some civilians. On 4 May 1973 a grenade was thrown at then Minister for Works and Transport Prayag Raj Singh Suwal in Kathmandu by NC activist Shiva Prasad Kangala but it missed the target and injured civilians instead leading to public criticism and a government crackdown in which 401 people were arrested. Later on 18 April 1974 Barn Bahadur was arrested while attempting to bomb a police barrack in Phusre Dharan. These incidents intensified state repression against the armed democratic movement. Bomb Aimed at Government Officials in Jaleswar: A powerful bomb was exploded at a place called Bajrahi Math which was targeted at the zonal commissioner the chief district officer and high ranking police officers who were returning from a dinner party late at night. Although zonal commissioner Lila Raj Bista was the main target of the bomb the CDO was seriously injured by it. Assault on the Janakpur Police Post: Soon after Jaleswar incident an assault was made on the police post of Janakpur in which a bomb was exploded and a revolver was also used. This assault was made at the initiative of youths affiliated with the Nepali Congress. In connection with this incident even the priest of Janaki Mandir could not avoid suspicion of the terror stricken administration. A lot of students and youths were arrested by the local administration. Jadukoha Firing Incident: A procession was organized there on September 13 1972. On September 15 the local administration arrested a student Mahendra by name. After the arrest a big crowd of students rescued him while police was taken to Janakpur. On September 17 the students of Jadukoha organized a joint procession. As the procession of about 250 students proceeded from Jadukoha high school towards the market the police charged batons upon it. The police administration was awaiting an opportunity to take revenge so it opened fire. A 17-year-old ninth grade student of Jadukoha high school Kameswar Mandal sustained a bullet injury. Another injured student of Dhabauli high school Kanni Goit died in the evening the same day while undergoing treatment at the local health post. Still another student Kusheswar Mandal who had received three bullets in the leg also died in the evening the same day. A 50-year-old woman of Jadukoha and Makka Raj of Macho village and Sabakat Kabari of Nanupatti also fell victim to bullets. A total of 42 students and 75 ordinary citizens sustained injuries in the repressive firing incident. Timurbote Kanda: The strategists of this incident were Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa and some others Gopal Rai Agam Mani Rai Balraj Karki and Kshetra Dhwaj Basnet. Led by Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa with key figures including Gopal Rai Agam Mani Rai Balraj Karki and Kshetra Dhwaj Basnet a group of 53 fighters planned to capture the Okhaldhunga army barracks. But how practical it was for some ex-soldiers to take up their limited weapons and move against 700 well-trained and equipped royal soldiers is a different question. The group was divided into units commanded by Agam Mani Rai L.B. Gurung Mahesh Kormocha and Dhak Bahadur Gurung while Yagya Bahadur commanded Gopal Rai Ram Upadhyay and Laxman Upadhyay. Armed with grenades Sten guns pistols revolvers and ammunition they advanced toward Okhaldhunga but their plan was exposed and the Royal Army surrounded them at Timurbote. On 15 December 1972 they planned coordinated attacks on the police post jail and CDO office in Solu but the Royal Army bombed their hideout and crushed the operation. Many fighters including Agam Mani Rai Shyam Kumar Gurung Padam Prakash Puri Shiva Kumar Rai Maila Rai Man Bahadur Bakhim Man Bahadur Magar Lal Bahadur Magar Chandra Bahadur Tamang Ram Upadhyay Laxman Upadhyay Prajalal Rai Mahesh Koirala Netra Bahadur Karki Krishna Bahadur Limbu and Peshal Kumar Dahal were killed. Others including Harka Bahadur Karki Ambar Bahadur Khadka Bhim Bahadur Katuwal Shamsher Bahadur Karki Ram Kumar Sunuwar Tika Ram Rai Homisher Rai and his son were later killed while being transferred to jail. Kam Bahadur Basnet and Bhabendra Bahadur Basnet disappeared while Lok Bahadur Gurung and Jas Dhan Rai escaped. Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa was captured and later executed. Biratnagar Bomb Explosion: In the course of the second armed struggle being conducted by the Nepali Congress a bomb was exploded in Biratnagar during the king's visit on March 14 1975. The persons targeted at escaped safe from the explosion but unfortunately dozens of innocent citizens sustained injuries. Leaders like Bhim Narayan Shrestha were arrested in the incident. Realization: Meanwhile Subarna Shamsher Rana openly opposed the Nepali Congress's armed struggle and Krishna Prasad Bhattarai who was in prison also disagreed with the strategy. On 25 June 1975 Indira Gandhi declared the Emergency in India and arrested opposition leaders including socialist leader Jayaprakash Narayan a close associate of BP Koirala. As a result India was no longer a favorable base for the Nepali Congress movement. BP then decided to renounce armed resistance in favor of a nonviolent movement within Nepal. Adopting the policy of National Reconciliation (Melmilap) with the monarchy he returned to Nepal on 31 December 1976. With this the Nepali Congress's second armed struggle formally came to an end in failure having inflicted heavy losses on the party.

events.title: Pro-reformist Panchayat Leaders Arrested
events.detail: Surya Bahadur Thapa had previously served as Prime Minister during the early stages of the partyless Panchayat system. He grew disillusioned with its failure to modernize and give ordinary citizens a voice. Following the death of King Mahendra King Birendra ascended the throne in early 1972. Thapa and other leaders saw the transition of power as a crucial window to push the new monarch toward a constitutional democracy triggering his famous Itum-Bahal address. Surya Bahadur Thapa was arrested and imprisoned in Nakkhu Jail after delivering a historic public speech at Itum-Bahal. He championed a 13-point resolution that called for sweeping democratic changes to the Constitution the restoration of basic human rights and the reinstatement of democratic elections. Following the declaration the state detained key figures including Thapa and Rishikesh Shah prompting a subsequent 21-day hunger strike by Thapa in 1974 that forced their release and significantly weakened the monarchy's authority paving the way for the 1979 student uprisings.

events.title: Jhapa Revolt And Sukhani Kanda
events.detail: King Mahendra introduced land reforms in 1964 to set ownership ceilings and protect tenants, but local landlords ignored these rights, causing severe tenant frustrati. In 1967 the Indian government launched a massive crackdown on the Naxalite movement. Naxalite leaders such as Kanu Sanyal, Charu Majumdar, Deepak Biswas and Jangal Santhal used to take shelter in Jhapa where Nepali communist leaders met them. The Jhapa District Committee of CPN (Amatya) independently coordinated with Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist). One of the revolt’s goals was to seize rice and distribute it to farmers and establish the rights of tenants. The political resistance transformed into an armed insurgency in 1970. The party created armed squads in areas with high concentration of landless farmers. Each unit was supposed to create a guerrilla squad equipped with weapons which would then collect firearms from landlords and security agencies. The Jhapa Revolt was launched on 17 May 1971. The first victim was Butan Chaudhari himself a farmer. He was perceived as a threat to the party because of his anti-communist ideology. After Chaudhari various other landlords were ambushed and murdered. The Panchayat regime stepped up a search operation in the east after the murder of landlords. Police rounded up almost all the leaders who were labeled “anti-national elements” in a matter of one year. Five communist rebels Ramnath Dahal, Netra Ghimire, Biren Rajbanshi, Krishna Kuinkel, Narayan Shrestha were arrested and later killed in a fake encounter in Sukhani forest bordering Jhapa and Ilam on March 4 1973. Leftist movement continued to be unified and widespread being inspired by the brutal torture undergone in Jail by Mohanchandra Adhikari ,C.P. Mainali, Radhakrishna Mainali, KP Oli, Durga Prasad Adhikari, Dhanendra Basnet, Naresh Kharel, Chhabi Lal Rajbansi, Bhogendra Rajbansi, Mangal Mani Satar, Namakumar Tamang, Manakumar Gautam, Amar Karki, Amar Adhikari, Panbir Viswakarma, Bhishma Dahal, Sita Khadka, Gaura Prasai, etc. but also by the self-sacrifice of Netra Ghimire Krishna Kuikel Ramnath Dahal Dhauren Rajbansi Chandra Bahadur Dangi Narayan Shrestha and others.

events.title: Royal Nepal Plane Hijacking
events.detail: NC's armed struggle had been on hult after the Sino-India War of 1962. After BP's release party started another armed struggle but it was running out of money as Subarna Shumsher didn't help this time. BP had asked Indian PM Indira Gandhi for weapons and even Rs 1 Crore for that. However as the possibility of support from Indira began to diminish BP began looking for other sources. Especially after giving away collected weapons to Bangladesh's Mukti Bahini the party went broke. Therefore they came up with the plan of plane hijack. The operation masterminded by Girija Prasad Koirala and executed by party activists including Durga Subedi Basant Bhattarai Nagendra Dhungel and Vinod Aryal targeted a Nepal Airlines Twin Otter transporting about IRS 30 Lakh in government bank cash from Biratnagar to Kathmandu. Shortly after takeoff from Biratnagar the hijackers entered the cockpit at gunpoint and forced the pilots to divert the aircraft to an improvised landing strip at Forbesganj India. There waiting party members unloaded the cash before allowing the aircraft and its passengers to continue safely to Kathmandu. No passengers or crew were harmed. The money was delivered to BP Koirala's network in exile and was used to finance the Nepali Congress's armed campaign against the Panchayat system including the purchase of weapons. However within a year all hijackers were arrested in India except Nagendra Dhungel. After the 1975 Emergency in India ended they were released on bail.

events.title: Singha Durbar Fire
events.detail: On 9 July 1973 a huge fire broke out in Singha Durbar engulfing all three wings of the palace except the front facing wing. To prevent the front wing from catching fire cannons destroyed three wings facing North South and West. Employees working at Singha Durbar the then prime minister Kirti Nidhi Bista and ministers did their best to contain the fire on the night but its scale was overwhelming. Flames engulfed large sections of the palace and continued to burn into the next day. Little of substance could be saved. One individual named Sher Bahadur Shahi was assigned to investigate the cause of the fire but the responsibility was far too big for a single person. Therefore the truth was never uncovered. After the fire was put out the whole area was rebuilt on the old foundation. It took approximately 40 to 50 years for parts of Singha Durbar to be renovated and restored and made ready for reuse. The exact cause of the fire which started at midnight remains a mystery. Prime Minister ⁠Kirti Nidhi Bista took moral responsibility for the event and resigned one week later on July 16 1973.

events.title: Nagendra Prasad Rijal
events.detail: 1st Term

events.title: OPEC Oil Embargo and Economic Problem
events.detail: The 1970s oil crisis began in October 1973 when Arab members of OPEC declared an oil embargo against nations that supported Israel during the Yom Kippur War. This shock fundamentally changed the global economy triggering a period of "stagflation" and Nepal was no exception. Nepal's economic growth had stayed below 2% for last 4 years and locals faced rising commodity prices every week. Government was unable to control prices of essential commodities. Stung with bitter citicisms government came up with few measures. It increased the interest rate budget promised to provide minimum necessities to fixed income groups at "reasonable" prices and rice exports were to be institutionalized starting November 18 1974. Though the programs were welcomed but they lacked proper implementation. The "minimum necessity program" became only limited to rationing oil and kerosene. As for rice government released 1200 tons of paraboiled rice at fixed prices in Kathamndu like it had done previous years. In fact government didn't even botehr to find out who were to be included in the fixed income groups cited in the budget. The rice nationalization policy also failed badly as the program started very late then the announced date and had to rely on old network of traders who exploited the government to the maximum.

events.title: Release of Rastriya Panchayat Members
events.detail: Government released the 3 members of Rastriya Panchayat from graduate constituency Dr. Prakash Chandra Lohani Ratna Prasad Kharel and Krishna Prasad Bhandari who had criticised the government demanding reforms of panchayat system. All 3 had been jailed under Security Act 17 months earlier.

events.title: Press Statement Politics
events.detail: Leaders like Tanka Prasad Acharya and Subarna Shumsher resorted to frequent press statements as a way to criticize the Panchayat Government as they lacked cadres and proper political program behind them.

events.title: Prithvi Highway Inagurated
events.detail: The 174-kilometre-long highway connecting Naubise of Tribhuvan Highway 26km from Kathmandu and Prithivi Chowk Pokhara was built with Chinese aid. The construction of the highway started in 1967 and completed in 1974

events.title: Mechinagar (Kakarbhitta) – Dhalkebar Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: Though India was initially hesitant of the assistant they jumped in after Soviet Union started constructing the Dhalkebar - Pathalaiya section of the highway. Under India's assistance the construction of 258 km road began in 1967 and was completed in 1974.

events.title: Harre Barre Peasant Movement
events.detail: The Harre Barre Struggle was a leftist peasant movement in Harre and Barre of Arghakhanchi district inspired by growing communist influence among peasants. Led by Keshar Mani Pokhrel who returned from India after differences with Pushpa Lal Shrestha the movement attempted to implement armed struggle by targeting the property of local feudal figures. Along with Beduram Bhusal Pitambar Bhusal Devaraj Bhar Buddhi Rayamajhi Netra Prasad Dhungana and others he targeted the house of local landlord and Panchayat supporter Shobhakhar Belbase who was accused of exploiting peasants through usurious loans and forged debt documents. After an exchange of gunfire the group burned debt records forced Belbase to promise to stop exploiting farmers and seized cash and valuables worth about Rs. 25000. Their objective was not to kill but to end feudal exploitation. The government launched a major crackdown after the incident. Nine of the fifteen participants were arrested—many after being betrayed by infiltrator Shashidhar Acharya. Keshar Mani Pokhrel spent nearly seven years in prison before being released under a royal amnesty in 1980.

events.title: Nepal-China Trade and Payments Agreement
events.detail: Principle of Equilibrium: Both countries did not want huge trade imbalances as both were short of foreign reserve. SO they agreed that trade should be regulated as far as possible on the principle of equilibrium. MFN Treatment: We will treat each other's goods at least as favorably as goods from other countries. Official Trade Routes: The treaty officially recognized only three major trade routes Kodari – Nyalam Rasuwa – Kyerong and Yari – Purang. 30-km Border Trade Rule: People living within 30 km of the border can continue traditional barter trade without normal trade restrictions. Payment System: Overseas trade payments are to be made in freely convertible currency while overland trade payments are to continue in the "traditional customary way". For overseas trade China and Nepal each opened an account in Kathmandu and Beijing respectively providing £300000 swing credit or overdraft facility. Logistics and Shipping Terms: Nepal exported on an F.O.B. basis and China exported on a C.I.F. basis at Calcutta or other transit ports.

events.title: Mohan Bikram SIngh Faction CPN's Fourth National Convention
events.detail: When Nepal’s communist movement was fragmented a Central Nucleus was formed on December 4 1971 under leaders like Manmohan Adhikari to pursue unity but talks with Pushpa Lal failed. The Fourth Congress held in Varanasi in 15 September 1974 instead caused another split leading to the formation of CPN (Fourth Convention) under Mohan Bikram Singh which later fragmented into groups including Masal and the Maoists. At the time the Central Committee of the party consisted of Mohan Bikram Singh (general secretary), Nirmal Lama, Jaya Govinda Shah, Bhakta Bahadur Shrestha, Khampa Singh, Mohan Baidhya, Rishi Devkota, Suryanath Yadav, Khubiram Acharya, Chitra Bahadur K.C., Gangadhar Ghimire and Bhardhwaj. Mohan Bikram Singh faction later formed Communist Party of Nepal (Masal) in 1983. Meanwhile the Jhapa District Committee decided on armed struggle in 1971 leading to the Jhapa Uprising under leaders such as C.P. Mainali. This stream formed the All Nepal Revolutionary Coordination Center (Male) in 1975 and later established CPN (Marxist-Leninist) in 1979 which became the main root of today’s UML. Rejecting the Fourth Congress CPN (Male) held its own Fourth National Convention in 1989.

events.title: Nakkhu Jail Murder
events.detail: On 29 September 1974 four political prisoners from Okhaldhunga—Lila Nath Dahal Thagi Raj Dahal Gokarna Bahadur Karki and Khagendra Raj Dahal—were taken from Central Jail under the pretext of being transferred to Nakkhu Jail. Lila Nath Dahal and Thagi Raj Dahal were arrested by state authorities while transporting explosives and were arrested at the Thankot checkpoint in Kathmandu while other two for resistance against government. Instead of transfering them they were executed in a rice field near Jawalakhel–Nakkhu by security forces. The Panchayat government claimed they were shot after attempting to escape and seize weapons from guards but this explanation was widely rejected because the prisoners were handcuffed and heavily restrained.

events.title: Pokhara Industrial Estate Established
events.detail: The Pokhara Industrial Estate was established in 1974 with investment from the Government of Nepal. It spans a total land footprint of 472 ropanis. The district currently hosts 86 total establishments within which 77 are active manufacturing industries.

events.title: Revolutionary Coordination Committee emerged from alive Jhapa Rebelion Leaders
events.detail: Founded by Jhapa District Committee of the Communist Party of Nepal (Amatya) leaders such as CP and RK Mainali and the Morang District-based Nepal Revolutionary Organisation (Marxist–Leninist) led by Madhav Kumar Nepal. On 30 August 1977 Mukti Morcha Samuha led by Madan Kumar Bhandari merged into the party. In August 1978 a section of the Dhanusa District Committee of the Communist Party of Nepal (Amatya) merged into the party.

events.title: Strain on Balance of Payment
events.detail: Although Nepal's economy was stagnant at just below 2% growth it had generally maintained a healthy balance of payments. By the mid-1970s however its trade deficit with India had grown so large that the government had to use convertible foreign exchange to buy Indian rupees for imports. Exports to third countries also failed to expand despite the export bonus scheme remaining stuck at around Rs. 12 Crore (about US$12 million). Meanwhile imports kept rising and in 1974/75 foreign exchange spending exceeded government plans. If this trend continued Nepal was expected to face a serious balance of payments crisis within three years. A major 1974 reform institutionalized the rice trade through joint government-private participation to reduce revenue leakage improve tax collection and retain Indian currency. However results were disappointing: bank credit on export bills increased by over 300% between April 1974 and April 1975 while Indian currency reserves at Nepal Rastra Bank fell by 40%. Inflation continued in 1974/75 with prices rising about 1% faster than during the same period in 1973/74. However falling prices in India caused Nepalese agricultural prices to decline by up to 40% benefiting urban consumers but reducing farmers' incomes and Nepal's earnings of Indian currency.

events.title: Narayanghat–Butwal Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: This section of the road was built with the economic aid from United Kingdom. The construction was carried out by the Ministry of Public Building and Works UK. The cost was provisionally estimated at about £4¼ million over 5 years half of which was provided by grant and half as an interest-free loan repayable over 25 years. The construction was divided into 2 sections: Eastern and Western. By 10 March 1970 of the 75 miles due to be constructed 30 miles of forest had been cleared and surveyed and approximately 12 miles were under construction. By 1972 the western section had been completed and inaugurated and following three years after that the eastern section was completed i.e. 1975.

events.title: Butwal Industrial Estate Established
events.detail: The Butwal Industrial Estate was established in 1975 with investment from the Government of Nepal. It spans a total geographic area of 434 ropanis. The estate hosts 71 industries that have received operational permits. Around 64 to 70 units remain continuously active on leased lands.

events.title: Purwanchal Congress Formed
events.detail: Gajendra Narayan Singh's political journey began with active participation in the movement against the Rana regime. He started his political career affiliated with the Nepali Congress and remaind with NC even after formation of Terai Congress. In the 1959 general election, he was the District President of the Nepali Congress in Saptari. After the royal coup, he went to India on exile and was arrested multiple times. Later in 1975, following disagreements with some top leaders of the Nepali Congress, Madhesi leaders within the Nepali Congress formed the Purbanchal Congress. Ramjanam Tiwari, Rajeshwor Nepali, Ramchandra Mishra, and others involved in this group, formed under the coordination of Gajendra Narayan Singh, continued to raise the issue of Terai-Madhes for a few years while living in India. Bhadrakali Mishra also supported him. The referendum held in 2036 BS also ended that. Later it led to their split from NC forming Nepal Sadbhavana Parishad in 1985

events.title: Integrated Rural Development Projects Started
events.detail: Integrated Hill Development Project: The IHDP was one of Nepal's earliest experiments with genuinely integrated rural development and was launched in 1975 with Swiss assistance, covering Dolakha and Sindhupalchok. It was implemented jointly by the Government of Nepal and the Swiss Association for Technical Assistance (SATA/SDC), and operated until 1990. Its approach went well beyond agriculture: it combined agricultural extension, livestock, forestry, irrigation, drinking water, health, local infrastructure, rural industries and institutional development, while its famous Tuki system attempted to mobilize respected local farmers as voluntary village-level development agents. Its major legacy was therefore institutional and technological rather than simply the physical infrastructure it constructed: it demonstrated that rural development could be organized around local participation, extension services and community-level institutions, although later evaluations of Nepal's IRDPs generally found that coordination among government departments and the sustainability of project institutions remained major weaknesses. Rasuwa–Nuwakot Rural Development Project: The Rasuwa–Nuwakot Rural Development Project, launched in 1976–77, was the first major World Bank/IDA-supported rural development project of its type in Nepal and became a model for subsequent IRDPs. The first phase was financed through IDA Credit 617-NEP, with UNDP technical assistance, and targeted agriculture, livestock, irrigation, forestry, rural infrastructure, health, water supply and institutional development in two very different hill districts. The project was deliberately multisectoral, containing roughly 19 components, including agricultural extension, research and training, veterinary services and improved livestock, about 570 hectares of small irrigation, roads and trails, water supplies, health facilities and support for cottage industries. Its achievements were mixed: around 85% of the project population benefited directly from production-oriented components, and the project succeeded in bringing agricultural, livestock and other government services into extremely remote areas. But the project also exposed the central problem of the IRDP model: putting many ministries and technical agencies under a supposedly integrated programme did not automatically produce integration. The experience eventually led to a second phase, approved as the Third Rural Development Project, again focusing on Rasuwa and Nuwakot. Kosi Hills Area Rural Development Project: The Kosi Hills Area Rural Development Project, generally dated from around 1977/79 to 1984, was a British/UK-supported integrated development programme covering the eastern hills around Bhojpur, Dhankuta, Terhathum and Sankhuwasabha. Its central idea was to use the Dharan–Dhankuta road corridor and emerging service centres to connect isolated hill communities with markets and government services, while simultaneously improving agriculture, livestock, forestry, rural infrastructure, health, water and local administrative capacity. Evaluation found that roads, market access, agricultural technology, extension services and new economic opportunities produced durable changes in parts of the region, although benefits were uneven and many of the original institutional arrangements did not survive intact. Sagarmatha Integrated Rural Development Project: The Sagarmatha Integrated Rural Development Project was launched in 1978 and ran until 1988, covering Siraha, Saptari and Udayapur and becoming one of Nepal's largest early IRDPs. It was financed jointly by IFAD, the Asian Development Bank, the European Economic Community and the Government of Nepal; the total cost was about US$37.2 million, comprising approximately US$13 million from IFAD, US$14 million from ADB, US$3.75 million from the EEC and US$6.45 million from the Government, and it was designed to benefit approximately 50,000 households. The project attempted to address both the Terai and hill dimensions of the zone through agricultural extension, irrigation, roads, livestock, markets, health, drinking water, soil and water conservation and alternative employment. Its physical achievements were substantial: six major link roads totalling about 110 km, 2,843 shallow tube wells, 15 deep wells and 12 other tube wells, 40 irrigation schemes covering about 27,004 hectares, 27 agricultural and livestock service centres, milk collection and chilling facilities and rural markets were established. The Government's groundwater agency confirms that the project subsequently produced approximately 14,510 hectares of irrigation through shallow and deep tube-well development in Siraha, Saptari and Udayapur. Mahakali Hills Integrated Rural Development Project: The Mahakali Hills Integrated Rural Development Project was launched in 1979/80 in Darchula, Baitadi and Dadeldhura, principally with World Bank/IDA financing and UNDP technical assistance. The original project cost was estimated at roughly US$10.9 million, with an IDA credit of US$8 million and US$500,000 of UNDP technical assistance; a subsequent second rural-development credit was approved for US$11 million. Its programme included agricultural extension and improved varieties, horticulture and marketing, livestock services, small dairy facilities, irrigation, input supply and credit, soil-erosion control, health centres, drinking water, trails and footbridges and cottage industries. mplementation, however, was considerably more difficult than anticipated: the project fell behind schedule, suffered from funding and staffing problems and was hit by a major earthquake in 1980; the US$11 million credit eventually closed in 1988, around three and a half years behind schedule, with approximately US$4.63 million undisbursed and cancelled. Its outcome was therefore mixed: some agricultural, livestock, irrigation and infrastructure services were established, but the project fell substantially short of its original integrated-development ambitions. Rapti Zone Integrated Rural Development Project: The Rapti Zone Integrated Rural Development Project was one of the most ambitious US-supported IRDPs, beginning in 1980/81 and covering the difficult western hill districts of Dang, Pyuthan, Salyan, Rolpa and Rukum. USAID provided the principal external financing and technical assistance, with the project implemented for the Government by a large multidisciplinary team; the first phase ran approximately 1980–87, followed by a second phase beginning in 1987. Its six major components were farming systems, renewable-resource management, employment and skills/rural industry, education and appropriate technology/alternative energy, rural works including roads and small self-help projects, and institutional development. Execution proved difficult: the 1985 final evaluation concluded that the components remained too separate rather than genuinely integrated and that fragmented management meant only about 54% of planned targets were achieved. Karnali–Bheri Integrated Rural Development Project: The Karnali–Bheri Integrated Rural Development Project was a Canadian-supported programme launched around 1981, focusing particularly on the extremely remote Surkhet, Dailekh and Jumla area, with subsequent phases extending the programme. The project attempted to create a series of locally based, self-sustaining development activities combining agriculture, livestock, forestry, infrastructure, health, education, rural industry and institutional development. Historical project listings identify a first phase in 1981–84 and second phase in 1985–89, financed by Canada/CIDA. The project was designed for a particularly difficult environment where weak transport links, low agricultural productivity, limited markets and extremely weak state services made conventional development programmes difficult to implement. Its principal achievements were therefore in establishing local development institutions, agricultural and livestock services, small infrastructure and community-level development capacity. The experience reinforced a lesson shared by the other IRDPs: remote-area development required roads, markets and local institutions before sectoral investments could achieve their full effect. Dhading District Development Project: The Dhading District Development Project, initiated around 1983, was supported by GTZ/Germany and represented a later generation of Nepal's integrated rural-development experiments. Its principal objective was to improve living conditions across Dhading while promoting off-farm employment and rural economic diversification, rather than treating agriculture as the sole route out of poverty. Evaluations increasingly recognized that simply supplying agricultural technology was insufficient in densely populated hill districts: rural households needed roads, markets, non-farm employment and stronger local institutions. Seti Zone Rural Development Project: The Seti Zone Rural Development Project was an ADB-supported programme launched in the mid-1980s and implemented roughly 1986–95, covering five districts of the Seti region. ADB financing was approximately US$20 million; Nepal's development portfolio records an ADB loan of about US$14.9 million with implementation extending into the 1990s. The project had four major components: transport infrastructure, deep-tubewell irrigation, agricultural-support facilities and rural-development support, with the broader objective of increasing food and cash-crop production and creating rural employment. Mechi Hills Irrigation and Related Development Project: The Mechi Hills Irrigation and Related Development Programme, later organized into several phases, operated from roughly 1986 to 2001 in Ilam, Panchthar and Taplejung with Swiss/Netherlands-style development cooperation through SNV and the Government of Nepal. The programme's budget across its phases was approximately €9.18 million. The first phase worked with the Departments of Irrigation, Forests, Agriculture and Livestock on sectoral development, while later phases shifted increasingly toward strengthening district NGOs, village groups, DDCs and VDCs so that local communities could identify, plan and implement their own development activities. In this respect Mechi represented an evolution of the IRDP philosophy: instead of simply delivering a package of government services from above, it increasingly emphasized local institutional capacity, participatory planning and coordination. Gulmi–Arghakhanchi Rural Development Project: The Gulmi–Arghakhanchi Rural Development Project (GARDP) was a later European-supported IRDP, with the first phase beginning around 1990 and a second phase extending into the late 1990s/early 2000s. It focused on sustainable improvement of rural socioeconomic conditions and poverty reduction through four major components: natural resources, human welfare, infrastructure and business enterprise. The second phase used a strongly participatory bottom-up sub-project model, with roughly 962 sub-projects covering the four components and an estimated 500,000 beneficiaries. Infrastructure outputs included approximately 40 km of roads in each district and 15 irrigation sub-projects covering about 369 hectares, while the project also supported agricultural/livestock enterprises, social services and natural-resource management. Palpa Development Programme: The Palpa Development Programme, beginning around 1988/89, was another later integrated rural-development initiative associated with European/Swiss and German development cooperation. It sought to improve living conditions and rural economic opportunities in Palpa by combining agriculture, infrastructure, natural-resource management, local institutions and rural enterprise rather than relying exclusively on a single sector. The programme's importance lies particularly in the institutional transition it represented: Nepal's rural-development policy was gradually moving away from large donor-designed regional packages toward district-level planning, local government participation, community groups and smaller demand-driven investments.

events.title: Coronation of King Birendra And Zone of Peace
events.detail: On February 24 1975 King Birendra was coronated in presence of high level dignitaries from over 60 countries including international figures like the crown princes of U.K. and Japan. Welcoming his foreign guests on the lawn of his palace on the coronation day the King proposed that Nepal be declared a "zone of peace." This diplomatic move was explicitly designed to secure global guarantees for Nepal’s sovereignty and legally prevent India from executing a Sikkim-like political intervention. China and the U.S.S.R. welcomed the King's initiative but India and the U.S. have remained silent.

events.title: Sikkim Officially Became The 22nd State of India
events.detail: Prior to its integration with India Sikkim was a hereditary monarchy ruled by the Chogyal (king) of the Namgyal dynasty since 1642. In the 19th century Sikkim and Bhutan became a British protectorate. This status transferred to India after it gained independence in 1947. India signed a treaty with both Sikkim and Bhutan in 1950 making then Indian protectorate. India assumed responsibility for Sikkim and Bhutan's defense external affairs and communications while the kings retained internal sovereignty. In Sikkim growing dissatisfaction among the majority Nepali-ethnic population against the ruling minority Bhutia-Lepcha monarchy led to widespread political turmoil. In 1973 major protests erupted outside the Chogyal's palace demanding democratic reforms and adult franchise. The Chogyal requested Indian assistance to maintain law and order. A treaty was signed between the Chogyal political parties and the Government of India establishing a constitutional monarchy and setting up legislative elections. The pro-India Sikkim National Convention won an overwhelming majority in 1974 elections and Kazi Lhendup Dorjee became the Prime Minister. The new assembly passed a resolution seeking closer association with India. The Indian Parliament subsequently passed the 35th Amendment designating Sikkim as an "associate state" of the Indian Union. The relationship between the Chogyal and the newly elected democratic government continued to deteriorate rapidly. Fearing the Chogyal might subvert democracy the Sikkim Assembly removed the king and voted for full integration with India in 1975. On April 14 1975 Sikkim held a special referendum. A total of 97.55% of voters approved the abolition of the monarchy and voted to join India. The Indian Parliament passed the 36th Amendment to the Constitution. The President of India signed the bill on May 16 1975 formally making Sikkim a full state of India. Unlike Sikkim Bhutan did not have internal ethnic-political polarization. Bhutan recognized the risk of absorption and actively asserted its independence on the global stage. With India’s eventual sponsorship Bhutan joined the Universal Postal Union in 1969 and became a full member of the United Nations in 1971. Gaining UN sovereignty made a future annexation geopolitically impossible for India. On March 2 2007 India and Bhutan formally updated their treaty. They completely scrapped Article 2 officially recognizing Bhutan's full sovereignty and freedom over its own foreign and military policies. Bhutan officially became a democratic constitutional monarchy on July 18 2008.

events.title: All Nepal Communist Revolutionary Coordination Committee (Marxist-Leninist) Formed
events.detail: This committe was formed with the initiative of second-tier leaders who were left after Jhapa revolt and the merger of Nepal Revolutionary Organisation (Marxist–Leninist), an organisation in Morang emerged in 1973 and led by Madhav Kumar Nepal. On 30 August 1977, Mukti Morcha Samuha, a faction split from CPN (Pushpa Lal) led by Madan Bhandari, also merged into the party. The party inspired by the Naxalites carried out a peasant-led anti-feudal movement in Jhapa District.

events.title: Indira Gandhi's State of Emergency
events.detail: Immediate Cause: On June 12 1975 Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha of Allahabad High Court found Prime Minister Indira Gandhi guilty of electoral malpractices during her 1971 campaign. The court declared her election to parliament void stripped her of her seat and banned her from holding public office for six years.Instead of resigning Gandhi moved the Supreme Court which granted her only a conditional stay. She was allowed to remain Prime Minister but lost her right to vote in Parliament rendering her position politically untenable. While the court ruling was the final spark deep-seated political and economic crises had been building across India for years. The JP Movement And Opposition Coalition: Jayaprakash Narayan launched a massive nationwide agitation against Gandhi’s government targeting rampant corruption inflation and unemployment. Crucially JP called upon the police paramilitary forces and the military to disobey illegal government orders which Gandhi interpreted as an incitement to a military coup. Economic Stagnation: India’s economy was reeling from the financial strain of the 1971 war with Pakistan consecutive monsoon failures leading to severe food shortages and the 1973 global oil shock. Inflation peaked at over 30% fueling widespread public anger and historic labor strikes including a massive national railway strike in 1974. The "Foreign Hand" Narrative: Paranoid about foreign intervention—particularly after the Western and Chinese backlash to India's recent nuclear test (1974) and the annexation of Sikkim (1975)—Gandhi genuinely believed or strategically argued that external intelligence agencies (like the CIA) were funding the domestic opposition to destabilize and balkanize India. Suspension of Fundamental Rights: On June 25 1975 Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency across India by citing internal and external threats to the country. The order bestowed upon the prime minister the authority to rule by decree allowing elections to be cancelled and civil liberties to be suspended. Over 100000 politicians journalists student leaders and activists were jailed without trial under the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA). High-profile prisoners included future prime ministers Atal Bihari Vajpayee Morarji Desai and protest leader Jayaprakash Narayan. The government established strict pre-censorship guidelines. Editors were legally forced to submit all newspaper layouts articles and headlines to government censors before printing. Outraged newspapers like The Indian Express and The Statesman left their editorial columns blank in protest. The government passed constitutional amendments—most notably the 42nd Amendment—which stripped the courts of their power to review executive decisions or protect the fundamental rights of citizens including Habeas Corpus. Authoritarian Domestic Policies: With the opposition jailed Sanjay Gandhi championed a controversial "Five-Point Programme" of family planning eradication of illitracy tree plantation abolition of dowry and slum clearance. In a brutal campaign to control population growth millions of men—particularly from marginalized poor and Muslim communities—were subjected to enforced vasectomies. Local authorities were given strict quotas leading to police roundups and forced medical procedures. Massive urban "beautification" drives resulted in the destruction of slums. The most infamous event occurred at the Turkman Gate in Delhi where police opened fire on residents protesting the demolition of their homes killing dozens and displacing thousands overnight. The state banned 26 political and cultural organizations including the right-wing Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and left-wing Naxalite groups driving their activities completely underground. To gain public compliance Indira Gandhi launched the "20-Point Programme" aimed at restoring economic order. Strikes and labor unions were banned government officials were forced to arrive on time and prices of essential goods were artificially stabilized. While it temporarily reduced inflation and improved train schedules it came at the absolute cost of human freedom. Call For 1977 Election: Indira Gandhi terminated emergency and called for the 1977 elections due to flawed intelligence a desire for democratic legitimacy and an underestimation of the opposition resulting in a crushing defeat. Key factors included inaccurate reports suggesting a landslide a need to counter international criticism and a desire to regain control from her son Sanjay Gandhi. The Janata Party and its allies won a commanding majority with 345 seats in the Lok Sabha. The Congress Party was reduced to just 154 seats failing to win a single seat across most of northern India. The electorate directly punished the orchestrators of the Emergency. Indira Gandhi lost her own parliamentary seat in Rae Bareli and her son Sanjay Gandhi was heavily defeated in Amethi.

events.title: Hetauda Textile Industry Established
events.detail: The ⁠Hetauda Textile Industry was established in July 1975 with technical and financial assistance from the Chinese government. At its peak, it directly employed over 1,200 people. Industry faced huge losses, largely due to cheap Chinese and Indian imports that have almost destroyed the Nepali textile industry. Its accumulated losses add up to Rs 230.5 million, about half of which was incurred during fiscal year 1998-99, according to the Ministry of Finance.

events.title: Fifth Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 8.83 billion spent ; ~48% from foreign aid; ~77% implemented; 9 PEs established; 1,840 km of roads built; Pokhara-Surkhet highway sections commenced; Kulekhani Hydroelectric Project Phase I construction accelerated; Gandak power station finalized; 95,000 hectares of land added to irrigation networks; Integrated Rural Development Projects (IRDPs) introduced for hill areas; chemical fertilizer distribution subsidized; "Primary Education Free" policy declared; Nepal’s 5th development region (Far-Western) created; basic health posts established in remote districts to decentralize healthcare; agriculture and irrigation took the historical top priority at 34.8%; transport and communications followed closely at 31.8%; social services received 22.4%; major shift in priority toward agriculture and social services; actual GDP growth (2.3%) failed to catch up with population growth (2.6%).

events.title: Tulsi Giri
events.detail: 3rd Term

events.title: Second Ammendment of 1962 Panchayat Constitution
events.detail: On 16 December 1974 King Birendra formed a Constitutional Reform Advisory Committee to recommend reforms to strengthen and revitalize the Panchayat system. The committee included leaders from diverse political backgrounds including D.P. Adhikari (former communist) Kirti Nidhi Bista (Panchayat leader) Shri Bhadra Sharma (former Nepali Congress) and Ram Hari Sharma (Praja Parishad) all of whom agreed to work under the King's leadership. The committee submitted its report in December 1975 leading to the Second Amendment of the 1962 Panchayat Constitution. Gaun Farka Abhiyan: It Strengthened the Back to Village National Campaign (BVNC) as the sole organization responsible for directing Panchayat political workers. It expanded the BVNC's organizational network down to district and village levels under the King's overall leadership. It received constitutional recognition and gained the power to approve candidates contesting Panchayat elections. This transformed Gaun Farka into a major center of political controversy. Candidates could not contest elections at any level of the Panchayat system without approval from Gaun Farka officials. Many Panchayat politicians became anxious because their political careers depended on approval from the organization. Even Rajeshwor Devkota a former Chairman of the National Panchayat was denied approval to contest. Village and Nagar Panchayat: Provision was made for the formation of a village panchayat of 47 people, including the Pradhan Pancha and the Upa Pradhan Pancha. An ordinance issued in 1977 stipulated that the Pradhan Pancha and Upa Pradhan Pancha should bring 50 percent of the votes cast. Provision was made for the term of office of the village panchayat members and office bearers to be 4 years. CPAA: Commission for the Prevention of Abuse of Authority (CPAA) was formed as constitutional anti-corruption agency in Nepal. The CPAA had massive powers. It acted as an investigator a prosecutor and a judge all at once. Giving one agency the power to investigate prosecute and decide punishments was too heavy of a workload. It became difficult for the CPAA to function fairly. : When Nepal changed to a multi-party democracy in 1990 the government wanted better checks and balances. The CPAA was transformed into the CIAA. Graduate Constituency: It abolished the Graduate Constituencies ending the direct election of four graduate representatives to the National Panchayat. Leadership: Initially BVNC was under the direct leadership of the King. After the constitutional ammendment it got new leadership: Bedananda Jha (1973-75) Khadga Bahadur Singh (1975-77) Bishwabandu Thapa (1977-78) and Kamal Raj Regmi (1978-79). Interesting anecdote: Bishwabandu Thapa had gone to receive the Dashain tika on October 11 1978 from his former leader B.P. Koirala due to family ties. But the Panchas who found this unacceptable harshly criticized him. Subsequently King Birendra made him resign.

events.title: Kathmandu Trolleybus System Started
events.detail: The trolley bus system was opened in 28 December 1975 with a Rs40 million grant from China for 22 standard trolley buses adapted to left-handed operation. Ten newer model buses were donated in 1997. The line was operated by the Nepal Trolley Bus Service a branch of the Nepal Transportation Corporation (NTC). In 19 December 2001 the NTC was dissolved and the trolley bus operation was suspended as it did not turn any profit since 1990. The reasons for NTC’s failure were stringent government bureaucracy and overstaffing coupled with cronyism in management that resulted in poor technical expertise and inept operational policy. After 18 months Kathmandu Madhyapur Thimi and Bhaktapur municipalities agreed to restart the service and the trolley buses rolled again. Less than a year later the Madhyapur Thimi and Bhaktapur municipalities opted out of the scheme as the service failed to attract riders and continued to lose up to Rs2 million a month. Consequently the line was reduced to only between Tripureswor and Tinkune and most wirework beyond city limits was removed. Operations on the system were suspended again and for the final time in late November 2008 and the system was formally closed (without ever resuming operation) in November 2009.

events.title: Securities Exchange Center (SEC) Founded
events.detail: SEC was founded in Nepal in 1976 to manage capital markets under the Companies Act acting as sole entity managing both market operations and regulatory tasks in the country. It was later split into NEPSE and SEBON in 1993. It was set up as a collaborative effort between the central bank, ⁠Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) (holding a 49% stake), and the Nepal Industrial Development Corporation (NIDC) (holding a 51% stake). For its first seven years, the SEC operated without a dedicated, legally binding securities statute. The promulgation of Securities Exchange Act (1983) provided the SEC with its first formal legal framework. Following this, the SEC officially opened its internal trading counter to the public in 1984.

events.title: Nepal Aid Group Formed
events.detail: The Nepal Aid Group was a multilateral consortium formed in 1976 under the patronage of the World Bank to coordinate international financial assistance, technical support, and development policy for Nepal. It centralized aid from Western countries (such as the United States and the United Kingdom), Japan, and various United Nations agencies to prevent project duplication and streamline resource management. By 1987, the consortium had expanded to include 16 donor nations and 6 international agencies. Over time, this coordination framework evolved to address broader institutional reforms, human capacity building, and environmental conservation. The group eventually transitioned into the modern Nepal Development Forum, which continues to serve as the unified platform for Nepal's international donors.

events.title: KPB Becomes Acting President of NC And Party Division
events.detail: When BP was in exile they required party organization to function in Nepal which was why KPB was made an acting president of NC. It was also as part of preparation for BP's return later that year (December 1976) under the policy of "National Reconciliation." Establishing Bhattarai as the acting president ensured a stable domestic organizational base to support this shift from armed rebellion to peaceful dialogue with the King. On January 17 1988, KPB transioned to full president following a consensus among the party's top leadership. However NC became divided after Koirala appointed Bhattarai as Acting President. Senior leaders aligned with Subarna Shamsher Rana opposed the move and reaffirmed the party's 15 May 1968 declaration which had offered "loyal cooperation" to the monarchy within the Panchayat framework. Opposition divisions deepened when 36 NC leaders criticized Koirala's reconciliation policy as too vague and refused to recognize K. P. Bhattarai's leadership arguing he had not accepted the party's 1968 declaration. So the well known 36 group or "chhattise" formed a new party Nepali Congress (Subarna) in 1977 under leadership of Bakhan Singh Gurung and Surya Prasad Upadhyaya.
