The party contested the 1981 Rastriya Panchayat election launching 36 candidates as 'independents'. Four of its candidates were elected Dr. K.I. Singh, Bakhan Singh Gurung, Kashi Nath Gautam, and Bhagwat Yadav. Bakhan Singh Gurung became the minister of land reform and law and justice in his tenure.

events.title: Hetauda Cement Industries Established
events.detail: Hetauda Cement Industries Ltd. was established in 1976 under an investment by the Government of Nepal and loan assistance from the Asian Development Bank. It started cement production in 1986.

events.title: Policy of National Reconciliation
events.detail: The Nepali Congress’ armed struggle (1973–1975) had failed to overthrow the Panchayat system.Operations such as the Timurbote campaign resulted in heavy losses arrests and executions. B.P. concluded that armed resistance was harming the democratic movement and that a new strategy was needed. After Indira's emergency declaration Indian political environment became hostile to NC. Many Indian socialist leaders close to B.P. including Jayaprakash Narayan were imprisoned. The Nepali Congress could no longer operate effectively from India. Likewise the incorporation of Sikkim into India in 1975 deeply affected B.P. He feared that political instability and internal divisions could make Nepal vulnerable to external pressure. Earlier in December 1976 King Birendra had pardoned Bhadrakali Mishra and 11 other former NC leaders stating that those who accepted the basic principles of the Panchayat system could receive pardon and participate in politics. On 30 December 1976 B.P. Koirala and Ganesh Man Singh returned to Nepal from exile in India and were immediately arrested. After their arrest Koirala and Singh refused to accept the Palace’s conditions for release. After that government turned more hostile towards the democratic demands. The government accused them of supporting armed rebellion during their exile. A special court was established on 23 January 1977 to handle cases related to the accusations. Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa and Bhim Narayan Shrestha were later sentenced to death for armed rebellion. Meanwhile the Palace continued implementing the 1975 Panchayat constitutional reforms. Local Panchayat boundaries were reorganized. The “consensus election” system (candidate selection through the Gaun Farka expanded. National Panchayat members increasingly depended on Palace or BVNC approval rather than direct voter support. Radical communist groups rejected reconciliation and intensified anti-government activities. They were particularly active in Jhapa Ilam Janakpur and other eastern Tarai districts where clashes with police arson and looting occurred in the late 1970s.)

events.title: Kathmandu Valley Ring Road Built
events.detail: The 27-kilometer ring road was constructed between 1973 and 1977 entirely through Chinese government aid and technical assistance. In 2018 the 10.5 km Kalanki-Koteshwor section was expanded to eight-lanes in cooperation of the Chinese government. In the same year an agreement was signed with Chinese government to upgrade 8.2 km Kalanki-Basundhara section under Chinese grant. The project is delayed mainly due to delay in local site clearance.

events.title: Nepal's Relationship in Gulf Established
events.detail: The year 1977 was the single most explosive year for Nepal's diplomacy in the Gulf region as it established ties with four major Middle Eastern nations in that year alone. The countries were: Bahrain (January 13) Qatar (January 21) UAE (January 22) Saudi Arabia (March 15). Nepal did so to protect its sovereignty from Indian influence gain endorsement for its Zone of Peace proposal secure foreign aid and establish labor markets for its citizens.

events.title: External Support and Release of BP Koirala
events.detail: The unexpected victory of the Janata Party in India changed the political environment. The party was formed during emergency by merger of Bharatiya Lok Dal (BLD) led by Charan Singh Congress (O) led by Morarji Desai Jan Sangh (BJS) backed by RSS and led by figures like Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Lal Krishna Advani and Socialist Party led by George Fernandes and Madhu Limaye under the guardianship of Jayaprakash Narayan. Indian socialist leaders with ties to B.P. Koirala openly supported democracy in Nepal and called for his release. 34 Indian MPs appealed to King Birendra to release Koirala on humanitarian grounds. While Indian Prime Minister Morarji Desai and Foreign Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee maintained a policy of non-interference other Janata leaders expressed support for Koirala. Carter administration in Washington had ranked Nepal in the lowest category of nations respecting human rights. It was also believed that carter wrote personal letter to KIng requesting BP' release which is also backed by him writing a public letter thanking the King for BP's release. Even Prime Minister Bhutto of Pakistan stated publicly that Nepal had no real election system. Shortly after Janata party president Chandrashekar's unofficial visit to Kathmandu to encourage some compromise between the Palace and Koirala BVNC Chairman Khadga Bahadur Singh a strong supporter of strict Panchayat control was replaced by Bishwabandu Thapa who favored greater political openness. The King instructed the BVNC to emphasize popular participation and hinted at changing the consensus election system. On 8 June 1977 B.P. Koirala was finally released for medical treatment in the United States though charges against him remained.

events.title: Nakkhu Jail Break
events.detail: In 1977 political prisoners of the Jhapa movement carried out a daring escape from Nakkhu Jail. Beginning in February 1976 they secretly dug a nearly 100-foot tunnel using simple tools like cooking spoons while hiding the soil and disguising their work. On 25 March 1977 CP Mainali, Pradip Nepal, Dhanendra Basnet, Naresh Kharel, Narad Wagle, Bhisma Dhimal, Madhav Paudel and Bir Bahadur Lama escaped through the tunnel. Although the government launched a nationwide search and recaptured some prisoners the escape became a powerful symbol of courage and resistance.

events.title: Jugedi Kanda
events.detail: The Jugedi Struggle was a left-led peasant uprising in Jugedi Chitwan organized mainly among the marginalized Chepang community against exploitative moneylenders food insecurity and the Panchayat regime. Around 400 villagers led by activists including Naresh Sharma Neupane ("Madan") Ruplal Bishwakarma and local organizer Sundar Chepang seized food and goods from a trader's shop for redistribution. Police intercepted the group during their retreat opening fire and killing Dasharath Chepang and Santa Bahadur Chepang while several others were arrested. Initially portrayed by the state as a robbery the incident later became recognized as a symbol of Chepang political awakening and peasant resistance with the two victims officially declared martyrs after the restoration of democracy.

events.title: Carpet Scandal And Tulsi Giri's Resignation
events.detail: India became concerned about Nepal being used as a route for smuggling luxury goods. Nepalese carpet exporters allegedly inflated export invoices by up to 40 times the actual value (and in some cases up to 150 times during April–July 1977) to obtain larger import permits. Nepal resisted strict action because the practice supported carpet exports and could generate about Rs. 40 million in import duties. After Commission for Prevention of Abuse of Authority got constitutional status it investigated the case. Prime Minister Tulsi Giri was directly implicated and was eventually forced to resign in 1977 due to the mounting pressure and judicial scrutiny of the scandal. Likewise Finance Minister Dr. Bhekh Bahadur Thapa and Planning Commission head Harka Gurung were also heavily entangled in the allegations and subsequent investigations. However after three years all were given clean chit.

events.title: Kirti Nidhi Bista
events.detail: 3rd Term

events.title: BP Returns From Treatment in US And Gets Jailed
events.detail: On 5 September 1977 through a famous television interview in the US BP announced that he would return to Nepal and continue his campaign for national reconciliation. The Palace then abandoned signs of compromise. Kirtinidhi Bista replaced Tulsi Giri as Prime Minister and Khadga Bahadur Singh became Home and Panchayat Minister signalling a tougher approach toward opposition forces. Although the Second National Panchayat Convention proposed reforms to reduce BVNC control implementation remained uncertain. The government improved its international image by releasing many political prisoners pardoning some NC leaders and allowing six banned newspapers to resume publication. However police harassment of NC leaders and press censorship damaged this image. By the end of 1977 reconciliation had failed. B.P. Koirala still demanded a role for political parties and greater civil liberties. King Birendra insisted that the core principles of Panchayat — partylessness class coordination decentralization and “traditional democracy” — would not change. On 10 November 1977 BP returned to Nepal. Upon his return the government rearrested him and the trial against him was resumed ending hopes of a negotiated reconciliation between the Palace and Nepali Congress.

events.title: Improved Relation With India And China
events.detail: India accepted Nepal's long-standing demands for separate Trade and Transit Treaties and an overland transit route to Bangladesh with the treaties signed on 17 March 1978. Despite warmer ties with India major disagreements remained unresolved such as Nepal's Zone of Peace proposal and joint river and hydropower projects especially the 3600 MW Karnali Project where India wanted a bilateral project while Nepal and Bangladesh favored broader international participation. On 31 August 1978 Nepal and China signed an agreement allowing Royal Nepal Airlines to operate a trans-Himalayan air route to Beijing with possible extension to Tokyo via Shanghai. China also agreed to provide US$40 million to establish sugar and paper factories in Nepal. Prime Minister Kirti Nidhi Bista visited China in September 1978 where he met Hua Guofeng and Deng Xiaoping.

events.title: Ammendment of Forest Act 1961
events.detail: In 1973 an Institute of Forestry was established under the umbrella of Tribhuvan University. An important change in forest legislation began in response to the National Forestry Conference-1974 held in Kathmandu. In that conference a community-oriented group of foresters working in the various districts strongly favoured for people to be involved in forestry protection and management work that became later known as Community Forestry. Prior to 1978 the Forest Act of 1961 had nationalized all forests. It treated local villagers as a threat which led to severe conflict and rapid deforestation. The 1978 rules reversed this approach through two key management systems. In 1978 a serious and revolutionary wave was made in forestry sector with the emergence of the Panchayat Forests (PFs) and Panchayat Protected Forests (PPFs) Rules-1978 based on the amendment of Forest Act-1961 in order to handing over of accessible government forests to village Panchayat as a community forests. The PFs and PPFs rules allowed for the transfer of responsibility for forest protection and management from the government to the local Panchayat as PFs and PPFs. Up to 125 ha of degraded forest could become a Panchayat Forest. Up to 500 ha of better forest could become a Panchayat Protected Forest. Local communities received rights to fuelwood fodder grass and some forest products. Income from Panchayat Forests largely stayed with the local Panchayat with part earmarked for forest protection and development. These rules formally recognized community participation in forest protection management development and use. Despite the policy shift only a small portion of forests was actually handed over and many areas continued to degrade. The main weakness was the absence of clearly defined forest user groups; forests were often not transferred to the actual users and protectors.

events.title: Deteriorating Trade Balance
events.detail: Food production declined by 5.2% by the end of July 1978 due to unfavorable weather and total food grain production was 3.46% lower than the previous fiscal year. Foreign trade deteriorated during the first 11 months of FY 1977–78 as imports from India and overseas increased while exports to India fell by about 40%. Inflation accelerated sharply with the National Price Index rising by 11.2% in FY 1977–78 compared to 2.7% in FY 1976–77.

events.title: Kohalpur-Banbasa Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: India for long had prevented China from entering the Nepali tarai for its infrastructure projects. On the pretext of preventing China from spreading communism to Nepal it did not allow China to carry out agricultural projects. China on the other hand kept Nepal happy by offering show-case programs. The political and strategic importance India attached to its aid program of the 1950s and 1960s become fairly obvious as most of the aid allocated was used to build roads airfields and communication networks’. China and India sparred over building sections of the Mahendra east-west highway. China won the contract to build the Kohalpur-Banbasa sector with a low bid in a global tender. India panicked and Rajiv Gandhi sent his special envoy Panjalal Shiv Shankar to Kathmandu who met the PM and the King to halt the contract awarded to the Chinese company. Finally the cabinet decided to cancel the contract. The road which was going to be built by loan was then built by India under the grant. The construction of 203 km section of road began in 1973 and completed in 1978.

events.title: BP Released and Aquitted
events.detail: BP Koirala was released for the second time in February on medical grounds. He was subsequently acquitted of five of the seven charges against him. Before leaving he said he would not make political statements until meeting the King whom he called the "kingpin" of Nepali politics. Bp went to US for a follow-up medical trip during which the Nepalese government refused to pay forcing American committees and his nephew Shall Upadhaya to fund his treatment.

events.title: India-Nepal Treaty of Trade
events.detail: The 1971 Trade and Transit Treaty had expired in August 1976 but India’s Janata government allowed trade to continue under the old terms to avoid a crisis. India agreed to some Nepalese demands like allowing Nepal to export 30000 metric tons of rice to Bangladesh through Indian territory and to negotiate separate trade and transit treaties. However India insisted that Nepal first take measures against smuggling of Western goods through Nepal into India keeping transit access linked to border controls. India became concerned about Nepal being used as a route for smuggling luxury goods. Nepalese carpet exporters allegedly inflated export invoices by up to 40 times the actual value (and in some cases up to 150 times during April–July 1977) to obtain larger import permits. Nepal resisted strict action because the practice supported carpet exports and could generate about Rs. 40 million in import duties. Separate Trade Treaty: Separate Treaties for Trade and Transit but Trade Treaty has to be renewed every 5 years. Beyond MFN Status: Both sides agreed to give each other treatment no less favorable than that given to third countries over most favorable nation system. Duty Free Access: Duty-free and quota-free access for Nepali manufactured goods containing at least 80% Nepalese and Indian materials which was previously 90%. Preferential Treatment for Primary Products: Duty-free treatment was granted for many traditional products such as rice pulses flour timber honey milk products egg etc.

events.title: Another Development on Koshi Treaty
events.detail: To curtail resentment India funded renovation and extension of Chandra Canal Pumped Canal and distribution of the Western Koshi Canal

events.title: Death of Pushpa Lal Shrestha
events.detail: Pushpa Lal Shrestha founder and leading figure of the illegal Nepal Communist Party died. Living in exile in India since 1960 Pushpa Lal had closely followed BP's reconciliation efforts. The Nepali government refused to allow his body into Nepal though it permitted his ashes to be brought in where they were received by leaders of the banned opposition parties. Following his death his wife Sahana Pradhan took over the party's leadership advancing his vision of joint struggle. Pushpa Lal became the very first person to translate the Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels into the Nepali language. He also translated other vital works by Lenin Stalin and Mao.

events.title: BP Returns From Follow-up Treatment in US And Meeting With King Birendra
events.detail: After returning from the United States on 20 August 1978 Koirala faced demonstrations by Panchayat supporters but later held a one-hour meeting with King Birendra on 31 October 1978. He described the meeting as having "broken the ice" and said it strengthened his belief in national reconciliation urging the King to promote democratic institutions for Nepal's development.

events.title: CPN (Marxist–Leninist) Formed
events.detail: The party was formed as successor of All Nepal Communist Revolutionary Coordination Committee (Marxist–Leninist). General convention elected CP Mainali as the party's first general secretary of CPN (ML)

events.title: Communist Party of Nepal (Manandhar) was formed because of the failure of Keshar Jang Rayamajhi to support the Bhutto student protests and supporting the status quo. Manandhar accused Rayamajhi of being a royalist pointing to his appointment in the Raj Sabha.
BP Departs For Second Follow-up Treatment in US
events.detail: He departed Nepal on January 19 1979 to receive specialized cancer treatments in New York. While he was away and undergoing medical care Captain Y.B. Thapa and B.N. Shrestha were executed.

events.title: Execution of Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa And Bhim Narayan Shrestha
events.detail: Captain Yagya Bahadur Thapa and Bhim Narayan Shrestha of the Nepali Congress who had been found guilty respectively of treason and attempted assassination of King Birendra in 1974 were executed by hanging in Hetauda on February 9 1979. Significantly they had been sentenced to death by a tribunal whose decision was subsequently endorsed by the Supreme Court in 1977. According to law capital punishment must be carried out within six months of the court's verdict. In these cases the sentences were carried out two years later. The royal government delayed the executions for two years as a tactical leverage tool to deter the Nepali Congress from launching protests while BP Koirala was on trial and to test whether his policy of national reconciliation would pacify the opposition without the palace losing absolute power. However after BP's successful "ice-breaking" meeting with King Birendra in late 1978 hardline royalist factions within the Panchayat government led by Kritinidhi Bista grew deeply threatened. They finally carried out the sentences in February 1979—strategically waiting until Koirala was out of the country in the United States—to minimize public backlash and successfully sabotage the growing peace between Koirala and the King. They had anticipated that it would prevent Koirala from returning to Kathmandu after treatment.

events.title: BP Returns From Second Follow-up Treatment in US
events.detail: BP returned to Kathmandu on March 6 1979. The execution of two NC activists convicted on charges of treason and terrorism—the first in over 15 years—was met with further protests and when BP Koirala returned to Nepal after treatment in the US pro-government supporters encouraged demonstrations against BP during which several Congress members were injured.

events.title: Nepali Students Protest On Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's Death And Referendum Announced
events.detail: On 6 April 1979 Tribhuvan University students clashed with police on the way to Pakistani Embassy while protesting the execution of Pakistan's former Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. Students then issued 24 demands including dissolving the state-backed Bidyarthi Mandal and restoring free student unions. Series of violent incidents continued acorss the campuses in Kathmandu. KIng Birendra constituted a Royal Commission to investigate the incident. Despite the fulfillment of almost all the students' demands including the dissolution of the RSVM and allowing student unions to be established on the campuses the situation became more tense on May 23. Students connected with the disbanded RSVM declined to abide by the decision of the three negotiating leaders. Two of the three student leaders were subjected to the humiliation of having their faces smeared black being made to wear garlands of shoes and being taken around the city on a pushcart. The climax of the drama was reached when the police tried to rescue the two leaders Bal Bahadur K. C. and Saran Malla from the angry mob near the Royal Nepal Airlines building. The mob set fire to four RNAC vehicles and to the building housing the two official dailies Gorkhapatra and Rising Nepal. No actual figures were available but it was reported that some deaths occurred during the riot. The movement eventually spread across to 40 of Nepal's 75 districts. Police repression and violence escalated with around 30 people killed. The government arrested major opposition leaders including B.P. Koirala Ganesh Man Singh K.P. Bhattarai and pro-Moscow communist leader Keshar Jung Rayamajhi but this failed to stop the protests. But these actions also proved ineffective. On the contrary after BP Koirala's house arrest in the last week of April the movement was internationalized as the foreign mass media gave it more attention. On the morning of May 24 King Birendra to the astonishment of the nation as a whole announced a nationwide referendum based on universal adult suffrage. Voters would choose between a reformed partyless Panchayat system or a multiparty democratic system. Prime Minister Kirti Nidhi Bista resigned and pro-reformist Surya Bahadur Thapa became caretaker Prime Minister. A 15-member Election Commission was established under the chairmanship of Bhagwati Prasad Singh. The Gaun Farka was suspended. Freedom to campaign for either side in the referendum was granted and all political prisioners were released. B.P. Koirala welcomed the referendum calling it a success for his National Reconciliation policy but opposition parties demanded suspension of all Panchayat institutions formation of a neutral government and guarantees of free and fair campaigning. Although political parties remained officially banned they openly campaigned. Some radical communist factions (especially Marxist–Leninist and Naxalite groups led by Mohan Bikram Singh Nirmal Lama and others) boycotted the referendum arguing that changing the political system without changing class relations would solve nothing. Armed extremist activities increased in several eastern and central districts prompting government security operations.

events.title: The Referendum Campaign
events.detail: Pro-Panchayat Camp: After the announcement of referendum the panchas were divided among themselves. They appear to have fallen into four general categories: (1) Thoroughly demoralized Panchas i.e. some ground cadres; (2) Those who crossed over to the multi-party camp i.e. some junior leaders; (3) Advocates of a Pancha Party within Multiparty System i.e. leaders like Vishwa Bandhu Thapa Rabindra Nath Sharma and Shri Bhadra Sharma; and (4) Reformist Panchayat supporters i.e. majority leaders like Matrika Prasad Koirala Kirti Nidhi Bista Nagendra Prasad Rijal and Surya Bahadur Thapa. In June 1979 national convention of the Panchayat was held through which the Panchayat supporters reorganized and united around a strategy of "reformed panchayat". The convention proposed major democratic reforms such as direct elections at all Panchayat levels through universal adult franchise PM to be elected by the National Panchayat the Council of Ministers to be collectively responsible to the legislature greater fundamental rights including freedom of speech assembly association and equality before the law and abolition of the BVNC and greater local autonomy. A couple of months later the national legislature adopted a bill stipulating that all the elections from village to the national tiers of the panchayat system would be held on the basis of direct adult franchise. With the endorsement of this act by the king and the incorporation of the principles of collective responsibility of the cabinet as well as the election of the prime minister by the national legislature in the king's message of December 1979 the stalwarts of the panchayat system reconciled themselves to some of the changes demanded by the multi-party leadership. This allowed Panchayat supporters to argue that people could obtain democracy without restoring political parties. At the end of the year the panchas' strategy moved into its final phase. A number of leaders who so far had remained inactive-people such as Tulsi Giri became involved. Panchas campaigned the entire election on the issues of stability and an appeal to nationalism. Panchayat successfully portrayed the referendum as Panchayat = King and Multiparty = BP Koirala. This strengthened Panchayat support but also politicized the monarchy. Multi-Party Camp: Multi-party supporters initially became overconfident believing victory was likely. However they soon became deeply divided by ideological disagreements personality conflicts and rival leaderships. While there were calls for a united front BP Koirala rejected it. He believed Nepal needed democratic reconciliation—not an anti-monarchy revolutionary coalition—and because he refused to compromise the Nepali Congress's democratic socialist principles through opportunistic alliances with ideologically incompatible forces. It is worth noting that not all opposition leaders agreed. Leaders such as Ganesh Man Singh were generally more open to tactical cooperation with communist groups against the Panchayat whereas B.P. consistently insisted that any cooperation must not undermine the Nepali Congress's independent identity or its commitment to constitutional democracy. At that time Nepal's communist movement was fragmented. Some communist leaders believed that even though the referendum was not a fully free democratic election it was an opportunity to defeat the Panchayat system. Moderate communist leaders like Man Mohan Adhikari and Sahana Pradhan supported participating in the referendum and campaigning for the multiparty option. The Multi-Party Janabadi Morcha associated with figures such as Ram Raja Prasad Singh and Prem Krishna Pathak worked to create support for multiparty democracy. However radical communists like CPN (Marxist–Leninist) aka Male led by C. P. Mainali Madan Bhandari Jhala Nath Khanal KP Oli etc. and CPN (Masal) led by Mohan Bikram Singh and Nirmal Lama boycotted the referendum initially though though some factions later participated indirectly. The multiparty camp portrayed Panchayat as an undemocratic corrupt and economically unsuccessful system while presenting democracy as the path toward development national unity and stronger independence. King Birendra: After announcing the referendum in May 1979 King Birendra initially attempted to project neutrality between the two options. However as the referendum campaign progressed he gradually appeared more sympathetic toward retaining a reformed Panchayat system. By late 1979 he encouraged Panchayat leaders to unite around reforms and emphasized themes such as national unity stability sovereignty culture and territorial integrity themes that implicitly supported the argument that Panchayat was better suited to safeguard these interests. On Constitution Day (16 December 1979) King Birendra announced that irrespective of the referendum outcome Nepal would move toward significant political reforms including direct elections to the National Panchayat based on universal adult franchise a Prime Minister elected by the National Panchayat and a Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the legislature. These commitments endorsed the reform direction already approved through the Panchayat legislature and were intended to strengthen the argument that democracy could be achieved through a reformed Panchayat system without restoring political parties. Campaign Methods: Both sides used pamphlets posters wall graffiti public meetings and mass rallies. Panchayat side campaigned on the achievements of the Panchayat system and claimed political parties caused instability division and foreign influence. Meanwhile multi-party campaign themes criticized the Panchayat system as authoritarian corrupt undemocratic and responsible for suppressing civil liberties.

events.title: Surya Bahadur Thapa
events.detail: 3rd Term

events.title: Chhintang Massacre
events.detail: The Chhintang Incident took place in the Chhintang village of Dhankuta district in eastern Nepal and is considered one of the bloodiest political massacres of the Panchayat era. Influenced by underground communist cadres local peasants mainly from indigenous communities revolted against oppressive local landlords demanding fair wages land rights and an end to feudal exploitation. In November 1979 the Panchayat government deployed armed police forces to ruthlessly crush the growing leftist stronghold. State forces systematically executed 15 political activists and farmers in cold blood.

events.title: Soviet Invasion Of Afghanistan
events.detail: Emir Amanullah Khan declared full independence from British foreign influence following the Third Anglo-Afghan War in 1919. Born into the Barakzai royal family Mohammed Daud Khan rose through military ranks becoming PM in 1953. During his tenure he constituted major modernizations but was eventually pressured to step down in 1963 due to a diplomatic and trade crisis stemming from his hardline stance on creating an independent "Pashtunistan" along the Pakistani border. A subsequent 1964 constitution explicitly barred members of the royal family from holding political office sidelining him from open statecraft. It also granted women the right to vote and opening the doors for widespread university education and modern social liberties in major cities. On July 17 1973 while King Zahir Shah was abroad receiving medical care in Italy Daoud Khan orchestrated a bloodless coup d'état backed by the military and left-wing factions. He abolished the 225-year-old monarchy declared Afghanistan a republic and assumed office as its president. He originally leaned on the Soviet Union for military and infrastructure funding. He moved to centralize authority under his National Revolutionary Party cracking down on both religious conservatives and domestic leftists. In his later years he attempted to distance the nation from Soviet influence actively seeking closer ties with Western powers and Middle Eastern countries to diversify diplomatic dependencies. His crackdowns on local communist factions backfired causing the rival Khalq and Parcham wings of the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) to unify against him. On April 27–28 1978 a violent military uprising known as the Saur Revolution took place. Left-wing military officers stormed the Arg presidential palace in Kabul. The President Daoud Khan his brother and approximately 30 family members were summarily executed after refusing to surrender. His assassination ended the First Republic and installed a Marxist-Leninist government. The new communist regime forced radical agrarian secular and social reforms that deeply angered the traditional conservative Muslim populace of rural Afghanistan. Internal division split the PDPA. In September 1979 Hafizullah Amin orchestrated an internal coup to seize power. Fearing Amin's instability and the potential for a total Islamic uprising on its southern border Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev decided to intervene. On December 27 1979 Soviet special forces launched a rapid assault on the Tajbeg Palace in Kabul killing President Amin and installing the loyal puppet leader Babrak Karmal. A decentralized insurgent group called Mujahideen was formed funded and heavily armed by an international coalition including the United States (via the CIA's Operation Cyclone) Pakistan China and Saudi Arabia. In 1986 the U.S. began supplying shoulder-fired Stinger missiles neutralizing Soviet air superiority and making their armored helicopters highly vulnerable. Nepal: The invasion brought the Cold War directly to South Asia fracturing the unity of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) and causing friction between Nepal and India. In several occasions Nepal expressed grave concern over developments in Afghanistan called for the withdrawal of foreign troops from both Afghanistan and Kampuchea and indicated it was prepared to support any regional or other effort to resolve the Afghan crisis. To this end and in order to seek additional support for the King's proposal that Nepal be declared a Zone of Peace the King took several trips during the year first to neighboring countries in South Asia and South East Asia and later to the United Kingdom with stops along the way. The results were reassuring and gained Nepal additional support for its Zone of Peace initiative. India's reluctance to aggressively condemn the USSR put it at odds with Nepal's principled stance. Concurrently Nepal found common diplomatic ground with Pakistan and China both of whom were deeply involved in backing the anti-Soviet resistance.

events.title: Increasing Dependence On Foreign Borrowing
events.detail: Total budget expenditure for FY 1979-80 was Rs. 2.9696 Arba. Foreign loans financed about 63% of total expenditure.

events.title: Referendum
events.detail: Election: The referendum used adult suffrage but the voting age was 21 years. Voter registration began on 14 Shrawan 2036 BS. The final voter roll contained about 70 lakhs eligible voters. Voting took place from 9:15 AM to 5:15 PM across Nepal. There were 5913 polling stations and 4005 polling sub-stations. Each polling station had election officials appointed by the Election Commission. Representatives from both sides Panchayat and Multiparty side. They were allowed to observe the process. The ballot paper was very simple. It was approximately 4 inches × 4 inches with two colored sections yellow for Panchayat system with reforms and blue for multiparty democratic system. Results: There was 66.92% voters turnout among which 7.63% votes were invalid. Among the valid votes reformed Panchayat system got 54.79% and multiparty system got 45.21%. The multiparty option won in 19 of Nepal's 75 districts including Kathmandu Valley Morang Sunsari Kaski Chitwan Rupandehi and several western districts. Panchayat's Advantage: Nepal's literacy rate was only about 19% limiting the impact of reformist multi-party side. Neither side conducted extensive door-to-door campaigning but Panchayat supporters already had a nationwide organizational network through village Panchayat officials. The pro-pancha forces did not need to resort to extensive campaign. Many panchas who lived at the village level supported the status quo perceived the referendum as a critical survival issue and consequently mobilized their own resources in favor of the panchayat system. The 1979 movement that forced the referendum was overwhelmingly student-led but despite popular demand of keeping voting age to 18 panchayat government sticked with status quo. This helped to keep agitated student population out of voting process favoring the panchayat side. Aftermath: Most of multi-party side leaders including Ganesh Man Singh within NC were in favor of rejecting the referendum results alleging of rigging and state-sponsored manipulation. However BP was the only top leader who accepted the referendum result despite believing there had been irregularities for three reasons: 1. He could not be certain that supporters of the multiparty camp had not also committed irregularities. 2.) He believed that complaints about electoral malpractice should have been made before the results not only after losing. 3.) Rejecting the result could have triggered civil conflict or civil war a responsibility he was unwilling to bear. His acceptance of the 1980 referendum despite believing it was flawed reflected his conviction that constitutional and democratic legitimacy was more important than short-term political victory. His refusal to incite violence or reject the verdict became one of the defining features of his political legacy.)

events.title: Sixth Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 22.09 billion spent; ~48% from foreign aid; ~65% implementation rate; development to be carried out through public Panchayat and private sectors; emphasized decentralized development and greater participation of local Panchayats through the National Development Council; 2,120 km of roads built; Kulekhani I (60 MW) and Devighat (14 MW) Hydroelectric projects completed; Marsyangdi Hydro project commenced; Hetauda-Narayangadh highway sections paved; sought to improve the living standards of the nearly 40% of the population living below the poverty line; prioritized agriculture rural development employment generation and basic needs; agriculture and irrigation received 32.4%; transport and communications took 26.8%; social services received 25.7%; introduced private sector participation in banking and industry.

events.title: Damauli Jail Break
events.detail: The Damauli Jail Break took place on 1 August 1980 after Bamdev Gautam politically organized prisoners and raised their awareness during imprisonment. Led by Ram Bahadur Tiwari with an action committee consisting of Dhan Bahadur Gurung Narayan Bastola and Tiwari the prisoners launched a planned escape. During the attempt they seized weapons from the jail overpowered guards and escaped. The government responded by mobilizing the army leading to clashes near the Gandaki River where some escapees including Dal Bahadur Thapa and Durga Thapa were captured. The incident became a major challenge to the Panchayat regime and highlighted growing resistance.

events.title: Bhairahawa Jail Break
events.detail: The Bhairahawa Jail Break occurred on 17 August 1980 when nine communist activists including Modanath Prasrit were arrested while bringing underground materials of the Communist Party of Nepal (ML) into Nepal and charged under the crime against the state. The prisoners secretly prepared an escape by making a rope ladder from window pieces and jute strings to cross the 15-foot jail wall. Six prisoners including Modanath Prasrit successfully escaped at 4 PM becoming a major boost for the democratic and left movements against the Panchayat regime. Prasrit was later rearrested and faced further attempts on his life during transfers between Pokhara and Kathmandu prisons.

events.title: Third Amendment to The 1962 Constitution
events.detail: King Birendra promulgated the Third Amendment to the 1962 Constitution on 16 December 1980 implementing reforms promised after the referendum. The amendment was a compromise within the Panchayat camp of liberals led by PM Surya Bahadur Thapa who favored meaningful reforms and purists who wanted to preserve the traditional Panchayat system with minimal change. Transition to Direct Election: After the ammendment 112 members of the National Panchayat would be directly elected by universal adult franchise while the King still retained the power to nominate 28 members meaning the legislature was not fully elected. The National Panchayat would recommend a single candidate for Prime Minister. The King would then appoint that candidate. Council of Ministers would be collectively responsible towards National Panchayat. Moreover, Pradhan Panchas and Upa-Pradhan Panchas of Gaun/Nagar Panchayat were were also to be elected through direct election. Reaction From Multiparty Camp: Most political groups with allegiance to the multiparty cause declined to accept the constitution claiming that it did not represent the aspirations of 45% of the electorate that voted for the multiparty system in the referendum. One exception was the pro-Moscow faction of the erstwhile communist party; another was the Nepali Congress "group of 38." B. P. Koirala found himself in a Hamlet-like dilemma and vacillated while his more aggressive colleagues--K. P. Bhattarai Ganesh Man Singh and G. P. Koirala and also M. M. Adhikari of the erstwhile communist party--issued statements asserting that the constitution was undemocratic and unacceptable. BP Koirala adopted a cautious middle ground. He described the constitution as disappointing overall unlikely to promote national reconciliation and yet containing enough positive features that democrats should not reject it outright.

events.title: Worsening Economic Conditions
events.detail: The government abolished the dual exchange-rate system but the new exchange rate made luxury imports cheaper increased the cost of some essential goods and reduced the profitability of exports. Nepal recording a record trade deficit of Rs. 3 billion in year 1980–81. Finance Minister Y. P. Pant proposed a budget with a 100% increase in development spending but few believed it was realistic because it was not accompanied by meaningful policy or administrative reforms. Prime Minister Surya Bahadur Thapa faced criticism in the newly elected Rastriya Panchayat particularly from a group of 13 dissident members who accused his government of lacking a coherent economic program and tolerating widespread corruption. The group included leaders like Lokendra Bahadur Chand Padma Sundar Lawati Pashupati Shumsher JBR Sribhadra Sharma and Dr. Prakash Chandra Lohani. However this opposition remained weak because the partyless Panchayat system discouraged organized opposition and legislators depended on government support to deliver development projects to their constituencies.

events.title: Growing Superpower Competition
events.detail: In late 1981 Nepalese customs officials at Tribhuvan International Airport intercepted and detained a massive unauthorized cargo consignment flown into Kathmandu. Although the shipment was explicitly addressed to the Soviet Embassy inspection revealed it contained non-diplomatic high-value consumer goods—most notably a vast quantity of watches. It raised questions about Nepal's commitment to non-alignment and created unease in relations with the Soviet Union. Subsequently Both the United States and the Soviet Union increased their diplomatic engagement with Nepal reflecting growing Cold War competition. It added more credence when U.S. Ambassador Coon stated that the U.S. had a "strategic interest" in Nepal's stability and opposed the imposition of foreign ideologies. The usual American practice of skipping Nepal when high-level dignitaries visit the region was changed when U.S. Permanent Representative to the UN Jeane Kirkpatrick visited Nepal in August. The Soviet Union kept up the momentum by dispatching its First Deputy Chairman Kuznetsov in December. High-level exchanges resumed with visits by Indian President Neelam Sanjiva Reddy and Foreign Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao. However major bilateral issues like King Birendra's Zone of Peace proposal cooperation over Nepal's vast water resources and Transit problems at Calcutta Port remained unresolved. Meanwhile China remained a strong supporter of Nepal's Zone of Peace proposal. During Premier Zhao Ziyang's visit both sides discussed improving regional cooperation and the implications of improving Sino-Indian relations.

events.title: Second Rastriya Panchayat Election
events.detail: First direct election under Panchayat to elect 112 seats elected and 28 appointed by the King. Election Boycott: BP had stated that he would participate in the elections only if they were free fair impartial and free from unnecessary restrictions. Meanwhile the government accelerated election preparations while BP and his allies sought a postponement and demanded the allotment of the same election symbol to all NC candidates, one manifesto, abolition of the class organization membership requirement, and an interim government for holding elections. When these demands were not met the Nepali Congress and multi-party camp decided to boycott the 1981 Panchayat elections. The boycott by the major opposition parties effectively left the elections to competing Panchayat factions undermining the broader political opening initiated by King Birendra's 1979 referendum. This outcome represented a victory for conservative ("purist") Panchayat leaders who preferred preserving the status quo while the opposition missed an opportunity to participate in the reformed system and gradually push Nepal toward greater democratization from within. Surya Bahadur Thapa's Consolidation: After the Nepali Congress and other major opposition groups boycotted the 1981 elections internal rivalries resurfaced. Panchayat candidates competed not only against unofficial candidates but also against one another exposing deep factionalism. Surya Bahadur Thapa used his control of the government during the elections to weaken potential rivals. He reportedly helped defeat Matrika Prasad Koirala who was considered a possible challenger for the premiership along with several other rivals. Former Prime Ministers Tulsi Giri Kirti Nidhi Bista and Nagendra Prasad Rijal did not even contest. By eliminating competitors before the new National Panchayat convened Thapa ensured that King Birendra had little choice but to reappoint him Prime Minister. Election Results: Voter turnout was 52% lower than the referendum's 67% but still respectable despite the opposition boycott. 1096 candidates contested 112 seats. More than 70% of the official Panchayat candidates lost and 57 of the 112 elected members were newcomers. Nani Maiya Dahal an unknown candidate won Kathmandu a result widely interpreted as a protest vote against the political establishment. Direct elections based on adult suffrage led voters in politically aware districts to reject many traditional elites. Government And Aftermath: Despite many new legislators Lokendra Bahadur Chand did not challenge Thapa for Prime Minister. The National Panchayat overwhelmingly nominated Surya Bahadur Thapa while Marich Man Singh was elected Chairman unopposed. King Birendra appointed Thapa to head a 28-member Council of Ministers on 16 June 1981. Throughout 1981 Thapa called on opposition leaders to accept the constitution and join the "national mainstream." The most notable defection was Parshu Narayan Chaudhary a close associate of BP Koirala who accepted the constitution after the elections. However neither the Panchayat establishment fully embraced Choudhary nor did his departure significantly weaken BP Koirala's faction which remained the principal democratic opposition.

events.title: Nepal-China Trade and Payments Agreement
events.detail: Payment System: Scraped clearing-account and swing-credit mechanism. It mandated that all payments for overseas trade be made in "freely convertible currency". For overland trade it simply stipulated that payments "remain to be made in the traditional customary way". Logistics and Shipping Terms: Chinese exports could be C.I.F. Calcutta (or another agreed port) or F.O.B. a Chinese port. Conversely Nepalese exports could be F.O.B. Calcutta (or another agreed port) or C.I.F. a Chinese port. This allowed for more varied logistical arrangements depending on the specific trade contract.

events.title: BP Koirala's Illness and the Future of the Nepali Congress
events.detail: By late 1981 BP Koirala was seriously ill and had returned to Kathmandu. His illness prompted discussions about reuniting the fragmented factions of the Nepali Congress as leaders from different Congress groups appeared together at a public meeting in December 1981. Leaders like K. P. Bhattarai S. P. Upadhyay and Rishikesh Shah who belong to different Nepali Congress groups and other politicians including ex-Premier T. P. Acharya were present to address a mass meeting. BP's faction also planned meetings in early 1982 to determine the party's future organization leadership and strategy.

events.title: Jhala Nath Khanal Became The General Secretary of CPN (Marxist-Leninist)
events.detail: After the referendum the party changed its political approach and started to focus more on mobilizing mass movements for a democratic change. Though party din't participate in referendum amid KP oli's stance to participate. CP Mainali, clearly identified with the initial militant phase of the party, was removed from his post of general secretary by party's central committee and replaced by Jhala Nath Khanal.

events.title: Economic Decentralization Efforts
events.detail: The government promoted decentralized development allocating around 50% of land tax revenue to District Panchayats but many local bodies lacked the technical capacity to use these resources effectively. King Birendra personally initiated several “crash development programs” during regional visits including support for agriculture irrigation education health and infrastructure. While these projects benefited local communities critics argued that bypassing normal budgeting processes weakened government planning.

events.title: Nepal's Policy of Non-Alignment in Action
events.detail: Nepal government criticized Soviet military intervention in Afghanistan and Vietnam's intervention with Soviet assistance in Kampuchea in the UN and other international forums. With regard to relations between some Middle Eastern countries and Nepal Nepal asked for an end to the war between Iraq and Iran. Nepal's good relations with Iraq have resulted in the importation of 250000 tons of oil. Nepal denounced the Israeli military operation in Lebanon and the massacre of Palestinians in two camps in Beirut.

events.title: Kulekhani-I Hydropower Project Built
events.detail: Kulekhani-I Hydropower Project was Nepal's first major storage-type (reservoir) project located in Makwanpur District. storage-type (reservoir) project. It remains critical today for maintaining grid stability and meeting peak winter demands. The Kulekhani-I Hydropower Project was built with financial and technical assistance from the World Bank (IDA) Japan (OECF) the Kuwait Fund and the UNDP and was completed in between 1977 and 1982. Kulekhani II was commissioned in 1986 through loan assistance from Japan and a third power station the 14 MW Kulekhani III was funded entirely by domestic resources from the Government of Nepal and was operational in April 2018.

events.title: Hetauda–Narayanghat Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: Under USOM's Rapti Valley Development Project a 52-mile double-lane gravel Hetauda-Narayangadh road was first built in 1956. Later in 1972 an ADB loan was approved for the upgradation of the 77 km road which was completed in 1982.

events.title: Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper Mills Established
events.detail: Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper Limited was a major state-supported paper factory in Gaindakot, Chitwan, established in 1982 with Chinese assistance and privatized under the ⁠Golchha Organisation in 1992. It was capable of producing roughly 42 metric tons of paper per day.

events.title: Gorkha/Mugling-Narayanghat Highway Inagurated
events.detail: The Gorkha-Narayanghat Highway (officially known as the Madan-Ashrit Highway for its Narayanghat-Mugling section) was built with financial and technical assistance from the Government of China. The 61-kilometer highway was officially completed and handed over to Nepal by the Chinese side in January 1982. The Chinese Minister of Communications Peng Deqing visited Nepal for the inauguration of the Chinese-aided Gorkha-Narayanghat Highway. This project came as an answer to India who blocked China from constructing Kohalpur-Banbasa section of East-West highway. Through the critical Gorkha-Narayangadh highway corridor they reduced the use of the India-assisted Tribhuvan highway. Chinese aid was also perceived as being attached with fewer strings and was rendered ‘with great fanfare’ making grant conditionalities as attractive as possible ‘without regard to what this might do to the economic utility of the aid’44. For example Chinese technicians employed on projects would be paid by China but ‘not out of the grant’.

events.title: BP Koirala Dies
events.detail: The final weeks of B.P. Koirala's life in July 1982 were a race against aggressive lung cancer set against his unwavering commitment to his political ideology. Despite suffering from worsening throat and lung issues Koirala refused to halt his advocacy. In January 1982 he delivered his final public speech. He actively promoted national reconciliation between the crown and democratic forces to avoid foreign intervention in Nepal. By the summer of 1982 the cancer had metastasized. His family arranged for immediate medical intervention abroad. On the morning of his departure from his Chabahil residence author Ganesh Raj Sharma arrived with a tape recorder to capture the final segments of Koirala's autobiography Atmabrittanta. Lying bedridden and visibly exhausted Koirala was asked how he wanted the Nepali people to remember him. He provided his final reflections while surrounded by his niece Shailaja Acharya and his sister-in-law Nona Koirala. BP was flown to a hospital in Bangkok Thailand for specialized cancer treatment. Unfortunately his condition deteriorated rapidly and he eventually slipped into a coma. Recognizing that the illness had reached a terminal phase his son Dr. Shashank Koirala made the decision to bring him home so he could spend his final moments on Nepali soil. On July 21 1982 a charter flight brought the comatose leader back to Kathmandu. He was moved from the airport to his home where he passed away peacefully just two hours after landing. When BP passed away in 1982 the tone of King Birendra's message was almost taunting: "It is natural for us to feel aggrieved at the death of any Nepali." The state-controlled media and the government downplayed the passing of the country's first democratically elected prime minister. The autocratic Panchayat government refused to grant Koirala an official state funeral or standard national honors. In complete defiance of the palace the response from the public was an unprecedented emotional outpouring of grief and mass mobilization. An estimated 500000 people poured into the streets of Kathmandu for his funeral procession to the holy banks of the Bagmati River at Aryaghat. It was one of the largest public gatherings in modern Nepali history.

events.title: Wost Economic Performance in Several Years
events.detail: Performance of the economy during 1982-83 was the bleakest in several years with signs of economic mismanagement apparent in most areas. Budget deficits were the highest ever. The trade gap widened enormously. Foreign exchange reserves fell sharply and for the first time in several years exports declined substantially even in absolute terms. A negative growth rate of GDP along with a high rate of population growth resulted in a lower standard of living for the vast majority of the people. The new Lokendra Bahadur Chand government introduced limited measures such as reducing rice and electricity prices and cutting the development budget by 14% but these were considered insufficient. The government largely continued the policies of the previous Surya Bahadur Thapa government despite criticizing its economic failures. Although export promotion measures including subsidies were introduced they were unlikely to significantly improve the economy. The new two-year economic program mostly repeated existing plans without addressing deeper structural problems. Panchayat governments focused on short-term popularity rather than long-term reforms because of political insecurity. As a result major structural changes—such as agrarian reform stronger economic institutions and resolving issues with neighboring countries on water resources and migration—were unlikely under the existing political system.

events.title: Fall of Surya Bahadur Thapa
events.detail: The year 1983 saw increasing conflicts among Panchayat leaders with divisions moving from internal debates in the Rastriya Panchayat to public protests press conferences and rallies. Opposition to Prime Minister Surya Bahadur Thapa grew among Panchayat members especially over corruption economic mismanagement food shortages and failure to address national problems. Panchayat conventions organized by the Panchayat Policy and Evaluation Committee (PPEC) raised fears that the old Back to the Village National Campaign (BVNC) style of political mobilization was returning. Prime Minister Surya Bahadur Thapa was removed from his post through a no-confidence motion in the Rastriya Panchayat in the leadership of Lokendra Bahadur Chand, Padma Sundar Lawati, Pashupati Shumsher JBR, Sribhadra Sharma and Dr. Prakash Chandra Lohani etc. 41 members submitted the motion accusing Thapa’s government of weakening Panchayat principles and partylessness widespread corruption failure to solve food shortages and economic indiscipline. The motion passed overwhelmingly with 108 votes in favor 17 against and 10 abstentions. The motion passed without serious debate. Ministers who had been part of Thapa’s government also voted against him. King-nominated members of the Rastriya Panchayat supported his removal. Thapa publicly criticized an "underground gang" (Giroha) working against his administration, revealing a tense power dynamic between Singh Darbar and the royal palace. His allusions used to be towards Gyanendra and Dhirendra who wanted to remove him. Even insuch bleak condition 17 members of Rashtriya Panchayat supported him and were long known as 'Satra Bhai' parallel to 'Satra Bhai' in Dhir Shumsher's Rana family. Thapa’s fall showed increasing instability within the Panchayat leadership. Many ministers resigned before the vote and on 12 July 1983 Lokendra Bahadur Chand became PM.

events.title: Lokendra Bahadur Chand
events.detail: 1st Term

events.title: CPN (Masal i.e. मसाल) Formed
events.detail: In November 1983 the followers of Mohan Bikram Singh faction of CPN (Fourth Convention) held a separate conference, and formed Communist Party of Nepal (Masal). Amongst those who followed MBS were Chitra Bahadur K.C., C.P. Gajurel, Mohan Baidhya, Khampa Singh, Bachaspati Devkota, Bhairav Regmi, R. Shrestha as well as future Maoist leaders like Pushpa Kamal Dahal and Baburam Bhattarai. The remainder, led by Nirmal Lama, continued to work under the name of CPN (4th Convention). In a simplified manner one might say that the key issue behind the split was diverging opinion on who was the main enemy of the party. MBS claimed that the main enemy was Indian expansionism, which was backing up the royal house in Nepal. Since the Nepali Congress, according to him, were Indian puppets cooperation with them was not feasible. According to Lama was feudalism as the main enemy, and that the royal regime was propping up the feudal system. The main priority was to fight against the royal regime for a democratic opening, and thus fight against feudalism itself. To Lama, the Nepali Congress was a potential ally in this struggle. In November 1990, CPN (4th Convention) merged with Communist Party of Nepal (Mashal i.e. मशाल) and other smaller fractions, forming the Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre)

events.title: Rise of Panchayat Political Control Through PPEC
events.detail: Despite growing divisions within the Panchayat leadership and fears of outside political influence some leaders were trying to transform the Panchayat system into a one-party style structure. The Panchayat Policy and Evaluation Committee (PPEC) began functioning like a central party organization by monitoring political activities and guiding government policies. Its creation of a Decentralization Committee and plans to establish zonal and district-level subcommittees indicated an attempt to extend centralized political control throughout the country similar to a party network.

events.title: American and French Support for King's Zone of Peace Proposal
events.detail: King Birendra visited US in December 1983. President Ronald Reagan expressed support for Nepal’s proposal to declare Nepal a Zone of Peace. France had also supported the ZOP proposal after President François Mitterrand’s visit to Nepal in July 1983 the first visit by a Western head of government. However both the US and France emphasized that Nepal needed cooperation with its neighbors to make the proposal successful.

events.title: Factional Conflict Within the Panchayat
events.detail: The politics was dominated by a power struggle between the Lokendra Bahadur Chand and Surya Bahadur Thapa factions (samuhas) exposing deep divisions within Panchayat system. Soon after Chand became PM after voting out Thapa another no confidence motion was filed against him by more than 30 members. Although rejected on technical grounds it showed that political instability continued. The frequent challenges suggested that Panchayat politics remained dominated by factional competition. Chand Faction: It united many Panchayat leaders dissatisfied with Surya Bahadur Thapa's leadership corruption allegations and style of governance. Key leaders included Lokendra Bahadur Chand Padma Sundar Lawati Pashupati Shumsher JBR Sribhadra Sharma Dr. Prakash Chandra Lohani Marich Man Shrestha etc. Thapa Faction: This faction consisted mainly of Thapa's loyalists. Around 42 National Panchayat members remained his core supporters after Chand formed the government. Hardline Panchayat Conservatives: Beyond mainstream two factions this third faction mostly consisted of opportunists within the system who wanted to restore the original Panchayat system and roll back the Third Amendment. It consisted Tulsi Giri Kirti Nidhi Bista (at times) Dr. Mohammad Mohsin Yajna Prasad Acharya (NC district secretary in 2006 BS Communist Party district secretary in 2010 BS) etc. Chand's Survival Tactics: Soon after coming to power Chand government tightened rules on no-confidence motions. When the no confidence motion was tabled by the Thapa faction Marich Man Singh chairman of the National Panchayat and of the Panchayat Policy and Inspection Committee came to the government's rescue and made his controversial decision against the motion. Chand also expanded his cabinet to strengthen political support bringing in new figures such as Parashu Narayan Chaudhary a former Nepali Congress minister who had joined the Panchayat system.

events.title: Good Monsoon Driven Economic Relief
events.detail: A GDP of $2.5 billion against a population of about 16 million gives a per capita GNP of $170 one of the lowest among the least developed of the developing countries. Although GDP grew by 7.4% agricultural output rose sharply by 18.4% and inflation eased in 1984 these gains were largely attributed to a good monsoon rather than government policy. According at a data During 1971-2000 the year 1973 1975 and 1984 seemed to be generally much more rainfall than normal throughout the country and on the contrary at the same period 1972 1982 and 1992 seemed to be much lower rainfall than the normal throughout the country.The incoming finance minister Prakash Chandra Lohani adopted past budget and its principles and later without going to the legislature made ad hoc changes to reduce by 15% what he called a bloated budget. The reduction was mostly in development expenditures producing in the process a curious amalgam. That regular expenditures increased in 1983 by 13.5% while development expenditures did so only by 1.6% tells its own tale. The 1984–85 Chand government budget emphasized development spending and introduced measures such as higher public sector salaries and greater competition. Exports increased mainly because of the carpet industry while new international air routes to Singapore and Abu Dhabi via Karachi reflected efforts to expand economic links.

events.title: Piskar Massacre
events.detail: The Piskar Massacre took place on 15 January 1984 when thousands of villagers gathered in Piskar Sindhupalchok to celebrate Maghe Sankranti. Following recent political activities by the Communist Party of Nepal (Marxist–Leninist) (CPN-ML) the festival featured songs and performances criticizing the Panchayat system and feudal landlords. Police backed by local officials and landlord Devi Jang Pandey surrounded the gathering and opened fire killing Bir Bahadur Thami Ile Thami and five others while injuring many more. The government subsequently arrested around 60 people including 12 women with many detained for years without trial tortured or disappeared. The massacre became a symbol of the Panchayat regime's violent suppression of political dissent. Piskar later became the underground shelter of the then president of UML Jhalnath Khanal vice president Ashtalakshmi Shakya and other famous leaders. From this incident leaders like Madhav Paudel and Amritkumar Bohra rose to the level of parliamentarian minister and national level.

events.title: Surajpur Kanda
events.detail: The Surajpur Incident in Devdaha Rupandehi was a major act of political violence during the Panchayat era. On Mar 4 1984 pro-Panchayat Mandales attacked a banned Nepali Congress gathering at the residence of Congress leader Pushpananda Giri where leaders like Girija Prasad Koirala Ram Chandra Poudel and Sher Bahadur Deuba were present. The attackers entered the private residence vandalized property looted belongings and assaulted participants. Yadunath Alok was killed on the spot and Ram Prasad Chaudhary later died from injuries. Around 272 people were injured including 27 seriously wounded. Sher Bahadur Deuba was also injured and leaders including Girija Prasad Koirala had to be hidden to save them from attack. The incident forced Girija Prasad Koirala to cancel his nationwide political tour and intensified public opposition to the Panchayat system. Rather than accepting compensation offered later by the state Pushpananda Giri demanded punishment for the perpetrators and restoration of democracy. The Surajpur Incident remains a symbol of state-backed political violence and repression under the Panchayat regime and it strengthened the movement for multiparty democracy.

events.title: Nabil Bank Founded
events.detail: Nabil Bank, formerly known as Nepal Arab Bank Limited, is the first private and foreign joint venture commercial bank in Nepal, established in 1984. Its Dubai government-owned majority share was purchased in 1995 by CG group. Nabil bank had acquired Nepal Bangladesh Bank in July 2022.

events.title: CPN (Mashal i.e. मशाल) Formed
events.detail: CPN (Mashal) was formed in November 1984, following a split in the Communist Party of Nepal (Masal i.e. मसाल). The split was caused by dissatisfaction with Mohan Bikram Singh's authoritarian leadership methods. Mohan Baidya (alias 'Kiran') became general secretary of the new party. Other Central Committee members elected at the Gorakhpur conference were Chitra Bahadur K.C., Ramsingh Shris, Bhairav Regmi, Govindsingh Thapa, Pushpa Kamal Dahal, Khambasingh Kubar, Bachaspati Devkota, C.P. Gajurel, Dev Gurung, Ishwari Dahal, Bishnu Pokhrel and Bhakta Bahadur Shrestha. In 1986, Mohan Baidya was acting as General Secretary of the CPN (Mashal) when he called for an armed uprising against King Birendra. These attempts were ultimately unsuccessful leading to the arrest of several revolutionaries known as the Sector Incident. It saw Baidya face severe internal criticism culminating in his resignation and replacement with Pushpa Kamal Dahal (Prachanda). In 1991 CPN (Mashal) merged with Communist Party of Nepal (Fourth Convention), and formed Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre).

events.title: Butwal-Kohalpur Section of East-West Highway Completed
events.detail: Similar to Mechi-Dhalkebar section this section was also built with economic assistance of India. However this section was only agreed after the eastern section was completed. The construction began in 1973 and completed in 1985.

events.title: Koshi Highway Completed
events.detail: The 390 km Koshi Highway (Rani-Itahari-Dharan-Dhankuta-Dhankuta-Hile-Kimathanka Road) was built of five different sections. The Rani-Itahari and Itahari-Dharan section was built by Government of Nepal. First during the 1930s a road connecting Biratnagar to Dharan was built via Itahari. Before this to travel from Itahari to Dharan commuters had to go through Pakali Ramdhuni and Chatara. The roads were later upgraded by ODA (UK Aid Project) in 1996. The Dharan-Dhankuta and Dhankuta-Hile section were also constructed with the assistance of UK between 1976 and 1985. The Hile-Kimathanka section due to difficult terrain track has been recently opened so the road is not paved yet.

events.title: Mahakali Highway Partially Completed
events.detail: The 364 km Mahakali Highway (Mohana Bridge- Attariya- Syaule(Dadeldhura)- Dadeldhura- Satbanj(Baitadi)-Khalanga(Darchula)-Tinkar) was completed in parts. The original Mohana Bridge-Attariya section was initially established by Nepal Government and paved in the decades following the regional malaria eradication and planned settlement programs of the late 1960s and 1970s serving as the primary southern link to the Mahendra Highway. The Attariya-Syaule-Dadeldhura-Satbanj section was completed between 1967 and 1980 by US assistance. The Satbanj-Khalanga was opened in the late 1980s with construction beginning in 1985. However the track of Khalanga-Tinkar hasn't been opened yet. On the closure of roads from Darchula to India by the Indian side on various excuses Nepal decided to extend the road from Darchula Khalanga to Chhangru and Tinkar. Chhangru Tinkar and Khalanga are all inside Nepali territory but one has to pass through Indian territory to get from Khalanga to these two villages as there were no roads or foot trails on the Nepali side. Since 2020 Nepal Army is working to open a track from Tusarpani to Tinkar in Darchula district.

events.title: Nepal Sadbhawana Parishad (Later Party in 1990) Formed
events.detail: In 1983, a andmark Report on Internal and International Migration in Nepal was prepared by Dr. Harka Gurung. The report stated that the dominance of immigrants, i.e. people of Indian origin, was increasing in the Terai districts. It recommended regulation of India-Nepal border and the provision of compulsory work permits for Indians. In reality the report was an indication from the Nepali ruling authorities that the government was not happy with the unequal, vague and stiff provisions of the 1950 treaty signed between Nepal and India. Gajendra Narayan Singh strongly opposed the terming of Madhesh residents as foreigners. Gajendra Narayan Singh, along with Ram Janam Tiwari, submitted a memorandum to the Royal Palace opposing the commission's report. Protests against this report also took place in the district headquarters of the Terai-Madhes region. Since political parties were banned at that time, Singh opened the Nepal Sadbhavana Council, whose objective was the development of the language and culture of the Terai-Madhes. The then NC president of Mahottari, Ram Chandra Mishra was also among the founding leaders. Nepal Sadbhawana Parishad participated in the democratic movement in Nepal. After the People's Movement of 1990 the Parishad transformed itself into Nepal Sadbhawana Party which won 6 out of 205 seats in 1991 election. Gajendra Naryan Singh advocated for five provinces in Nepal based on social, economic, and community homogeneity: Eastern Hills, Eastern Terai, Kathmandu Valley, Western Hills, and Western Terai, but that did not materialize. In the year 1993, Sadbhavana made various demands to the government. At that time, it demanded the group recruitment of 'Madheshi' in the Royal Nepali Army as separate regiment, easier distribution of citizenship certificates, reservation in employment, restructuring of constituencies, constitutional status of Hindi as the national language, establishment of federal government, and solution of squatter problems. After those demands were not met, Gajendra Narayan Singh sat on a 9-day hunger strike. The government agreed to form a high-level committee to investigate and resolve issues surrounding citizenship distribution and state discrimination against the Madhesi population. Again, the party staged a 10-day coordinated hunger strikes across 10 districts in Nepal to protest government inaction on regional and minority demands. The protests led to the mass arrest of approximately 250 party activists and members. The strike was defused after PM Girija Prasad Koirala formally offered to open government negotiations regarding their core demands. However, the demands remained largely unfulfilled.

events.title: Nepal Television Established
events.detail: NTV was established as a state broadcaster in 1985. Nepal signed an agreement with the French firm Sofratev in February 1982 for a 30-day feasibility study. Broadcasts officially began on January 30, 1985, with a 30-minute daily schedule and only 400 TV sets nationwide. Technical support was provided by Finnish experts via the Worldview International Foundation, and Nepal later sought additional Japanese technical assistance. The founding chairman of NTV was senior film actor and director Nir Shah. NTV became a corporation under the Communication Act in February 1986, moving to Singha Darbar from temporary Lazimpat facility. Later NTV gained autonomy in April 1990 when Nepal's 30-year ban on political parties was lifted.

events.title: Nepali Congress Launched National Satyagraha
events.detail: The banned Nepali Congress launched a peaceful civil-disobedience campaign demanding political reforms. Picketing before central and local offices was one form of this satyagraha. Leaders including Ganesh Man Singh, Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, and Girija Prasad Koirala were arrested, along with communist leaders such as Man Mohan Adhikari and Tulsi Lal Amatya. However, the satyagraha largely remained peaceful and was able to cause some tension within government and the National Panchayat between reformists and advocates of status quo. In June, a series of bombings in Kathmandu, including near the Royal Palace and Singha Durbar, marked a new and more dangerous phase of opposition. The Jana Mukti Morcha, associated with Ram Raja Prasad Singh, claimed responsibility. The bombings led to the suspension of the satyagraha and the collapse of the immediate no-confidence threat. The government subsequently passed an Anti-Terrorism Act, which opponents criticized for its implications for civil liberties.

events.title: Seventh Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 48.15 billion spent; ~95.5% execution rate; foreign aid financed ~58% of the development budget; 1,745 km of roads built; Marsyangdi Hydroelectric Project (69 MW) completed; Kulekhani II (32 MW) commissioned; major expansion of domestic airport runways; Structural Adjustment Program (SAP) initiated under World Bank/IMF guidance; primary education enrollment reached 78%; social services jumped to the top at 31.5%; agriculture and forestry received 24.3%; transport and communication took 14.5%; Interrupted in its final year by the 1989 trade/transit deadlock with India and the 1990 democratic movement, leading to an interim planning holiday (1990–1992).

events.title: Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Established
events.detail: NEA was established on August 16, 1985, under the Nepal Electricity Authority Act, 1984. It unified the Department of Electricity, the Nepal Electricity Corporation, and local development boards to manage power generation, transmission, and distribution with domestic funding and international loans.

events.title: Nepali Rupees Devaluated
events.detail: In order to improve Nepal's trade imbalance, Nepal decided to devaluate Nepali rupees against all foreign currencies. The most visible consequence was against the Indian rupee i.e. 100 Indian rupees went from costing Rs 145 to Rs 170.

events.title: SAARC Formed
events.detail: The seven South Asian countries met in Dhaka in December 1985 and formally established the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC). Nepal officially became the headquarters of SAARC when its permanent Secretariat was established in Kathmandu on January 16, 1987. Afghanistan joined as the eighth member in April 2007.

events.title: Gorakhkali Rubber Industry Limited Inagurated
events.detail: Gorakhkali Rubber Industry Limited (GRUL) was established under PPP model in 1984. Government of Nepal held 21% of the equity, STC held another 21%, ADB held 13% equity, Nepal Oil Corporation held 5% and rest was held by other government institutions. While the capital was structured via the PPP-ADB model, the physical creation of the factory was driven entirely by Chinese bilateral development assistance. Government of China assisted with turnkey plant construction, machinery, and technical manpower. As company showed signs of financial distress, severe operational inefficiencies, and heavy political interference, in 2003, ADB sold its 13% ownership block directly to STC. During the 1990s and 2000s, the global automotive market rapidly transitioned to radial tyres, which offer better fuel efficiency, a smoother ride, and longer lifespans. However, company continued using outdated bias-ply (nylon) technology. The company failed to invest the necessary capital—estimated later to be over 1 Arba rupees—to upgrade its machinery. As vehicle owners naturally switched to modern radial imports, demand for Gorakhkali's old-fashioned tyres evaporated. Moreover the company was plagues by politicization, internal mismanagement, and increased foreign imports of cheap tyres. Gorakhkali Rubber Industry Limited officially ceased operations in March 2015.

events.title: Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip's Second Nepal Trip
events.detail: Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip stopped over in Kathmandu again in 1986 for a four-day visit on their way to Australia and New Zealand. King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya were at the airport to greet them as they stepped off a British Airways L-1011 Tristar. The highlight of the trip was the Queen’s meeting with 200 British Gurkha veterans, among them seven surviving soldiers who had been awarded the Victoria Cross in previous wars. Queen Elizabeth walked across Kathmandu Darbar Square to the 16th century Kasthamandap accompanied by Kathmandu’s mayor Kamal Chitrakar. This time there was no royal hunt, Chitwan had been turned into the Royal Chitwan National Park. While the Queen visited Gurkha camps,  Prince Gyanendra flew down to Meghauli with Prince Philip for a morning safari and lunch at Tiger Tops in South Asia’s first natural world heritage site. However, the Queen's public congratulations to King Birendra on the 25th anniversary of the partyless Panchayat system caused controversy. Nepali Congress leader K. P. Bhattarai criticized the Queen for appearing to endorse Nepal's political system.

events.title: Nagendra Prasad Rijal
events.detail: 2nd Term

events.title: Sector Kanda
events.detail: Under the leadership of Mohan Baidya ('Kiran') the Communist Party of Nepal (Mashal) adopted Maoism as its ideological line.
