As part of the new line, the party called for armed struggle, seeking to ignite a mass popular uprising against the panchayat regime, and for boycott of the panchayat elections. According to the policy taken by the party, the attack on the police sector/beat was planned by the then Bagmati Bureau, whose in-charge was Dev Gurung. On April 1, 1986 the statue of King Tribhuvan at Tripureshwor in the capital Kathmandu was painted black and a number of police posts were attacked by the party at 4 am. Contrary to the expectations of the party leadership, the April 1 actions failed to inspire popular militancy. On the other hand, the action revealed the underground activities of the party. A number of Mashal party cadres were arrested.

events.title: Gorkhaland Movement
events.detail: In April 5, 1986, Subash Ghisingh formally declared the mass agitation program and introduced the "Do or Die" resolution for Gorkhaland at Gitangay Dara in Chowk Bazar, Darjeeling. The Gorkha National Liberation Front pushed for a separate Gorkhaland state in the Darjeeling hills, constitutional recognition for the Nepali language, and the revision or scrapping of Article 7 of the 1950 India-Nepal Treaty to protect the distinct national identity of Indian Gorkhas (i.e. open boarder). The first physical protest kicked off on the Nepali New Year i.e. April 13, 1986. The police fired on an agitation meeting of the Gorkha National Liberation Front (GNLF) held on 27 July 1986 at the Mela Ground of 9th Mile, Kalimpong. Thirteen persons were killed, while 38 others were wounded in this incident. This day is observed every year as 'Shahid Diwas' or Martyrs' Day in Darjeeling-Kalimpong hills. A tripartite agreement was signed by Subash Ghisingh (GNLF leader), Jyoti Basu (then Chief Minister of West Bengal), and C.G. Somiah (then Union Home Secretary) on on August 22, 1988 forming Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council, an an autonomous governing body in Nepali-speaking region. GNLF leader Subhash Ghising even asked King Birendra to help challenge the 1950 treaty. Nepal, however, carefully avoided taking sides, maintaining that Gorkhaland was an internal Indian matter.

events.title: Third Rastriya Panchayat Election
events.detail: In April, a new government headed by Nagendra Prasad Rijal, a former Prime Minister, was formed to carry on the day-to-day administration for a maximum period of three months until a new PM is elected. Rijal opened dialogues with the NC for it to participate in the elections. However, these talks ended in a fiasco, and the NC decided to abstain from the electoral process as it was not ready to take oath of allegiance to partyless system. A few groups, including the CPN (Marxist-Leninist), decided to contest, explaining that in the given situation when the prospect of "extra systemic" opposition was not bright, the struggle could be intensified within the system. In the May election, 60.32% of the voters cast ballots, compared with 52% in 1981. The abstention of some parties had no apparent impact on the turnout. In the process, about 20% of the candidates were elected either on the basis of their oppositional backgrounds or for other reasons unpalatable to the power elites. Of the 112odd elected members, eight came from various leftist groups and others were pro-party democrats. But many of them did not like to be identified with any of the "outlawed" parties. A few senior panchas who tried to project themselves as probable candidates for the post of Prime Minister preferred to keep quiet when Marich Man Singh Shrestha, the former Chairman of the NP and PPEC, became the lone candidate for the post.

events.title: Ammendment to Sino-Nepalese Treaty of 1956
events.detail: Border residents now needed border resident certificates registration and they could no longer freely wander across the frontier. More importantly they could not travel deeper into the other country.

events.title: Assasination Attempt on Padam Thakurathi and Arrest of Rup Chandra Bista
events.detail: Padam Thakurathi was a royalist and the founding president of Bidyarthi Mandal. Capitalizing on his loyalty to the system, Thakurathi was elected as a member of the Rastriya Panchayat representing Kanchanpur in 1977. By the early 1980s, Thakurathi grew disillusioned with the mounting internal rot, smuggling rings, and economic distortions taking place under the guise of the palace. He transitioned into journalism in 1982, editing papers like Saptahik Manch and Saptahik Bimarsha. Because he had spent years on the inside, he knew exactly where the regime's financial bodies were buried. When he began using his pen to expose the corruption of top-tier Panchayat elites (such as the Gauchan brothers and Sharad Chandra Shah), his former allies viewed his reporting not just as criticism, but as a deep, structural betrayal. Thakurathi was shot at 3:10 AM on September 6, 1986 while he was sleeping but assasination attempt failed. The shooter Vikas Gurung was arrested in July 1987 along with the planner Jagat Gauchan. Same Jagat Gauchan was made minister by King Gyanendra when he took direct control. However, the operatives Ganesh Thapa, Shankar Vishwakarma, and military aides Dipendra's ADC Bharat Gurung and IGP DB Lama were let free. On the other hand Rup Chandra Bista, a two-time (1981,1986) independent Rastriya Panchayat member, Saptahik Bimarsha published a highly critical, satirical poem titled "Hoshiyar" ("Beware") on October 3, 1986. The piece directly targeted government ministers, parliamentarians, and the broader failure of state leadership. The authoritarian Panchayat government retaliated immediately in early October 1986 by banning Saptahik Bimarsha and arresting paper's editor, Keshav Raj Pindali. Rup Chandra Bista was subsequently arrested and charged under the Treason Act for "spreading malice and hatred toward the King". He was detained until April 1987, when he was ultimately released without formal conviction. During 1986, the government was reported to have banned 19 newspapers, imposed fines on five, issued warnings to four newspapers, and arrested five editors.

events.title: Birendra's Foreign Trip and Nepal Becoming Headquarter of SAARC
events.detail: King Birendra's participation in both the eighth summit conference of nonaligned nations held at Harare, Zimbabwe, in the first week of September, and in the second summit of the South Asian heads of state and government held at Bangalore, India, on November 16-17, was considered significant. King Birendra and Queen Aiswarya paid informal visits to the Seychelles, Tanzania, Zambia, Kenya, and Oman en route to and from Harare. The state visit to West Germany on September 20-26 and some economic agreements concluded by the two countries were other highlights of the year. More important, the unanimous decision to make Kathmandu the venue for the secretariat of the SAARC was a diplomatic success for Nepal. SAARC also decided to hold its next summit in Kathmandu, for which King Birendra thanked the South Asian leaders for providing him with an opportunity to be the host.

events.title: 15th World Buddhist Conference
events.detail: On November 27, Prince Gyanendra opened the 15th World Buddhist Conference of the World Fellowship of Buddhists in Kathmandu. A controversy arose over the failure of the Dalai Lama, the spiritual leader of Tibet, to participate. There were reports that the sponsors had in fact invited both the Panchen Lama and the Dalai Lama, but that the Nepal government had ordered them to cancel the invitation to the Dalai Lama on the alleged grounds that this would harm relations between Nepal and China. Instead, the Panchen Lama, who was also the vice chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress of China, was invited by the vice chairman of the NP. In this context, a Nepali daily newspaper regretted that religion had been mixed with politics by denying participation to the most popular and respected Buddhist leader, who had a far greater number of followers than any one else.

events.title: CPN (Marxist) Formed
events.detail: Formed through the merger of the Communist Party of Nepal (Manmohan) led by Man Mohan Adhikari and the Communist Party of Nepal (Pushpa Lal) led by Sahana Pradhan. While Manmohan Adhikari took the role of party Chairman, Sahana Pradhan served as the General Secretary

events.title: NC's Participation and Poor Performance in Local Election
events.detail: In February the NC leader, Ganesh Man Singh, categorically stated that his party was not going to "participate in any panchayat elections," as almost all the twelve regional NC conferences, held to ascertain the opinion of party workers, had decided to abstain.' Subsequently, however, all the NC leaders presented a rationale for joining in the local elections, arguing that participation would not mean an acceptance of the partyless system because of the developmental nature of local units. The claim of the acting president, Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, that his party would wrest control of at least 23 of the 33 town panchayats was proved wrong when the results came in. Pitted against heavy odds, the party's poor performance was anticipated by political observers. Some left-oriented candidates, who called themselves "pro-people," did relatively better in some prestigious town panchayats and village panchayats, thus encouraging the left parties to challenge the NC's claim of being the alternative to the existing system. Several anti-NC newspapers termed it an explosion of the congress myth.

events.title: DDC MIlk Boycott Politics
events.detail: The government faced another major controversy when reports emerged that milk powder imported from Poland might have been contaminated by radiation associated with the Chernobyl disaster. The government cancelled import licenses and banned imports from potentially affected countries. The public boycotted Dairy Development Corporation milk for months. Opposition politicians used the controversy to attack government incompetence. But, crucially, the opposition could not transform popular anger into an organized political movement. This episode illustrated a recurring pattern: there was considerable public dissatisfaction, but no opposition capable of converting it into systemic political change.

events.title: Journalist Harihar Birahi Arrested
events.detail: Journalist Harihar Birahi was arrested after publishing an interview with Yogi Narhari Nath criticizing the country's deteriorating situation. This time the yogi poured his wrath on the worsening state of affairs in the country and urged King Birendra to firmly resolve the crisis facing the nation. His newspaper's registration was subsequently cancelled. The incident reinforced concerns about press freedom and political repression under the Panchayat system. Amnesty International report pointed out this specific case in its report.

events.title: Unusually Active Royal Diplomacy
events.detail: King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya, along with several foreign leaders visiting Nepal, kept foreign relations unusually active. Romania: Nicolae Ceaușescu visited Nepal and endorsed Birendra's Zone of Peace proposal. Nepal also signed an agreement to diversify bilateral trade. West Germany: Chancellor Helmut Kohl visited Nepal. West Germany remained an important development partner, particularly in agriculture, hydropower and urban development. Spain: King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia visited Kathmandu. China: Birendra visited Beijing and met Deng Xiaoping. Nepal sought to reassure China about its delicate balancing between India and China. China also provided grant assistance for the Kathmandu International Convention Centre and water/irrigation projects.

events.title: Udayapur Cement Inagurated
events.detail: The Udayapur Cement Factory was inagurated in Jun 14 1987 with funding support and development grants from the Government of Japan. It was designed by Onoda Engineering Co. Japan and constructed on a turnkey basis by a consortium of Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Tomen Corporation.It is a state-owned enterprise known for producing "Gaida Cement".

events.title: Nepali Expelled From Meghalaya
events.detail: The signing of the Assam Accord in 1985 served as a massive blueprint for student bodies across Northeast India. The Assam Movement was led by student unions demanding that the federal government identify, disenfranchise, and deport millions of undocumented migrants, primarily from neighboring Bangladesh, who they argued were altering the state's political, economic, and cultural landscape. The Assam Accord was signed which established March 24, 1971, the eve of the Bangladesh Liberation War, as the strict cutoff date for regularizing citizenship and deporting immigrants. The Khasi Students’ Union (KSU) in Meghalaya inspired from Assam launched an aggressive "anti-foreigner" agitation in July 1986. The movement that had been quietly building for two years rapidly transformed into a violent, widespread anti-foreigner and anti-outsider campaign. Migrant workers and long-settled populations of Nepali origin became the primary targets. More than 7,000 Nepalis were reported to have come to Nepal after being expelled from Meghalaya State in India. Criticizing both the government of India and the Nepali authorities for their callous indifference to the problem, various political group leaders and newspapers considered it a violation of the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship. Responding to the widespread concern, the Ministry of Home Affairs of Nepal issued a statement on November 13 stating that the government had already taken up "through proper channel" the matter of people of Nepali origin coming to Nepal after being evicted and displaced from different parts of India. On the other hand, some cases of harassment of Indian hawkers and vendors in Kathmandu were reported in the local press.

events.title: First SAARC Summit Held in Kathmandu
events.detail: The biggest diplomatic achievement of 1987 was hosting the first SAARC summit in Kathmandu from November 2–4. It elevated Nepal's diplomatic visibility, strengthened Kathmandu's role as a regional diplomatic centre, produced agreements on a SAARC food security reserve and cooperation against terrorism, and opened discussion about broader regional cooperation in trade, energy, finance and monetary affairs. For King Birendra, SAARC fit naturally with his vision of Nepal as a neutral and constructive regional actor.

events.title: Birendra's Aggresive Foreign Policy
events.detail: Nepal continued its highly active and successful foreign policy under King Birendra, particularly through SAARC. As SAARC chairman, Birendra visited six South Asian capitals. Nepal's international image of a peaceful country was further enhanced when the agreement between Nepal and the United Nations was signed on June 9 to have the U.N. Regional Center for Peace and Disarmament established in Kathmandu. Further, the number of countries endorsing Nepal's Zone of Peace proposal reached 99. India and the Soviet Union are the only major countries among those who have diplomatic relations with Nepal who have avoided endorsing the proposal so far.

events.title: Chinese Arms Purchase
events.detail: Following 1965's secret Defence Agreement that gave India monopoly over Nepal's military imports, in the early 1980s, Kathmandu approached India regarding the purchase of antiaircraft guns, but for several years there was no reply from Delhi. Meanwhile, King Birendra reportedly ordered negotiations with China for the arms deal in March 1988. A National Panchayat delegation that visited China that month was received by Politburo members Qiao Shi and Peng Zhen, both of whom reiterated China's "sincere support" for Nepal's zone-of-peace proposal. The Nepali arms purchase negotiators may have been included in this delegation. The first consignment of arms-500 truckloads worth $20 million began arriving in Nepal in June over the Lhasa-Kathmandu highway. The convoys of canvas-covered trucks reportedly moved under heavy security. Included in the shipment were light arms and ammunition, uniforms and boots, and 16 antiaircraft guns. Many Indian newspapers reported that surface-to-air missiles and medium range surface-to-surface missiles were included in the shipment. he Chinese principal in the arms transaction was apparently the North China Industries Corporation (NORINCO), China's major arms marketing firm, and presumably its motives were purely commercial. Once the arms sales issue erupted in 1989, Beijing justified it on the basis that military relations are part of the normal gamut of state-to-state relations. The sale did not take India by surprise, but it caused deep concern. New Delhi had got wind of Kathmandu's intentions and in December 1987 had warned Nepal of the consequences of purchasing antiaircraft guns from China. erhaps even more disturbing than the arms purchase was a secret agreement between Nepal and China providing for the exchange of intelligence between the two governments and signed sometime in 1988. Minister of State for External Affairs Natwar Singh flew to Kathmandu as Rajiv Gandhi's special envoy on July 22, 1988, carrying with him a letter from Gandhi to King Birendra asking for assurances that Nepal would not purchase arms from China again and that the weapons already purchased would not be used against India.12 Birendra refused to give any such assurances, insisting that it was Nepal's sovereign right to purchase weapons it considered necessary for its defense and insisting that the weapons were intended for internal security and antiterrorism and constituted no threat to India.

events.title: Dasharath Satdium Stampede
events.detail: The stadium was hosting Tribhuvan Challenge Shield final between Janakpur Cigarette Factory (Nepal) and Mukti Joddha Club (Bangladesh). The Dasarath Rangasala Stadium was a open terrace on three sides with the west side having the only grandstand. While the stadium was filled with 27,000 spectators, a strong hailstorm with 120 kph winds precipitated a human stampede at the stadium. A large hail began to lash the crowd, causing some panic. The crowd surged towards the west stand cover but was beaten back by the police. The spectators then returned to the south terrace where a crush developed in a tunnel exit. The crowd could not escape, because the stadium doors were locked and stadium staff failed to open enough exits, causing a fatal crush at the front killing 72 people and injuring 250. This incident shocked the nation as the loss of life and human injury was, in large part, caused by the lack of procedures to deal with emergency evacuation of the stadium grounds. After the disaster, the Minister for Education and Culture, Keshar Bahadur Bista, and president of the All-Nepal Football Association, Kamal Thapa, resigned. The stadium was later renovated for the 1999 South Asian Games with the help of the Chinese government.

events.title: India-Nepal Trade Treaty Expired
events.detail: In March 1 1988 India wrote to Nepal that Trade Treaty will expire on March 23 and demanded that trade and transit be combined into a single treaty, reversing the arrangement agreed in 1978. Nepal stood with the stand that they should continue with two treaties because trade was matter of convenience and subject to chnage periodically while transit was a permanent right for a land-locaked country. While two sides accused each other for delaying the treaty got two six-months extensions. But India on March 23 1989 declared the expiration of both the treaties and closed all but two entry points with Nepal.

events.title: 6.9 Mag. Udayapur Earthquake
events.detail: This was the largest earthquake in Nepal between 1934 and 2015. Despite being much smaller than the 1934 earthquake, it killed approximately 1,000 people and caused extensive damage. This is particularly significant because it exposed the continued vulnerability of Nepal's buildings after 1934.

events.title: Eaarthquake, Flooding, and Landslide
events.detail: Natural calamities marked the year 1987 for Nepal. Worst was the loss of life and property caused by the earthquake on August 21(6.7 on the Richter scale) epicentred in Udayapur, which took 721 lives and injured 1,551 people. Followed by numerous aftershocks, the disaster devastated the economy, destroyed more than 66,000 houses-rendering almost half a million people homeless and knocked down 1,202 school buildings and 14 campus facilities throughout the eastern region of the country. The physical devastation extended to the city of Bhaktapur within the valley of Kathmandu itself. The 1988 earthquake caused enormous human and economic losses, with property damage exceeding $200 million, disrupting development planning and requiring major relief efforts. Within weeks, excessive rains created heavy flooding and landslides that destroyed crops and other property, swept away thousands of head of livestock, and killed almost 300 people in the central and western regions that had previously been spared by the earthquake. Most notable of all was the event of 20 September 1988, when a huge rockslide occurred in the Darbang region of Myagdi. The landslide killed 109 people and buried all the houses in the right bank of the river.

events.title: Marich Man Singh Shrestha Became Hardliner
events.detail: Initially associated with attempts to make the Panchayat system more democratic and responsive, Shrestha increasingly appeared to move toward the authoritarian/right-wing wing of the Panchayat establishment. Prime Minister Marich Man Singh Shrestha reshuffled his cabinet three times. The decisive moment came in October, when he gave important ministries to conservative hardliners shortly after dismissing a proposed no-confidence motion against his government. Shrestha was successful in applying enough pressure upon the chairman of the National Panchayat and the Panchayat Policy and Evaluation Committee, Navaraj Subedi, to effectively suppress the resolution. In particular, it contravened the provisions of the Constitution as well as the directives of King Birendra, who has gone on record on several occasions in declaring that the prime minister must remain responsible to the National Panchayat.

events.title: Ganesh Man Singh Declared The 'demise' of NC
events.detail: In a formal interview with Saptahik Bimarsha, Ganesh Man Singh admitted that: "I was under the impression that the people were on our side. We thought that people would accept whatever we told them." Referring to poor performance during local Panchayat elections in which the banned party members had participated, he declared that it was "difficult even to find competent candidates. It was clear that we were deluding ourselves. We were entertaining the illusion of being a strong party because we had not had to face anyone . . . our committees in seventy districts were confined to paper." Because the party was banned, it never had to regularly test its popularity through competitive elections. Consequently, its leaders could maintain the belief that they represented the overwhelming majority without having contemporary evidence to prove it. The 1987 local elections shattered that assumption. The party therefore entered a period of strategic and organizational soul-searching.

events.title: Marsyangdi Hydropower Station Built
events.detail: The 69 MW Marsyangdi Hydropower Project in Tanahu District was inagurated in 1989. It was financed by World Bank Germany Kuwait Saudi and ADB at a cost of US$22 million. It is run-of-the-river hydropower plant which is still in operation.

events.title: Prachanda became General Secretary of Communist Party of Nepal-Mashal
events.detail: In 1986 Mohan Baidya was acting as General Secretary of the CPN (Mashal) when he called for an armed uprising against King Birendra. These attempts were ultimately unsuccessful leading to the arrest of several revolutionaries known as the Sector Incident. It saw Baidya face severe internal criticism culminating in his resignation and replacement with Pushpa Kamal Dahal.

events.title: India-Nepal Blockade
events.detail: Reasons: Among the irritants that may have motivated the Indian government action was a mid-1988 Nepal decision on Chinese arms purchases and the levying of a 55% tariff on Indian goods entering Nepal. The tariff violated the prevailing trade practice between the two countries and resulted in a price increase for some essential consumer goods, which irritated the price conscious Nepali consumer as well as the Indians. One other matter that aggravated the Nepal-India tension was Nepal's new law requiring non-Nepalese, including Indians, to have work permits. This arrangement was first introduced in 1987 and was stepped up in 1989. According to one reputed Nepali weekly, the issue was brought to the attention of the Nepalese foreign minister by his Indian counterpart on March 6th during the latter's visit to Kathmandu. Consequences: When the treaties expired without agreement, India declared that there was no longer a legal basis for normal trade and transit arrangements. It closed 13 of Nepal's 15 border transit points, leaving Raxaul and Jogbani open for essential goods such as medicines, baby food, and cement. Under international law a landlocked country has a right to only one transit route to the sea, thus, leaving two open was a gesture of Indian magnanimity. This also allowed New Delhi to deny that it was blockading Nepal. Nonetheless, the message, according to an Indian government spokesman was: "Be prepared to reciprocate if you want special privileges." Pressure continued to be further intensified. Government's Efforts: The government then started planning ways to end the blockade. Firewood was distributed at a subsidised price, and so were electric rice cookers and electricity. Nepal brought in fuel from Bangladesh and planned to bring in more from Tibet. The government prepared to import 50 per cent of the fuel from a third country and initiated the establishment of a stock tank in Panchkhal. World Bank and other donor agencies agreed to provide loans at a minimal interest rate. Government also made a secret plan was to bring in the oil pipeline from China till Xigatse in the first phase, Lhasa in second phase and Panchkhal in the third phase. After India discovered Nepal’s plan, it proposed to build a pipeline till Amlekhgunj, but the government rejected the offer. On March 31, an agreement allowing Nepal to obtain third-country petroleum through Indian infrastructure expired and was not renewed, creating a severe fuel shortage. In June, Nepal lost access to warehouse facilities at Calcutta port. India tightened controls at the remaining transit points and refused to provide railway wagons for Nepal-Bangladesh trade. Smuggling consequently increased sharply. The blockade severely affected Nepal's industries. Shortages of raw materials forced about half of Pokhara's industrial units and the Himal Cement Factory to suspend production, while power shortages reduced output at Everest Paper Mills. Biratnagar Jute Mills cut shifts and accumulated Rs. 51.6 million in unsold goods after India's 145% import duty crippled exports. Despite seeking government assistance, the mill eventually suspended production in September 1989. October 5, 1989, Nepali Foreign Minister Shailendra Kumar Upadhyaya commented at some length in the General Assembly on Nepal's situation. Upadhyaya did not directly mention India but his inferences were clear enough, for example, when he referred to the difficulties faced by landlocked countries "especially if actions taken by transit countries result in the denial or delay of unrestricted transit." Chinese Assistance: After India imposed an economic blockade, China provided limited but important assistance. Chinese aircraft initially transported about 300 tons of petroleum, followed by another 300 tons by road. By May, China began supplying fuel and food through Tibet, although Chinese fuel was expensive because of transportation costs. China also provided free salt. Additional border passes were opened for local trade, and China continued development assistance, including a $13.6 million grant in 1989 for infrastructure projects. During Premier Li Peng's visit to Kathmandu in November, China explicitly expressed support for Nepal's independence and sovereignty and gently urged India to be more "generous" toward Nepal. However, China's support had clear limits. China was itself facing severe economic and political turmoil in 1989, including the deterioration of relations with the West. It also did not want a major confrontation with India, particularly as Sino-Indian relations were beginning to improve. Geographic limitations also meant China could not realistically replace India's economic role. Importantly, China did not actively raise Nepal's case at the United Nations despite Nepal's attempts to internationalize the issue. Beijing ultimately encouraged Kathmandu to negotiate with India rather than prolong the confrontation. End of Blockade: Situation immediately eased after the success of the People's Movement. Later, in June, Krishna Prashad Bhattarai visited India for high-level talks with Indian Prime Minister V.P. Singh. New Delhi agreed to a separate trade and transit treaty as demanded by Katmandu and Nepal pledged to stop buying arms from Beijing taking into account India’s security concerns. Nepal also ended work-permit restrictions on Indian nationals.

events.title: NC's Opposition to Blockade And National Revival
events.detail: Opposition banned parties NC and Leftists potrayed it as government's failure. Ganesh Man Singh called for the dissolution of the existing Panchayat cabinet and formation of a national government including the NC, leftists, and Panchayat representatives to negotiate with India, arguing that the existing government lacked sufficient legitimacy. In September NC organized highly successful National Awakening Week in which 3500 party members were arrested including Ganesh Man Singh. Singh subsequently announced plans for a broader movement demanding an interim government, and multiparty elections. He was arrested on November 30 for advocating these demands. NC had formed a long overdue central committee this year. It met in Kathmandu on November 5-7 and passed a political resolution stating unambiguously that the party remained firm on the principle of attaining "democratic socialism" through the medium of parliamentary democracy under the constitutional leadership of the king. The committee decided to hold a national party conference in Kathmandu beginning on January 18, 1990, to decide the date and nature of the new movement.

events.title: King's Diplomatic Efforts to End Blockade
events.detail: King Birendra made several foreign trips such as 9th summit of NAM at Belgrade in September; 5-days visit to Czechoslovakia and Finland; visit to France Denmark and Rhodes in October. It is noted that in his meeting with French President he complained about India's blockade. Pakistani FM visited Nepal in June Bangladeshi PM visisted for five day in September and Chinese PM Li Peng visisted in November. At IMF and World Bank meetings too Nepal raised its tarade dispute. At the end of the years two things were evident Nepal did not get the support from international commmunity it expected and nepal wouldn't subbmit to Indian pressure that early.

events.title: Mainstream CPN i.e. CPN (Marxist-Leninist)'s Fourth National Convention
events.detail: After the deposition of CP Mainali and replacement with Jhala Nath Khanal the process of reform of CPN (ML) accelerated further in the Fourth Convention. With moderate Madan Bhandari elected general secretary, the party shifted it's ideological line toward embracing competitive multi-party politics. This convention marked a historic departure from the party's previous strategy of armed agrarian uprising and championed the idea of a unified mass movement alongside other democratic political groups. Barre Sangharsha Samuha and Nepal Workers and Peasants Organisation (D.P. Singh) had also merged into the party by 1986.

events.title: Revolutions of 1989 in Eastern Europe And Fall of Berlin Wall
events.detail: By the 1970s–80s, many Eastern European economies suffered from low productivity, shortages, debt, technological backwardness and declining living standards compared with Western Europe. Governments could no longer easily claim that socialism was delivering superior prosperity. Mikhail Gorbachev, when he became Soviet leader in 1985, introduced Glasnost (openness) and Perestroika (restructuring) and explicitly abandoned the Brezhnev Doctrine, meaning the USSR would no longer use military force to keep satellite states communist. Poland: In 1980, the Polish trade union Solidarity, led by Lech Wałęsa, became a mass movement challenging communist rule. The government eventually imposed martial law in 1981, but Solidarity survived underground. By 1989, the communist government was weakened enough to negotiate. The Round Table Talks between the government and opposition resulted in partially free elections. The opposition won overwhelmingly. A non-communist government emerged. This was enormously significant because it demonstrated a communist government could lose power without a Soviet invasion or a civil war. Berlin Wall: The "Monday Demonstrations" in East Germany grew rapidly, with hundreds of thousands of people in cities like Leipzig demanding civil rights, freedom of speech, and the right to travel. On November 9, 1989, East German spokesman Günter Schabowski was handed a draft of new, relaxed travel regulations right before a live broadcast. Unprepared, Schabowski mistakenly announced that citizens could cross the border immediately. Millions saw the broadcast and rushed to the checkpoints. Lacking clear instructions and outnumbered by the peaceful crowd, guards at the Bornholmer Straße crossing chose to open the gates rather than use lethal force. The Berlin Wall fell. Czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia had been communist since the 1948 Communist coup on democratic government. It had also experienced a major reform movement in 1968, the Prague Spring, when Alexander Dubček tried to create "socialism with a human face." The Soviet Union crushed that movement with military intervention. On 17 November 1989, a student demonstration in Prague commemorating a student killed by the Nazis in 1939 turned into an anti-communist protest. Police violently dispersed the demonstration. This became the spark. Rather than frightening people into silence, the crackdown produced larger demonstrations. The opposition created the Civic Forum, led by playwright and dissident Václav Havel. Slovakia developed a parallel movement called Public Against Violence. On 28 November, the Communist Party announced that it would abandon its monopoly on political power. By December, a transitional government had been formed. And on 29 December 1989, Václav Havel, a former political prisoner and dissident, became president. It was called Velvet Revolution for being remarkably peaceful and nonviolent. Romania: Its communist dictator Nicolae Ceaușescu had ruled since 1965 and had developed one of the most repressive regimes in Eastern Europe.In December 1989, authorities attempted to evict a Hungarian-speaking Protestant pastor, László Tőkés, who had become critical of the regime. People gathered to protect him. The demonstration became an anti-government protest. Security forces opened fire. News of the violence spread, and protests erupted across Romania. On 21 December, Ceaușescu organized a mass rally in Bucharest expecting the usual enthusiastic crowd. Instead, the crowd began booing and chanting against him. The event was broadcast live on television. For millions of Romanians, it was extraordinary: they could see that the dictator was losing control in real time. On 22 December, Ceaușescu and his wife Elena fled Bucharest by helicopter. They were captured and a military tribunal convicted them and executed the same day. Fighting continued around Bucharest because parts of the security forces remained loyal to the regime. Hundreds of people were killed. Bulgaria: The country had been ruled by Todor Zhivkov since 1954, making him one of the longest-serving communist leaders in Europe. But by 1989, the communist system was under pressure from economic problems, Gorbachev's reforms, and the collapse of neighboring communist regimes. On 10 November 1989, one day after the Berlin Wall fell, Zhivkov was removed from power by members of his own Communist Party. The Communist Party subsequently began negotiating with opposition groups and gradually allowed political pluralism, free elections, freedom of association, and constitutional reform. In 1990, the Communist Party renamed itself the Bulgarian Socialist Party and participated in multiparty elections. Albania: Albania was probably the most isolated communist country in Europe. Its dictator Enver Hoxha had ruled from 1944 until his death in 1985. After Hoxha's death, Ramiz Alia became leader. As protests intensified in 1990, the Communist Party eventually accepted multiparty politics. In December 1990, the Democratic Party was founded, ending the Communist Party's monopoly. By 1992, the opposition Democratic Party won the elections and Sali Berisha became president.

events.title: United Left Front Formed
events.detail: The Samyukta Bam Morcha was officially formed on January 15, 1990, when seven communist and left-wing factions united to mount a joint opposition against the absolute monarchy and the Panchayat system. The fornt consisted CPN (Marxist-Leninist), Nepal Workers and Peasants Party, CPN (Fourth Convention), CPN (Marxist), CPN (Burma), CPN (Manandhar), and CPN (Amatya) led by Sahana Pradhan (leader of the CPN-Marxist). They formed a tactical alliance with NC to launch the 1990 People's Movement.

events.title: NC Calls for The First People's Movement
events.detail: NC held party conference in Jan 18 1990 calling upon all political parties to participate in movement against the Panchayat calling for interim government and then multi-party elections. Also present was all-party delegation from India led by Chandra Shekhar at Ganesh Man Singh's residence in Chaksibari. He also delivered an impactful speech that the royal Panchayat government viewed it as a radical provocation. Officials immediately marched to his hotel room at The Kathmandu Sheraton and handed him an official protest letter, accusing him of dangerous foreign meddling and attempting to "incite a violent atmosphere" in Nepal. The conference decided to launch non-violent pro-democracy movenement on February 18. This was a direct, symbolic challenge to the regime, as February 18 was celebrated by the state as official "Panchayat Day."

events.title: First People's Movement
events.detail: NC and United Left Front started the movenent. In the eve of the movement government arrested national leaders of NC and ULF on Feb 17 and banned all opposition newspapers. Late in Month police fired on demonstration in Bhaktapur in which 12 died. Kathmandu Banda was announced for March 2 and other districts followed suites. In midst of confusion a high-level Indian delegation came to discuss trade and transit issue. On the eve of its visist the foreign minister SK Upadhaya resigned from his position citing differences with PN on protest handeling. Members of delegation returned home after staying in hotel for 3 days. A week later palace announced cabinet ressufle introducing some hardliners which alienated moderators. Soon professional groups supported the movement and also it got tacit supportf rom bureaucrats. On April 5 Army had to be called to control communist demonstrations in Patan which resukted in some death. The next day 2 lakhs people marched to palace where police again resorted to firing resulting more deaths. In efforts to distance itself from government the King dismissed PM Marich Man Singh and appointed Lokendra Bahadur Chand to negotiate with opposition. While talks were underway a mob surrounded the buildings of negotiations demanading immediate dissolution of the cabinet. Chand's car was smashed and the building was stoned while police watched helplessly. The next day palace announced the withdrawl of the ban on political parties and the movement was called off. The King dismissed the Chand government and invited Krishna Prasad Bhattarai to form interim governemnt. Interim government has 11 members 4 from NC 3 from ULF 2 from human rights groups and 2 nominated by King. After the interim government was formed, a major struggle emerged over who would control the constitution making process: the King or the elected political forces.

events.title: Lokendra Bahadur Chand
events.detail: 2nd Term

events.title: Rastriya Prajatantra Party Formed
events.detail: The RPP was formed by the ruling elite of the Panchayat era on 29 May 1990. The party split in the same year after another group also registered itself with the Election Commission. The two parties had the same name, ideology and statute but different flags and election symbols. The two parties, one led by Surya Bahadur Thapa and the other led by Lokendra Bahadur Chand, contested the 1991 elections. The two parties won four seats between them with Chand's party winning three seats and Thapa's party winning one seat. Following their performance at the elections the two parties agreed to merge into a single Rastriya Prajatantra Party on 8 February 1992.

events.title: Constitution of the Kingdom of Nepal 2047 Promulgated
events.detail: King insisted on not dissolving National Panchayat and introduce change but after government's pressure king disspolved it and transferred all legislative right to the cabinet. Palace made one last attempt to assert its authority by naming members of Constituency Recommendation Committee (CRC) under Justice Bishwanath Upadhaya without cabinet approval but when Bhattarai exerted pressure by threatening to resign the palace dissolved the CRC and named a new one proposed by cabinet again under Justice Bishwanath Upadhaya. The episode strengthened demands that sovereignty should explicitly belong to the people, rather than the Constitution being simply a "gift" from the King. A new nine-member CRC, again chaired by Justice Upadhyaya, was formed with greater consultation with political parties. Its members travelled around Nepal and collected public and political suggestions. The CRC submitted its draft to King on Sept 10 which he delayed for two month within which the King got time to suddenly produced his own draft, which significantly restored royal powers. The Palace Draft claimed that executive, legislative and judicial powers were vested in the king, gave him broad emergency powers, created a Raj Parishad under his control, and weakened the principle that the king acted on ministerial advice. It also changed the language on sovereignty from simply “sovereignty is vested in the Nepali people” to “sovereignty ... including His Majesty”, effectively trying to preserve the king's traditional political authority. The interim government, Nepali Congress, Left parties, student groups and civil society strongly rejected the draft. Prime Minister Krishna Prasad Bhattarai even offered to resign. Mass protests and the threat of renewed political unrest forced the palace to back down. After negotiations between the king, Congress leaders and Constitution Commission members, agreement was reached on the core principles. Sovereignty: Made the people, not the king, sovereign. Religion: Nepal continued remaining Hindu Kingdom, but the demand for secular state resulted in the granting of a right to all sects and denominations to run and maintain their own institutions. Language: While Nepali still remained only official language, all languages spoken as mother-tongues in the various parts of Nepal were identified as national languages of Nepal. It also allowed every community shall to run schools up to the primary level in their mother-tongues. Citizenship: Every provision from 1964 Citizenship Act upheld except the language requirement as all Nepali mother tongues were recognized as national languages. Requirement for Constitutional Positions: In order to be eligible for appointment to constitutional positions under this Constitution a person must either be a citizen of Nepal by birth or descent or be a person who as a naturalised citizen has resided in Nepal for at least ten years. Executive: Eecutive authority in Nepal is vested in the king and the Council of Ministers, and the constitution makes it clear that all functions discharged by the king (other than those explicitly stated by the constitution to be discretionary) should be discharged on the advice and with the consent of the Council of Ministers. Legislative: The legislature is to consist of three elements: the king, a House of Representatives consisting of 205 members each elected from a district constituency; and a National Assembly consisting of 60 members of whom 10 will be royal nominees i.e. reputed persons who have made distinguished contributions to national life, 35 (including at least three women) will be elected by the HoR, and 15 will be elected from the five development regions through an electoral college system. The term of the HoR will be five years, while the National Assembly will be a permanent body with one-third of its members retiring every two years. Judiciary: The constitution provides for a three-tier judiciary (previously four) i.e. a Supreme Court, Appellate Courts, and District Courts. The chief justice is to be appointed on the recommendation of a constitutional council (previously King), other justices of the Supreme Court on the recommendation of a judicial council (previously King). Administration: The zonal tier—which sat above districts as part of the 14 administrative zones i.e. Anchal Panchayat—was completely abolished. Gaun Panchayat was converted to VDC and Nagar Panchayat to Municipality. It allowed VDCs to be divided into 9 wards. Similarly, there was a system that allowed up to 35 wards to be formed into metropolises, sub-metropolitan cities, and municipalities. Chairperson/Mayor, vice-chairperson/deputy-mayor, one ward member from each ward were directly elected for both. Each members had a tenure of 5 years. At that time, the number of VDCs had reached 3913 and the number of municipalities had reached 58. The 75 district panchayats were reformed and renamed into District Development Committees. All the newly elected Chairpersons/Vice-Chairpersons of VDCs and Mayors/Deputy Mayors of municipalities within that district formed a massive regional body called the District Council. The district was divided into 9 to 13 sub-regions (Ilakas). Members of the District Council elected one executive DDC member from each Ilaka. The District Council also voted to elect the overall DDC Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson. To ensure connection with federal politics, all Members of Parliament (MPs) representing that specific district automatically held ex-officio seats on the committee. DDC worked as the chief executive body for local governance and regional planning at the district level. Elected DDC members served a term of 5 years. Political Parties: Almost total freedom to form political parties. However, a party must conform to certain rules if it is to be permitted to stand in national elections. It must not restrict membership on the basis of religion, community, caste, or region; its constitution and regulations must be democratic; its executive officebearers must be elected at least once every five years; and at least 5% of its candidates in elections must be women. Emergency Powers: Article 115 of the 1990 Constitution instead said that an emergency could be declared only in situations such as war, external attack, armed rebellion, serious threat to sovereignty/security, and extreme economic disruption. And crucially, the emergency proclamation had to be submitted to the House of Representatives for approval within three months. If the House did not approve it by the required majority, it ceased to operate. When Gyanendra assumed direct control in 2005, he invoked Article 115 which essentially allowed the king to issue orders to remove difficulties in implementing the Constitution. Gyanendra's government used this provision alongside the emergency declaration and other constitutional claims to justify the takeover. Amendments: Bills seeking to repeal or amend provisions of the constitution may be tabled in either house, providing they do not "contravene the spirit of the Preamble." Such amendments require a two-thirds majority and the king's approval, although the king must approve such bills if they are presented to him a second time. Army: King remained the Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Army but the National Security Council, headed by the Prime Minister, was responsible for major decisions concerning the army's mobilization and operations. The Commander-in-Chief was appointed by the king on the recommendation of the Prime Minister.

events.title: Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre) Formed
events.detail: Formed from the merger of Communist Party of Nepal (Mashal i.e. मशाल), Communist Party of Nepal (Fourth Convention), Proletarian Workers Organisation, and Communist Party of Nepal (Janamukhi); Soon thereafter a group led by Baburam Bhattarai and Shital Kumar who had left Communist Party of Nepal (Masal) joined the party. The party was led by Pushpa Kamal Dahal Prachanda. In 1994, a group led by Baburam Bhattarai and Pushpa Kamal Dahal broke away from CPN (UC) and formed a parallel CPN-UC which took the name Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) in 1996.
