events.title: Samyukta Janamorcha Nepal Formed
events.detail: The front was set up as the open mass front of the Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre) for election. Baburam Bhattarai was made its chairman. Prachanda and Baburam did not personally run as a candidate in the election. However, unlike Prachanda who operated strictly underground, Bhattarai played a highly visible, public leadership role in the election.

events.title: CPN (UML) Formed
events.detail: CPN (Marxist-Leninist) led by Madan Bhandari merged with the CPN (Marxist) led by Man Mohan Adhikari to form Communist Party of Nepal (Unified Marxist–Leninist) ahead of the 1991 general election. Man Mohan Adhikari served as the party's first chairman.

events.title: Citizen Investment Trust Established
events.detail: The ⁠CIT, known locally as Nagarik Lagani Kosh, was established as an autonomous statutory body under the Citizen Investment Trust Act, 1991. It is a government-backed institution helps government employees, private-sector worker or even NRNs to save money tax-free, invests those funds in major national projects, and returns the profits as retirement benefits. Contributors can also borrow up to 80% of their accumulated balance as low-interest loans.

events.title: 2048 General Election
events.detail: The new Constitution significantly expanded elected representation. Existing administrative districts became electoral districts, with 1–6 constituencies per district depending on population. The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18, prompting a major voter-registration exercise. Of 44 registered parties, 20 contested the election, alongside 397 independent candidates. Political Ideologies: Nepali Congress (NC) promoted centrist parliamentary democracy and democratic socialism, while increasingly accepting the emerging global trend toward economic liberalization and a mixed economy with a substantial private-sector role. UML called for a more radical and progressive form of democracy and deeper political transformation. Baburam-led Samyukta Janamorcha advocated more radical alternatives, including a people's republic. Nepal Sadbhavana Party emphasized equality and ending discrimination against Madhesis/Terai communities. RPP-Chand attacked the interim government over inflation, corruption and perceived concessions to India, while RPP-Thapa emphasized its governing experience. Even communist parties increasingly accepted the private sector and multinational investment, reflecting the collapse of communist regimes in Eastern Europe and the broader global movement toward economic openness. The NC itself had moved considerably away from its 1959 economic position toward a mixed economy. An important concern was the increasing politicization of the civil service, with government employees openly participating in politics. Nevertheless, an international observation team of 64 members concluded that the election was broadly “fair, free, and open.” Approximately 7.3 million voters, or 65.15% of registered voters, participated. Election Result: NC-110; UML-69; Samyukta Janamorcha-9; Nepal Sadbhavana Party-6, NDP (Chand)-3, NDP (Thapa)-1; Workers' & Peasants' Party-2 Krishna Prasad Bhattarai: Madan Bhandari defeated the incumbent PM Krishna Prasad Bhattarai in the election. Madan Bhandari had won the election by a margin of 751 votes. While Bhandari got 27,372 votes, Bhattarai got 26,621 votes. Madan Bhandari had immense popularity and sharp oratory skills, who captivated urban voters with his democratic Marxist vision. Additionally, Bhattarai faced quiet internal sabotage (antarghat) from rival factions within his own Nepali Congress party. Ultimately, his demanding role as interim Prime Minister left him too little time for grassroots campaigning to counter Kathmandu's strong anti-establishment wave. Even though Madan Bhandari won the election, he was not sure that he would win easily. That is why he also filed his candidacy in Kathmandu-5 and actually won both. Later he relinquished Kathmandu-5 seat. Girija Prasad Koirala became the PM.

events.title: Girija Prasad Koirala
events.detail: 1st term; Majority

events.title: Civil Administration Post-multi-party System
events.detail: Politicization of Bureaucracy During the People's Movement: As the movement was reaching its peak, the Supreme Commander of the People's Movement, Ganeshman Singh, called on the employees to join the movement to overthrow the Panchayat. Following Ganeshman Singh's call, the employees gathered in the open courtyard of the tennis court in Babar Mahal and announced their participation in the movement. During the French Revolution, parliamentarians gathered on the tennis court and took an oath not to leave until democracy was brought. This is called the 'Tennis Court Oath'. Employees in Nepal also started the 'Tennis Court' movement. After the end of the Panchayat system, some employees formed the 'Nepal NIjamati Karmachari Sangathan'. As soon as the interim government was formed, employees and teachers started a movement with their demands in Baishakh 1947. The movement ended after an agreement was reached to fulfill the demands within 15 days of the promulgation of the constitution. The new government was preparing for elections. Employees who were supposed to serve in the elections started a movement from Falgun 25, 1947. The teachers' movement also started. At that time, the organization that was carrying out the employee agitation was close to the CPN-UML. To 'counter' it, the Nepali Congress made another big mistake by forming the 'Civil Employees Association' with its supporters on Falgun 12, 2047. UML General Secretary Madan Bhandari had publicly commented that he had two 'bombs' (employees and students) in his hands and that if they exploded, the government would be overthrown within a few months. Not only UML MPs but also the very gentle leader Manmohan Adhikari were taken out in the street procession of the employees. The government started a cycle of repression, saying that politics had entered the employees' movement. At that time, many employees were retired. Later, after the UML minority government was formed, some were reinstated. Black Friday: Girija Prasad Koirala's government retired a large number of employees who were about to reach retirement age all at once. Since the announcement was made on a Friday, some call it 'Black Friday'. On the one hand, the government was suspicious of the administrators who had joined during the Panchayat period and had been active in suppressing the movement. On the other hand, there was dissatisfaction with the employee movement that had begun soon after the government was formed. Therefore, on the grounds of purging the administration, providing opportunities to the youth, and speeding up administrative work, approximately 300 employees who had completed 20 years of service were retired on Kartik 21, 2049 BS. Due to the negligence of the five minister panel who prepared the list of retirees, some employees who had not even completed twenty years of service were retired. The retirement was later stopped after the mistake was discovered. This decision was challenged in court and most of those who were retired were reinstated. On the same day, the Civil Service Regulations were amended and the retirement age was reduced from 60 to 58 years and service period of 30 years was set. As a result, approximately 3,000 experienced employees were retired at once. While giving retirement like that, pension facility was given on the assumption that one had worked till the age of 60. Due to this, due to the shortage of experienced staff, even secretaries from the Chief Secretary to the Secretaries had to be hired on contract. After this administrative accident, politicians seriously tried to correct it. The discussion on the Civil Service Act 2049 bill in Parliament focused more on the security of employees. The pamphlet system was abolished with the agreement of all parties. This was a major milestone in the field of administration. The 2013 Act on Civil Service Administration can be considered the first milestone, the 2032 provision banning political appointments in the administration the second, and the legal provision abolishing the pachar system the third. Party-based colonization by the UML: After the 2051 BS by-election, the UML formed a minority government. That government made major changes to high-ranking employees. Since the pachar system had been abolished, there was no legal basis for retiring employees. Therefore, the UML government sent secretaries who were said to be close to the Congress to the reserve. Those who had been removed by the Congress government and reinstated by the court were given important ministries. It also 'UMLized' the administration by transferring and bringing employees close to it to other positions. Employees from other services and groups were assigned to important revenue positions and as Chief District Officers. The civil service organizations close to the UML played a major role in these administrative changes. This started the tradition of the party-affiliated employee organizations dominating the administration. Politics further infiltrated the bureaucracy. To the extent of politicization, a probationary branch officer of the judicial service was made the CDO of Panchthar. One of the employees who was posted as the CDO was nowhere to be found in the civil service. Later, a person with the same name from the Curriculum Development Center was said to be the same person. Overall, the UML tried to 'party colonization' in the civil service. The administration, which had been shaken by the Congress's pamphlets, was completely shaken by the UML's saruwa and kaaj terror. Administrative Tsunami: The then King Gyanendra Shah, after assuming direct rule on Magh 19, 2061, initiated extensive changes in the administration. The royal regime initially began transferring, promoting, and retaining special ranks in the civil service. Eight secretaries were retained and eight joint secretaries were made acting secretaries. The Civil Service Act, which did not allow for more than a month in the reserve, was amended through an ordinance to allow for an indefinite period. Later, a royal commission was formed to harass those who were not liked. Tika Dutta Niraula, who was on the reserve, was detained in the Melamchi case. Dinesh Chandra Pyakurel, who was on the reserve, was shortened by the royal commission. Due to this tension, he committed suicide. Shashikant Mainali, Vijay Bhattarai, Lilaraj Sharma, and others retired from the reserve. The royal government amended the Local Administration Act and established tight control over the lower-level administration by politically appointing regional administrators and zonal administrators. These administrators were like loose bulls. They intimidated employees. The zonal administrator of Sagarmatha even physically attacked the local development officer and the chief district officer. The entire administration was terrified by the tyranny of inspection teams, known as Daudahas. As soon as the king became active, in 2059, when the ordinance on inspection teams was brought, an attempt was made to include a provision for snatching employees through pamphlets. The stance of the then Chief Secretary stopped this. Trade Union Attack on Merit: There was also a good participation of employees in the second people's movement of 2062/63. After the success of the people's movement, the employees' unions started demanding additional benefits as 'bonus' for participating in movement. They started putting pressure on the government to get trade union rights and salary increases. In 2064 BS, the Civil Service Act was amended to grant trade union rights to employees. As a result, employee unions began to open up on a party-by-party basis. Even some countries that considered themselves very liberal and democratic had not become party states to 'Convention 87 of the International Labor Organization'. Nepal, however, had already ratified it without understanding much. While employee unions should be focused on their own services and security, they seem to be more interested in transfers, promotions, and hiring. Some corporations even have a ridiculous system of having union representatives on the recruitment committees. Positives: After the Second People's Movement, the Good Governance Act-2064 was promulgated. This act has made provisions for clarity of the scope of work of ministers and secretaries, provision of platforms for voicing the voice of the people, and evaluation of employees. Similarly, the Right to Information Act-2064 was promulgated. It made provisions for making the functioning of public bodies transparent. The Constitution of Nepal has placed the work of filling posts in security agencies and organized organizations in addition to the civil service under the jurisdiction of the Public Service Commission. This is a major reform. It has made a very important provision by including public administration policy in the policy related to politics and governance. Civil Service Act-2049 was amended to provide reservation for 45 percent of posts in this service for women, indigenous people, Madhesi people, Dalits, people with disabilities, and backward areas. After this, this provision was also applied to security agencies and organized organizations.

events.title: Dissolution of Yugoslavia Began
events.detail: Tito died in 1980. He had held Yugoslavia together through a delicate balance with strong enough federation to keep the country together and enough autonomy for each republic to prevent Serbian/Croatian/Slovenian domination. After his death, collective leadership replaced him. But the system was much harder to operate because the republics increasingly pursued their own interests. During the 1980s Yugoslavia suffered high foreign debt, inflation, unemployment, falling living standards, and regional inequality. The richer northern republics, particularly Slovenia and Croatia, increasingly resented transferring resources to poorer regions. The 1974 Constitution had given enormous autonomy to Yugoslavia's six republics and Serbia's two autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina. Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia in the late 1980s and used Serbian grievances, particularly over Kosovo, to build political support. Through the "anti-bureaucratic revolution," Serbia reduced the autonomy of Kosovo, and Vojvodina. This gave Serbia much greater influence within the eight-member federal presidency. Slovenia and Croatia saw this as evidence that Yugoslavia was becoming increasingly dominated by Serbia. Slovenia and Croatia increasingly wanted a loose federation/confederation in which republics had substantial sovereignty. Serbia under Milošević increasingly wanted a stronger Yugoslav state and rejected sovereignty. Croatia and Slovenia argued that the republics have the right to leave Yugoslavia. Meanwhile Serbian leaders argued that if Croatia leaves, the Serbs living inside Croatia also have the right to decide whether they want to leave Croatia. In August 1990, Serbian rebels in Croatia began establishing control over parts of Serb-populated territory, including blocking roads. The Croatian government regarded this as rebellion against the Croatian state. Serbs regarded it as protection against an increasingly nationalist Croatian government. Slovenia and Croatia: On 25 June 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. That was the decisive escalation. The Yugoslav People's Army (JNA) attempted to enforce federal authority in Slovenia, producing the Ten-Day War. Slovenia's relatively homogeneous population and limited Serbian presence made the conflict short. Croatia had a large ethnic Serb minority. Backed by Belgrade and the JNA, these "Krajina Serbs" revolted, setting up their own breakaway state to remain unified with Serbia. Full-scale war erupted. Yugoslav forces subjected the city of Vukovar to a devastating three-month siege, flattening it, and shelled the historic coastal city of Dubrovnik. By early 1992, Serb rebels controlled roughly one-third of Croatia. A UN-brokered ceasefire in January 1992 temporarily froze the frontlines, though the war would linger until 1995. Macedonia: In September 1991, the southernmost republic of Macedonia voted overwhelmingly for independence. Unlike Croatia or Bosnia, Macedonia managed to negotiate a peaceful withdrawal of the JNA, entirely avoiding the initial outbreaks of violence. Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bosnia and Herzegovina, the most ethnically mixed republic (composed of Bosniaks, Serbs, and Croats), held an independence vote in early March 1992. Bosnian Serbs boycotted the vote, but Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats voted 99% in favor of seceding. Armed conflict exploded immediately. Backed by the JNA, Bosnian Serb forces launched a brutal campaign of systematic "ethnic cleansing" to expel non-Serbs. In April 1992, Serb forces surrounded the capital city, starting the Siege of Sarajevo—which became the longest siege in modern military history. Global outrage peaked after horrific massacres, notably the July 1995 Srebrenica genocide where over 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were executed, and the repeated shelling of civilians at the Markale marketplace in Sarajevo. The initial UN peacekeeping mission lacked a strong mandate to use offensive force finally inviting NATO to intervene in order to avoid greater European war and refugee crisis. The Bosnian War ended in late 1995 through the Dayton Accords, a peace agreement brokered by the United States following intense military pressure and NATO airstrikes against Bosnian Serb forces. Initialed in Dayton, Ohio, and formally signed in Paris on December 14, 1995, the treaty preserved Bosnia and Herzegovina as a single sovereign country but divided it into two highly autonomous governing entities: the Bosniak-Croat majority Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-majority Republika Srpska. Kosovo: Kosovo Liberation Army formed in the mid-1990s to launch armed attacks against Serbian police and state officials.: Clashes intensified, resulting in hundreds of deaths and hundreds of thousands of displaced civilians amid reports of heavy-handed crackdowns by Serbian security forces. : After diplomatic efforts failed and atrocities mounted, NATO launched air strikes against military and strategic targets in Yugoslavia without a UN Security Council mandate. Later, Yugoslav forces agreed to withdraw from Kosovo in 1999. Following years of provisional governance, Kosovo formally declared its independence in 2008, a status recognized by many nations but disputed by Serbia. Montenegro and Serbia: Montenegro declared independence after a referendum in 2006, and Serbia declared independence the next day, dissolving the union entirely

events.title: Bhutanese Refugee Crisis
events.detail: Nepali-speaking people had migrated into southern Bhutan mainly from the 19th century onward, and many had been recognized as Bhutanese citizens under the 1958 Nationality Law. But from the late 1970s, the Bhutanese monarchy increasingly pursued a policy of creating a more homogeneous national identity based on Drukpa/Ngalop culture. They were alarmed at the prospect of their Nepali speaking population, who were now perhaps the largest ethnic group in Bhutan, taking control of the country as their fellow Nepali-speakers had done earlier in Sikkim. The government introduced increasingly restrictive citizenship rules in 1977 and 1985. A 1988 census in southern Bhutan classified large numbers of newpali-speaking Lhotshampas as illegal immigrants or non-citizens. At the same time, the government introduced the "one nation, one people" policy, including compulsory Drukpa dress and cultural practices and the removal of Nepali from the school curriculum. This produced enormous resentment among the Lhotshampas. In September–October 1990, mass demonstrations broke out in southern Bhutan demanding political and cultural rights. The government responded harshly: demonstrators were labelled ngolops ("anti-nationals"), thousands were arrested, and human-rights organizations documented torture, ill-treatment and other abuses. Starting July 1991 a formal refugee camp was officially established on the banks of the Mai Khola in Jhapa, initially holding just 235 people. Although India had a treaty right to exercise ‘guidance’ over Bhutanese foreign policy, India put no pressure on Bhutan to take the refugees back. In the 1990s, the number reached to 106,000 Bhutanese refugees settled in seven U.N. supervised camps in eastern Nepal. After several failed discussions aimed at repatriating the refugees to Bhutan, most of the refugees have now been resettled to other international destinations with the help of the UNHCR and the International Organization for Migration. Since the start of its Bhutanese refugee resettlement initiative in 2007 the UNHCR has relocated over 100,000 refugees. The United States accommodated over 84,000 of these refugees, with the rest moving to Australia, Canada, Norway, New Zealand, Denmark, the United Kingdom and The Netherlands. Today, there are 2 active Bhutanese refugee camps remaining in eastern Nepal, down from the 7 original camps established in the early 1990s. Mass third-country resettlement programs led to the consolidation and closure of five locations.

events.title: Tanakpur Agreement
events.detail: While PM Girija Prasad Koirala was on his first India trip, he signed Tanakpur Agreement allowing construction of the 577 meters long bund. In return, India agreed to provide 28.34 m/s cusecs of water annually with 10 million units of electricity. However, the issue led to political turmoil in Nepal. Critics argued that Nepal was "cheated" out of its fair share of natural wealth. While India gained a fully functional hydropower plant, Nepal was initially only promised a marginal 10 megawatts of electricity and 150 cusecs of water as a "goodwill gesture". Consequently, in October 1992, a new Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed in which India agreed to provide 20 million units of electricity in exchange for the 2.9 ha land. However, the issue was much serious. Prime Minister Koirala signed the deal as an informal "understanding" rather than a formal treaty. Under Article 126 of the 1990 Constitution of Nepal, any formal treaty concerning the distribution and utilization of natural resources required a two-thirds majority approval in Parliament. The main opposition party, CPN-UML, and public critics accused the government of deliberately mislabeling the treaty to avoid parliamentary oversight, knowing the ruling party lacked a two-thirds majority. In December 1992, the Supreme Court of Nepal validated the protestors' claims by officially ruling that the agreement was, in fact, a treaty that legally required parliamentary ratification.

events.title: India-Nepal Treaty of Trade 1991
events.detail: More Flexible Rules of Origin: Previous required 80% local-content but now it gave full duty-free access and exemption from quantitative restrictions for >80% case-by-case duty-free access for 55–80% up to 50% tariff concession and exemption from quantitative restrictions for 40-55%. Explicit Export Promotion Strategy: 90 Nepalese industrial products eligible for preferential entry into India.

events.title: Hydropower Development Policy and Electricity Act Inacted
events.detail: Before 1992 the state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) solely developed and managed the country's power plants. In 1992 the introduction of the Hydropower Development Policy and Electricity Act dismantled state monopolies welcoming Independent Power Producers (IPPs) and FDI to accelerate energy generation bridge supply gaps and modernize national infrastructure. Today all private commercial hydropower projects developed by IPPs operate under the BOOT (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer) model. This means every private developer must secure a generation license that strictly requires transferring the plant back to the state after a set period which is currently 50 years.

events.title: NC Eight General Convention
events.detail: Krishna Prasad Bhattarai; NC held its long due general convetion after the 1992 election in Jhapa where Acting President Krishna Prashad Bhattarai became the President of the party. Girija Prasad Koirala and Mahendra Narayan Nidhi were elected General Secretary.

events.title: Civil Servant Protests and 12 People Died
events.detail: After the 2046 BS movement, employees staged a nationwide movement demanding a salary increase. At that time, the interim government of Krishna Prasad Bhattarai had agreed that the government formed after the election would increase the salaries of employees. However, after the election, Girija Prasad Koirala's government said that the agreement would be invalid, and a nationwide movement broke out in protest. Koirala took an extremely firm line and a number of government employees linked to the UML, which had sympathised with the action, lost their jobs. In addition, Koirala was felt by many to have secured an insufficient share of electric power and water for Nepal in an agreement legalising India’s construction of a dam on Nepalese territory at Tanakpur on the Mahakali River. Street demonstrations against these policies, in which the UPF and Masal took the lead, turned violent on 6 April 1992, the second anniversary of the Darbar Marg shootings during thejanandolan. At least 12 people died in police firing, partly because both training and equipment were inadequate, but also possibly because individual policemen wanted revenge for the killing of some of their colleagues the previous year. The extreme left groups responded with a campaign calling for the government’s resignation. The UML needed to preserve its own credibility as the main force on the left but also to maintain the image of a responsible opposition. It therefore participated in protests against the killings but demanded only the resignation of the home minister, Sher Bahadur Deuba, not that of the entire government; it abandoned the campaign after Congress agreed to an inquiry into the shootings.

events.title: 2049 Local Elections
events.detail: Voting was held in 2030 VDCs and 11 municipalities under the first phase on 15 Jestha 2049 and in 1965 VDCs and 25 municipalities under the second phase on 18 Jestha. Thus, in both phases, elections were held for 3995 VDC chairpersons/vice-chairpersons and 35955 members and 36 mayors/deputy mayors and 522 members in municipalities. The ruling Nepali Congress capitalized on its momentum from the 1991 general elections, securing a comfortable majority of seats nationwide. CPN UNL came second while RPP failed to capture major ground, solidifying the public's shift toward democratic parties. As part of this sweeping victory, prominent democratic leader PL Singh from the Nepali Congress was elected as the Mayor of Kathmandu Metropolitan City.

events.title: Eighth Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 91.48 billion spent; ~80.6% implemented; 20 PEs privatized or liquidated; 2,450 km of roads constructed; private sector hydel policy introduced; Khimti and Bhote Koshi private hydro projects signed; mid-hill highway tracking began; first plan after the restoration of multi-party democracy; aggressive adoption of economic liberalization, open markets, and privatization; poverty alleviation made a primary plan objective; agriculture and irrigation received 25.8%; social services received 31.2%; transport and energy took 23.5%; achieved an impressive GDP growth rate of 4.9% against a 5.1% target; successfully drew significant foreign direct investment (FDI) into telecom, banking, and hydropower.

events.title: Revision to Trade Treaty
events.detail: During P.V Narasimha Rao's visit to Nepal Trade Treaty was revised granting Nepalese manufactured goods duty/quota-free access to the Indian market provided they contained a minimum of 50% Nepalese or Indian labor/materials.

events.title: CPN (UML)'s Fifth National Convention
events.detail: People’s Multiparty Democracy i.e. JaBaJa adopted; path of democratic communism defined; Man Mohan Adhikari became Chairman and Madan Bhandari became General Secretary adopting the line of multiparty competition under People’s Democracy and electing Madan Bhandari as General Secretary. In November 1993, veteran communist leader Tulsi Lal Amatya's group also merged with the party

events.title: Nepal's Exchange Rate 1993
events.detail: 100 INR= 160 NPR

events.title: Madan Bhandari's Jeep Accident And Protests
events.detail: Madan Bhandari and Jivraj Ashrit were travelling in a jeep which plunged into the Narayani River at Dasdhunga. A government inquiry accepted the driver’s version that he had lost control of the vehicle but managed to jump clear himself. The UML and the other Communist parties, however, alleged there had been an assassination plot and demanded both a fresh inquiry and Koirala’s resignation. In renewed street disturbances, police again opened fire with the loss of 24 lives. Extensive flooding throughout most of the country later in the summer helped lower the political temperature, and the UML again reached an agreement with Congress providing for a fresh investigation. The smaller leftist parties continued the agitation on their own for some time. No definite evidence of a conspiracy was ever found and it was all too common for vehicles to plunge off mountain roads. In 1997 a Supreme Court ruling confirmed that the deaths had been accidental and the driver, who had been imprisoned for causing death through negligence, was released the following year. After Madan handari died Madhav Kumar Nepal became the General Secretary.

events.title: SEBON and NEPSE Established
events.detail: The older Securities Exchange Center (SEC) was divided the old SEC's duties into two separate, specialized entities in 1993 to align with open-market standards. The SEBON was established in June 1993 as the regulator of securities market to take over all the oversight, policy-drafting, and investor-protection duties. Meanwhile NEPSE was established in Dec 1993 as the marketplace to take over the core trading functions, allowing independent private brokers to step onto the trading floor for the first time starting from Jan 1994.

events.title: Central Nepal Floods
events.detail: Triggered by an unprecedented cloudburst between July 19 and 21, 1993, the disaster unleashed catastrophic flash floods, massive landslides, and overwhelming debris flows. Driven by a meso-scale convective system, the disaster dropped an unprecedented 540 mm of rain within 24 hours—the highest 24-hour rainfall ever recorded in the country. It completely devastated the river basins of south-central Nepal, primarily affecting the Bagmati, East Rapti, and Kamala rivers. Kulekhani hydropower deposited extremely large amount of sediments that reduced one-fourth (4.8 million m3) of reservoir dead storage (12 million m3). The torrential rain impacted the Bagmati barrage in Karmaiya and triggered many landslides and flash floods. The disaster officially claimed the lives of 1,336 people and injured hundreds more. Over 500,000 individuals across half the country were severely affected, destroying nearly 30,000 homes. Total property and infrastructural losses were estimated at approximately NRs 4.9 billion.

events.title: Forest Act of 1993 Inacted
events.detail: Despite introduction of Master Plan for the Forestry Sector (MPFS) 1988 with vision of increasing partiicpation of communities and strenthening forestry institutions only about 2% of potential community forests had been handed over. After the restoration of multiparty democracy Government formally empowered Forest User Groups (FUGs). District Forest Officers (DFOs) received authority to form FUGs. hand over forests and provide technical support. The Forest Act 1993 became the legal foundation of modern community forestry. FUGs became autonomous legal bodies. They could own property manage forests and undertake business activities. It classified forests into government community protected leasehold religious and private forests. Forest Regulations 1995 established procedures for handing over forests to FUGs and defined rules for forest management harvesting and user group governance. National workshops (1993 1998 2004 2008 2014) further strengthened community forestry by promoting good governance poverty reduction inclusion of women and marginalized groups and sustainable forest management.

events.title: Sagarmatha Highway Partially Completed
events.detail: The 323 km Sagarmatha Highway (Lahan-Gaighat-Diktel Road) whose construction started in 1990 by Government of Nepal remains still incomplete. The Lahan-Gaighat section was completed in between 1992 and 1994. However the Gaighat-Diktel section remains unfinished as contract has been revoked multiple times in the past. Though the project suffered from budget-related issues in its initial years the project officials said that the budget is no longer an issue.

events.title: Privatization Act of Nepal Inacted
events.detail:
The ⁠Privatization Act 2050 (1994) is the core legal framework in Nepal designed to transfer state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to the private sector by the formation of Privatization Committe under Finance Minister. Initial privatizations of state-owned enterprises began earlier via cabinet executive orders in October 1992 before the formal act was passed. Discussions on privatization had begun in mid-80s when nepal embarked on IMF's SAP. Donor pressure, especially that of the World Bank, USAID, and UNDP, has been instrumental in accelerating Nepal’s privatization program since 1988. They did not only dictate the government to set up a "privatization cell" but also assisted to make feasibility study to suggest potential candidates for privatization. A privatization cell was established in the Ministry of Finance in December 1989 to plan and implement the privatization program. Accordingly, the government came up with an ambitious plan to sell off 12 enterprises in 12 months. Yet, this plan never materialized during the Panchayat days because the public response was very poor, and the Panchayat regime was facing pro-democracy protests. Many enterprises in the past were enjoying some kind of protective market. Bansbari Leather and Shoe Factory had a secured shoe market for the army and police personnel; Nepal Film Development Company had monopoly for documentruy and newsreels for government departments; Raw Hide Collection and Development Corporation had monopoly business of collecting raw hides; Nepal Bitumen and Barrel Industty had a secured bitumen market for Nepal Electricity Authority; Tobacco Development Company had secured market for Janakpur Cigarette Factory until 1986; Nepal Foundry Industry had monopoly supply rights in Water Supply and Sewerage Corporation, Nepal Electricity Authority and Nepal Teleconununication Corporation.

Methods of Privatization: Government of Nepal implemented its privatization policy through five different methods. It started privatisation by selling assets and business of three public enterprises. After 2000, the government mostly went for liquidation. That was partly because the government wanted to get rid of the bleeding enterprises as soon as possible. Similarly, liquidation would be easier to administer compared to other modalities. The government was blamed and heavily criticised for selling the state owned enterprises below their value; arguably this was the main reason for opting for liquidation and dissolution of the SoEs in the latter stages of privatisation. For instance, of the total 15 SoEs privatised between 2001 and 2006, 10 were liquidated or dissolved 1. Sale of Shares: The government transfered partial or complete ownership by selling its stock to private individuals, institutional investors, or the enterprise's employees. 2. Sale of Assets and Business: The government sold the entire operational entity, including land, buildings, machinery, and inventory, as a package deal to a private operator. 3. Lease of Land and Assets: The ownership of the properties remained with the state, but the physical infrastructure and the right to conduct business were leased to private firms for a set period. 4. Management Contract: The government retained 100% ownership of the assets and properties but handed over day-to-day operations and administrative control to a specialized private management team. 5. Liquidation: The company was dissolved, and its individual assets (such as machinery, scrap metal, or real estate) were auctioned off independently to settle outstanding debts and employee liabilities.

First Phase of Privatisation (1992): In the first phase of the privatisation program, the government decided to privatise 3 PEs, based on the outcome of a joint study by the World Bank's IDA mission and the government. As it was the first ever privatisation in the country, and the Privatisation Bill was under consideration, the privatisation process centred around the high-level Privatisation Committee. A small and compact Privatisation Cell was centralised for all the responsibilities of the process. Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper Factory, Bansbari Leatherage Ltd., and Harisiddhi Bricks and Tiles Factory were privatized in this phase. Second Phase of Privatisation(1993-94): The Council of Ministers decided to privatise 14 PEs by September, 1994. As part of the second phase of the privatisation program, 4 PEs were privatised by June, 1994 and 2 PEs were liquidated. This was due mainly to the change in policy, which was a consequence of a change in the government. Unlike the first phase, all PEs were privatised through a method of share sale, except two liquidated enterprises. It is evident that the government was mindful of the criticism it received in the first phase due to adopting the asset sale method, so during the second phase it changed tack and utilised only the share sale method and liquidation. Nepal Film Development Company, Nepal Lube Oil Ltd., Nepal Bitumin and Barrel Industries Ltd., Balaju Textile Industry, Raw Hide Collection & Dev. Company, Tobacco Development Company (Liq.), and Nepal Jute Development &Trading Company(Liq.) were privatized in this phase. Third Phase of Privatisation(1966-67): In this phase government privatized 6 PEs. It also refrained from using the assets sale modality. In addition to the methods of second phase, lease and management contract methods were also introduced. Nepal Foundry Industry, Raghupati Jute Mills, Biratnagar Jute Mills (managment contract), Nepal Bank Ltd., Agriculture Tools Factory Ltd, and Bhaktapur Brick Factory Ltd.(leased) were privatized. Privatization After 1997: Though the Ninth Plan (1997-2002) set the objective of privatising 30 PEs only one was privatized during that period. The privatization process slowed down mainly due to the political instability in the country where none of the government was keen to privatise the PEs. All the PEs afterwards were privatised through equity sale, assets sale and liquidation. 15 PEs altogether have been privatized ever since.

The Perils: Legally, when the government sold factories like Bhrikuti Kagaj, Harisiddhi, or Bansbari, the sales agreements explicitly stated that the assets were being transferred to continue running the industries. The land was strictly designated for industrial operations, meaning it could not be subdivided, plotted, or sold for commercial or residential real estate. While the land was technically listed as an asset, its value was calculated using the government-registered land rate rather than the actual, booming open-market real estate rate. The evaluators also looked at the cash flow of the preceding which in most of the cases due to political interference, union strikes, overstaffing, etc looked negative. The machineries were also undervalued as they were valued at the price of establishment along with the decades of depreciation. Bansbari was brought by CG group which converted it to Champion Footwear. Later they turned it into CG Chandbagh Residency/Chandbagh School which was against the privatization terms. Later CG formally relinquished its claims over the disputed 10 ropani land, and the Supreme Court approved the withdrawal of their writ petitions, clearing the way for the Government of Nepal to officially re-claim and re-nationalize the property. In case of Bhrikuti Paper, Golchha Organization wanted to permanently shut down and clear the factory. However, they refused to pay over 50 million NPR in back-wages and pensions to the hundreds of permanent factory workers who were suddenly laid off. To prevent the owners from secretly selling off the real estate and running away with the cash, the Labor Office and Land Revenue Office stepped in and legally froze all 53 bighas of the factory's land. The case of Harisiddhi is different, though the factory is still running it is significantly downsized. However, the private owners have utilized that massive land as collateral at various commercial banks to secure huge financial loans for other purposes.

events.title: Krishna Prasad Bhattarai Loses By-election
events.detail: PM Girija Prasad Koirala appointed Dr. Ram Sharan Mahat, who was defeated in the 2048 BS election, as the Vice Chairman of the National Planning Commission. While Ganesh Man Singh wanted to make Dr. Durgeshman Singh the Vice Chairman of the Planning Commission. However, Singh was dissatisfied with Koirala when he did not fulfill his wish. Meanwhile, Koirala dismissed six ministers (Basudev Risal, Dhundiraj Shastri, Sheikh Idris, Taranath Ranabhat, Gopal Man Shrestha, and Chiranjibi Wagle) who were considered close to Bhattarai without consulting the party. And Kisunji also fell out with Koirala. Earlier, when the dispute between Singh and Koirala escalated, Kisunji, as the acting president of the party, had been mediating. Singh had planned to make Kisunji an MP and replace Koirala as the PM after the by-elections. Kisunji was unanimously elected as the candidate by the Congress Central Committee meeting. However, PM Koirala, who promised all possible support, did not ask for Kisunji's vote. 15 days before the election, in the 17-minute long statement, Koirala asked, "Unless the party president expresses his commitment to be an equal partner in the government's ups and downs, how can I, as the head of the government, participate in his election campaign?" Not only this, Koirala also played a secret game to defeat Bhattarai in the election. A three-member strategic committee was formed in Baluwatar, consisting of CPN-UML leader Pradeep Nepal, Nepali Congress leader Marshall Julum Shakya, and journalist Dev Prakash Tripathi. The committee's job was to monitor all of Kisunji's election campaign activities, report to the Prime Minister, and recommend necessary steps. A 22-point strategy paper was prepared to defeat Kisunji. The then Home Minister Sher Bahadur Deuba had tried to remain neutral in the dispute between Kisunji and Koirala. But Deuba did not openly try to win Kisunji. Since he did not trust the Home Minister, Prime Minister Koirala had taken direct reporting from the Police Chief throughout the election period. It is said that not only the police, administration, and political machinery were used to defeat Kisunji, but also money was used in the name of youth mobilization especially the activists of the Nepal Students' Union. Even on the day of the election, it is said that security was tightened in booths considered to be strongholds of the Congress and security arrangements were relaxed in booths considered to be strongholds of the Communists. Sushil Koirala was also very active in this campaign on behalf of the Prime Minister. Ultimately, Kisunji lost the election by a narrow margin. His defeat was due not only to Koirala's interference but also to the overwhelming sympathy he felt for UML candidate Bhandari. Initially, Kisunji was saying that if disciplinary action was not taken, arbitrariness would prevail in the party. But he came to the conclusion that using the stick of action would increase disputes and divisions in the party in the long run. Hundreds of cadres had staged a sit-in outside the Congress meeting demanding action against the conspirators. A group entered the party office, vandalized Koirala's office, and even burned Koirala's effigy. However, Kisunji announced that he would pardon those who committed the crime of conspiring and put them in oblivion.

events.title: Bhupi Sherchan Highway Inagurated
events.detail: The Bhupi Sherchan Highway (Pokhara-Beni Road) was built by the Government of China as a turnkey grant project for the Government of Nepal. The design and construction project was undertaken by the China National Complete Plant Export Corporation with planning beginning in 1986. Physical construction works on the highway began in 1988. The highway was completed and officially handed over to Nepal in June 1994.

events.title: Chhattise Group Fail Government's Policies and Programs
events.detail: Although Bhattarai himself ruled that no action should be taken against the ‘sabotage’ of his campaign,36 MPs opposed to Koirala stayed away from parliament in a vote on the Government's Policies and Programs resulting in its failure. Koirala then resigned and asked Birendra to call mid-term elections. In November of the same year, the country went to mid-term elections.

events.title: 2051 Mid-term Election
events.detail: The election took place after the NC government collapsed and King Birenda called new elections. The NC called on voters to stick with their party and not to entrust power to a Communist party they accused of being irresponsible. The UML called for land reform to break up large landholdings and give land to landless Nepalese peasants. Other pledges made by the party included running water and electricity for all voters and for each village to have at least one television. While the party called for foreign investment to be somewhat restricted and for privatisations to be limited, they also stressed that they believed in a mixed economy and did not support nationalisation. They accused the Nepali Congress government of having been incompetent and corrupt and said that a change in government was required. The results showed that the CPN (UML) won the most seats. Although the UML’s share of the total vote share (31.86% vs 34.47%) was less than that of Congress, they emerged as the largest party. CPN (UML)-88(+19); NC-88(-27); RPP-20(+16); Nepal Workers Peasants Party-4(+2); Nepal Sadbhavana Party-3(-3). The Samyukta Janamorcha of another communist groups failed to win any seats after the more radical wing led by Baburam-Prachanda, which was to launch the Janayudda two years later, had broken away and abandoned parliamentary politics. Neither Congress nor UML was successful in forming a coalition to hold a majority. After failed coalition negotiations, Man Mohan Adhikari became PM of a minority government, acquiring the support of the RPP and the Nepal Sadbhawana Party.

events.title: Man Mohan Adhikari
events.detail: Minority Government with RPP and Sadbhawana Party

events.title: Afno Gaon Afai Banaun, Briddha Bhatta, and Sukumbasi
events.detail: Finance Minister Bharat Mohan Adhikari delivered the landmark fiscal budget speech where he officially introduced the decentralization grants alongside Nepal's first-ever social security elderly allowance (Briddha Bhatta). Afno Gaon Afai Banaun: Under the Afno Gaon Afai Banaun, VDCs received grants of 3 Lakh rupees for local development projects which was increased to 5 Lakhs in another year. Briddha Bhatta: Likewise, the Briddha Bhatta program provided NPR 100 per month to citizens aged 75 years and above. Sukumbasi: The Krishna Prasad Bhattarai government in 1990 had first formed a mechanism to address the problems faced by the country’s landless people. But even before the commission could start its work, a new government was formed. The Girija Prasad Koirala-led government dissolved the previous commission and formed a new one led by Shailaja Acharya. Her work helped establish the administrative framework used by subsequent bodies (like the Lumsali and Alam commissions) to identify, measure, and allocate land to disenfranchised families. Thereafter, Rishi Ram Lumsali, Buddhiman Tamang, Tarini Datta Chataut, Mohmmad Aftab Alam and Gopal Mani Gautam led various commissions and distributed land to the landless at different times. The Adhikari cabinet also formed Rishi Raj Lumsali-led commission to resolve the problem faced by the landless families. The comission distributed the largest chunk of land – 21,900 bighas of land to as many as 58,340 families. There was also criticism that the 53,000 families eventually granted titles to land by the Landless People Problem Resolution Commission had been selected for their connections to the UML rather than on grounds of need.

events.title: CPN (Maoist) Formed
events.detail: The parallel CPN (Unity Centre), led by Baburam Bhattarai and Pushpa Kamal Dahal, went completely underground after the split in 1994 to begin preparations for its next phase of struggle. The party held its Third Plenum in March 1995, where the party renamed itself to the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist).

events.title: Arun III Hydropower Project Cancelled
events.detail: Arun III, a proposed 404 MW hydropower project on the Arun River in Sankhuwasabha, was identified by JICA and repeatedly confirmed through Nepal's least-cost power-generation studies as one of the country's most economically attractive medium-term projects. By 1994, it was estimated to cost about US$1.08 billion, but roughly two-thirds was already covered by highly concessional foreign assistance from the World Bank/IDA, ADB, Germany, Japan and others, with about a 70% subsidy element. The NC government approved it after extensive technical, economic, environmental and social assessments and public consultations, but the project became highly controversial, with Nepali political opponents and international and domestic NGOs criticizing its size, cost, environmental impact, debt implications and dependence on foreign contractors, while advocating smaller hydropower schemes instead. The controversy became decisive when UML leader Madhav Kumar Nepal wrote to the World Bank in October 1994 expressing serious reservations and promising a fresh review if the UML came to power; the World Bank subsequently postponed its approval. After the November 1994 election produced a hung parliament and the UML formed the government, continued uncertainty and attempts to redesign the project weakened the Bank's confidence. In August 1995, World Bank's new President James Wolfensohn cancelled Arun III, citing Nepal's management capacity, difficulty securing political support for necessary reforms such as tariffs, and anticipated cost overruns from delays. After the original 404 MW project was cancelled in 1995, Nepal later redesigned it as the 900 MW Arun-3 project and awarded it in 2008 to India's SJVN, a joint venture of the Indian government-owned NHPC and the Government of Himachal Pradesh, under a BOOT model. SJVN would finance, build and operate the project for a concession period, while Nepal would receive electricity, royalties, taxes and 21% of the generated electricity free of cost, after which the project would ultimately transfer to Nepal.

events.title: Man Mohan Adhikari Government Got Vote of No Confidence
events.detail: In June 1995, the RPP and the Nepal Sadbhawana Party, who helped to form a minority government supported the Nepali Congress's call for a vote of no-confidence in Adhikari's government in a special session of the House of Representatives. Adhikari attempted to dissolve parliament and call elections in an attempt to replicate the circumstances under which he assumed office in 1994. But a Supreme Court challenge led by the Congress saw this move deemed unconstitutional and the parliament was restored. The main rationale was that in 1995, unlike the previous year, there was the possibility of forming a replacement government from within the current parliament. The court also ruled that the right to bring a vote of no confidence in a special session took precedence over the prime minister’s right to seek a dissolution. The vote of no-confidence proceeded successfully. Sher Bahadur Deuba, who had replaced Koirala as leader of the parliamentary Congress Party after the mid-term election, became prime minister as head of a coalition with the NDP and Sadbhavana. Deuba emerged as a consensus candidate within party who could bridge the gap between the warring internal factions—principally those loyal to Koirala and those siding with Bhattarai-SIngh. As a prominent former Home Minister and a leader of the younger generation within the party, Deuba also commanded strong personal loyalty among the newly elected members of parliament. Due to heavy internal backlash for dissolving the parliament, Girija Prasad Koirala chose not to contest the PP leadership role, hence Deuba was selected unopposed as a consensus candidate to lead the NC parliamentary party after 1994 mid-term elections.

events.title: Sher Bahadur Deuba
events.detail: 1st Term; Coliation with RPP and Sadhbhawana Party

events.title: Operation Romeo
events.detail: In early November 1995, Home Minister Khum Bahadur Khadka launched Operation Romeo, primarily in Rolpa District. Officially, it was presented as a police operation to control increasing criminal activity and restore law and order. In practice, observers including Human Rights Watch concluded that its principal objective was to dislodge the militant communist movement and destroy its rural support base. The operation involved a major deployment of police and the establishment of additional police posts. Operation produced widespread allegations and documentation of arbitrary arrests, detention, torture and other human-rights abuses, with hundreds of political activists and suspected Maoist supporters targeted. Thousands of villagers were displaced; some accounts estimate around 6,000 people. Maoists believed that government-led violence worked in their favor as this created many sympathizers. Rolpa's Thawang was considered the de facto political and revolutionary headquarters of the CPN (Maoist) during the decade-long civil war.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 1996
events.detail: First Phase: The War' has been divided into three phases by the CPN (Maoist). The first phase had aimed to establish the politics of struggle, practically prove that the 'War' and the armies were the backbone of the struggle, and to prepare base and infrastructure for guerrilla warfare. Second Phase: On the second week of March 1996, the Central Politburo Meeting had adopted the second plan for the continuation of the "People's War". The motto of the second phase was to "develop the guerrilla war in a planned manner" as adopted by the Central Committee Meeting held on June 1996. This plan aimed to extend mass mobilisation for the favour of war, capture the arms and other equipment, centralise power for changing the base areas into the areas of guerrilla war. This phase of the Maoists movement concluded with propaganda programmes, warnings to stop corrupt activities of governmental and non-governmental organisations, collection of financial resources, capture of arms and ammunitions, seizure of bonds and bills from feudal landlords and so on. Home made weapons, guns and some modern arms had reportedly been in these incidences.Third Phase: The CPN (Maoist) declared its third phase effective from June 1996, in line with its phase wise `People's War'. The party declared its third phase with a theme of "uplifting the guerrilla warfare to a new height," through various political and military targets. Awareness and propaganda programmes, formation of local people's governments, development of revolutionary united front, are referred to as political programmes. Similarly, the military strategy aims to develop new war strategy to fight military suppression. 10 December: A petrol bomb was charged at the house of the then Home Minister Khum Bahadur Khadka at the night of 10 view to warning him.

events.title: The 40-Point Demand
events.detail: Baburam Bhattarai gave PM Sher Bahadur Deuba a letter with 40-Point Demand which was the Maoist movement's political ultimatum before launching the armed insurgency. It demanded: Nationalism: repeal unequal treaties, including the 1950 India treaty and Mahakali Treaty; regulate the open border; restrict foreign capital and influence. Democracy: abolish royal privileges, establish a new constitution, secularize the state, end political repression, and guarantee ethnic, linguistic, women's and minority rights. Livelihood: land redistribution, nationalization of major capitalist property, employment guarantees, free health and education, agricultural support, rural infrastructure and stronger action against corruption. The document warned that if the government did not respond by 17 February 1996, the United People’s Front would resort to armed struggle. The Maoists launched the insurgency on 13 February 1996.

events.title: Mahakali Treaty Signed
events.detail: Integration of Sharada Tanakpur and Pancheshwor Multipurpose Project; Sharada Barrage Agreement of 1920 to exchange land with British Raj to built barrgae; however Nepal has not yet received 36.67 Acre of land from India; In 1981 India started to construct Tanakpur barrage unilaterally on the land which was transferred to British India under the Sarda agreement; New treaty signed adding Pancheshwor with 3240MV and electricity to be shared equally; considered a relatively balanced agreement but the Pancheshwor project hasn't started yet.

events.title: Maoist Insurgency Began
events.detail: On 22 May 1994, the CPN (Unity Centre) was split in two. The militant faction led by Prachnada-Baburam later renamed itself the CPN (Maoist). This faction described the government forces, mainstream political parties, and the monarchy, as "feudal forces". The armed struggle began on 13 February 1996, when the CPN(M) carried out seven simultaneous attacks over districts like Rolpa, Rukum, Gorkha, Sindhuli, etc. The attack on the Holeri police post in Rolpa became one of the best-known opening actions. This is conventionally regarded as the beginning of the Maoist insurgency/Nepalese Civil War. Their strategy was to establish "base areas" in the countryside, weaken the state's presence and build parallel political institutions.

events.title: NC Nineth General Convention
events.detail: Girija Prasad Koirala; The ninth convention was held amid intense party infighting between Girija and Kishunji-Ganeshman faction. Parliament was dissolved by Girija and elections were held forming the first Communist government. Ganesh Man was angry with Girija and left the party eventually following 1994 mid-term election. Losing his closest ally, and fed-up with dirty internal party feud, Bhattarai politically isolated himself within the top leadership tier. Girija Prasad (1144 votes) Chiranjivi Wagle(254 votes) and Ramhari Joshi(12 votes) contested where Girija was elected the president. Sushil Koirala was nominated as the General Secretary.

events.title: India-Nepal Trade Treaty
events.detail: Full Duty and Quota-Free Access: Granted duty-free and quota-free access to the Indian market for all Nepalese manufactured goods with the exception of a small negative list like alcohol tobacco and explosives without any value-added criteria.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 1997
events.detail: 3 January: Maoists attack Bethan police post in Ramechhap. 11 March: UML-Sadbhabana-RPP coalition government presided over by Lokendra Bahadur Chand constitutes a taskforce led by Prem Singh Dhami to find a solution to the Maoist problem. The taskforce labels it "terrorist activity in a political disguise".

events.title: Maoists Attack Bethan Police in Ramechhap
events.detail: In one of the most daring acts since the initiation of the people's war in Nepal, the Maoist guerrillas raided a police outpost at Bethan in Ramechhap. Armed with local guns and pistol and home-made bombs, 29 guerrillas raided the armed police post. On the night of January 3, in a meticulously planned move the guerrillas surrounded the police outpost and ordered the policemen to surrender. However, as the mercenaries of the reactionary state shut themselves up in the building and resorted to indiscriminate firing on the guerrillas from the windows, there ensured a heavy exchange of fire for several hours. Meanwhile in the darkness of the night Com. Tirtha Gautam, the commander of the raid operation, was hit by a bullet on his head and attained martyrdom instantly. This fueled the fire and inspired the guerrillas to mount their attack more vigorously. In this course two of the running dogs of the reactionary state were killed and two others were seriously injured. On the guerrilla side two more fighters, Com. Dilmaya Yonjan, a young woman guerrilla squad member, and Com. Fateh Bahadur Slami, another guerrilla squad member, attained martyrdom. Finally the enemy was over powered; rifles, ammunitions and other valuable & utilities were seized and the police outpost was totally destroyed. Despite the loss of three precious lives of valiant guerrillas, this successful raid electrified the revolutionary aspirations of the toiling masses and sent chills down the spine of the reactionaries. It also signalled the steady development of the people's war to a higher stage.

events.title: Lands Act (Fourth Amendment)
events.detail: Introduced provision of 50-50 division of land into separate Lalpurja titles for mohi and talshing secured housing right of tenant by granting them full ownership of their house and path if built in the land. Allowed Cash Buyout Option for a localized market-rate purchase to prevent fragmentation.

events.title: 2054 Local Elections
events.detail: After 2049, local elections were held in 2054. At that time, the number of VDCs had reached 3913 and the number of municipalities had reached 58. And, the process of forming VDCs was also changed. This time, voting was required for the VDC chairperson, vice-chairperson, four ward members, and one female ward member (i.e. 20% female reservation for the first time). In the municipality, too, voting was required for the mayor, deputy mayor, four ward members, and one female ward member. Elections were held on 4 Jestha 2054 in the VDCs/municipalities of the districts under the three development zones of Sudurpaschimanchal, Mid-Paschimanchal, and Paschimanchal, and on 13 Jestha in the VDCs/municipalities of the Central and Eastern Development Zones. UML won a majority in the local bodies established it as the dominant local political force. RPP leader Lokendra Bahadur Chand was PM, while Bamdev Gautam was Home Minister. The opposition alleged that Gautam used the police and administration to benefit the UML. His replacement of the police chief and extensive transfers of officials, including CDOs, shortly before the election became a major source of suspicion. The election subsequently became associated with the label “Bamdev's election.” In western Nepal, the Maoists prevented candidates from registering in many places, forced some uncontested candidates to resign, and killed and attacked local candidates, particularly those from the Nepali Congress. The second phase saw serious clashes among Congress, UML and RPP cadres. Three people were killed on election day, while shootings and bombings occurred particularly in the Madhesh. In Siraha, 22 bombs exploded, injuring around 60 people, including children. Police also opened fire in Lagthigoth after an exchange of gunfire. Congress candidates Nawaraj Bhattarai and Baburam Bhattarai were attacked and injured in Sindhuli. By the following day, the reported death toll from election-related internal clashes had reached seven, with deaths reported in Bara, Siraha, Dhanusha and Sarlahi. Because of deteriorating security, the government postponed elections in hundreds of locations, including polling stations and areas across Morang, Rautahat, Siraha, Saptari, Dhanusha, Ilam, Sindhuli, Sarlahi, Dhading, Parsa and Ramechhap. The election demonstrated how Nepal's local democratic institutions were becoming caught between state-level partisan competition and the emerging Maoist insurgency.

events.title: Ninth Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 146.84 billion spent; ~77.4% implementation rate; Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC) formed; Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) established; Nepal Telecom converted to a corporation; Kali Gandaki 'A' Hydroelectric Project (144 MW) completed; Puwa Khola and Modi Khola hydro projects completed; Melamchi Drinking Water Project initiated; Local Self-Governance Act 2055 BS passed; introduction of Tenth Plan poverty mapping; expansion of rural sub-health posts to every Village Development Committee (VDC); social sectors received 35.8%; agriculture and forestry took 23.4%; transport and electricity received 22.1%; severely disrupted by the escalation of the Maoist insurgency and political instability (including the royal massacre), causing GDP growth to drop to an average of just 3.6%

events.title: Maoist Activities in 1998
events.detail: 11 June: US ambassador Ralph Frank warns of withdrawal of international aid if Maoist attacks on development infrastructure continue. 8 September: Alternative politburo member Suresh Wagle and Commander Bhimsen Pokharel killed in police encounter. 27 November: Maoists declare new campaign to create 'base areas'. 15 December: Minister Chiranjibi Wagle's house in Chabahil bombed.

events.title: CPN (UML)'s Sixth National Convention
events.detail: Oli advanced JaBaJa; UML split; Manmohan Adhikari as Chair and Madhav Kumar Nepal as General Secretary (Amid differing views on how to apply People’s Multiparty Democracy the strategy written and presented by K.P. Sharma Oli was adopted by an overwhelming majority. Soon after the congress the party split under the leadership of Bamdev Gautam centered on disputes over the ratification of the Mahakali Treaty. Gautam and other leaders broke away to form CPN (Male). However after failing to win a single seat in the 1999 election Gautam’s faction remerged with UML in 2001.)

events.title: Operation Kilo Sierra II
events.detail: Nepal's conflict had been going on for four years, the violence was spreading out from the Maoist ‘base areas’ of the mid-western mountains to other parts of the country. Teachers, farmers, students and traders were being extorted, tortured or killed. Government was relying strictly on the underfunded and ill-equipped Nepal Police. PM Koirala desperately wanted the army mobilized, but faced severe institutional roadblocks. King Birendra strongly resisted Koirala’s demands to deploy the army against civilian citizens. The Palace viewed the Maoist insurgency as a political and policing failure created by political parties, arguing that the army should only be used to defend national sovereignty, not for internal policing. Therefore, the Nepal Policed launched a brutal operation named ‘Kilo Sera II,’ characterized by the directive to ‘kill everyone, burn everything, and loot everything.’ During this operation, 500 civilians were killed by the police. The heavy-handedness of the police during Kilo Sierra II resulted in widespread human rights abuses and the deaths of hundreds of innocent civilians. Just like Operation Romeo, the harshness of KS2 drove thousands of terrified and angry rural youths straight into the arms of the Maoist rebels.

events.title: PPA Rates Fixed
events.detail: When the Electricity Act, 2049 was passed in 1992, it was highly progressive on paper. It officially allowed private companies to build power plants in BOOT model for the first time. However, from 1992 to early 1998, almost no major private domestic investments materialized. The state-owned Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) was—and still is—the only entity allowed to buy electricity and distribute it to the public. The 1992 framework expected private developers to sit down with the NEA and negotiate a purchase price case-by-case. Because the NEA was a bureaucratic monopoly, these negotiations dragged on for years. Corrupt officials could stall projects by demanding kickbacks, and there was no baseline formula to determine what a "fair price" for electricity was. When Shailaja Acharya took office as the Minister of Water Resources and head of the NEA Board in late 1997, she recognized that bureaucratic hesitation was suffocating the nation's potential.She bypassed the endless case-by-case negotiations by issuing a historic executive mandate that established Nepal’s first fixed and uniform Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) rates. For the first time, a private developer could take a government-guaranteed PPA contract to a commercial bank. The bank could instantly calculate the project’s future revenue streams, making it safe to issue large infrastructure loans. In over a century of history, the government grid had only managed to build about 661 Megawatts (MW) of power. Following her reforms, private developers flooded the market, building over 2,100 MW of electricity—effectively eclipsing the government's historic output.

events.title: Declaration of Base Area
events.detail: On 27 October 1998 the CPN (Maoist) declared to establish 'Base Areas' to continue its movement. It was also declared that the 'People's War' had entered to a new phase. With the theme "Let's move towards the grand path of the establishment of base areas", the new phase was said to have entered to the 4th phase of the 'People's War'. The decision of this effect was taken by the meeting of the Party held in the third week of August 1998. It was also said that the Party General Secretary had been entrusted to command and control the `People's War' and to establish a separate state administration in the Maoist affected districts. The same meeting adopted a policy of a signalman leadership of the General Secretary to command the army. Soon after the declaration, the Maoist activities were intensified in some districts beginning 26 and 17 October 1998. Various programmes including torch processions and bomb explosions occurred in the headquarters of Rolpa, Rukum, Salyan and Dang. Jewellery and cash were looted from the Nepal Bank Limited at Rukumkot, Rukum.

events.title: Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal Established
events.detail: Before its formation, the functions of the CAAN had been performed since 1957 by an agency within the Ministry of Work, Communications and Transport. On 31 December 1998, as a result of the Civil Aviation Act of 1996, the CAAN was established as an independent regulatory body. Currently, CAAN acts as both the referee and the player in Nepal's aviation sector. It regulates aviation safety while simultaneously operating the country's airports and generating revenue from air navigation services. International aviation watchdogs, including the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), have long identified this dual identity as an inherent conflict of interest. This structural flaw remains the primary reason Nepali airlines have been banned from European airspace since 2013.

events.title: Mechi Highway Completed
events.detail: The 268 km Mechi Highway (Kechna-Charali-Maikhola-Ilam-Phidim-Taplejung Road) was built in phases over four decades. The first phase spanning the 1970s to 1980s concentrated on the southern segments in Jhapa district establishing links to the Mahendra Highway at Charali. This initial development covering approximately 40 km of Kechana-Charali section was funded through the Nepal government itself. Currently India governemnt is upgrading the Charali-Kechana section under Phase-I of the ongoing Terai Roads Project in Nepal. The second phase was the Phidim-Taplejung section built between 1973 and 1987 also by the Government of Nepal. The final phase spanned from 1997 to 1999 under which the Charali-Maikhola-Ilam-Phidim section of the highway was built with the loan from ADB.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 1999
events.detail: 2 January: Bhatte Danda police post in Lalitpur attacked. 15 January: Maoists kill Hari Bhakta Oli, ex-DDC chairman and president of Rukum Nepali Congress. 5 March: Maoists kill Yadi Gautam, UML secretary of Rukum and candidate for general elections. 14 June: Maoists attack police post in Laha, Rukum. 30 December: Taskforce led by Sher Bahadur Deuba formed to study the Maoist problem and offer resolution.

events.title: Manmohan Adhikari died during 1999 election campaign; Party chair position abolished Madhav Nepal became the sole office bearer
Kargil War
events.detail: It was a limited armed conflict fought between India and Pakistan from along the Line of Control (LoC) in the Kargil district of Jammu and Kashmir. It remains unique as one of the very few direct military conflicts ever fought between two nuclear-armed nations. In early 1999 the Pakistani military secretly launched Operation Badr seizing vacant Indian military posts at altitudes up to 18000 feet. Pakistan aimed to cut off the main highway linking Srinagar to Ladakh isolating the region and forcing India to negotiate on Kashmir. India launched a massive counter-offensive operation called Operation Vijay to retake the vertical peaks through grueling uphill infantry assaults. India used Bofors heavy artillery for direct cliff-smashing and deployed fighter jets using precision laser-guided bombs. The recapture of strategic peaks like Tololing and Tiger Hill broke the back of the infiltration. Facing global isolation and pressure from U.S. President Bill Clinton Pakistan agreed to withdraw its forces. India cleared all infiltrators and reclaimed its territory. In Pakistan tensions over the failed war led to a military coup in October 1999 where Army Chief Pervez Musharraf overthrew the civilian government.

events.title: Hrithik Roshan Riots
events.detail: Mid-December 2000, a rumor began circulating that Bollywood actor Hrithik Roshan had said in a television interview that he hated Nepal and Nepalis. The rumor spread rapidly through newspapers, student organizations and word of mouth. It became particularly explosive because anti-Indian sentiment was already present in Nepal. On 26 December 2000, thousands of students demonstrated in Kathmandu. Gopi Krishna Hall showing Mission Kashmir, starring Roshan, was attacked. Police eventually opened fire after protesters attacked police and attempted to burn the cinema hall. Four people were killed and more than 180 injuried during the ensuing violence, including students killed by police gunfire. Violence continued on 27–28 December. Indian-owned businesses were attacked, the State Bank of India had its windows smashed, transportation stopped, schools and businesses closed, and Indian tourists were reportedly targeted. The government temporarily stopped cinemas from screening Hrithik Roshan films unless he apologized. Indian ambassador Dev Mukharjee played effective role by contacting Hritik Roshan and made him clarify in a video message via Nepal Television. By 30 December, the Nepal government itself described the trigger as a “media fabrication”, while businesses began reopening. Even after the issue was settled the mob violence shifted from targeting strictly Indian-owned businesses to targeting anyone perceived as "Indian-looking". At that time the entire Madhesi community of Kathmandu lived in terror while they were practically being hunted down. Madhesi students, vendors, and tenants were verbally and physically assaulted. It was the point the seed of forthcoming Madhesh Andolan was set. Dr. CK Raut has publicly claimed that his reason to come to politics was the discriminations he and his community faced during this incident.
