events.title: Alam Commission Distributed Land to Sukumbasi
events.detail: The Mohammad Aftab Alam-led commission in 2001 distributed 9,500 bigha (6,365 hectares) to over 15,000 families, the second highest after the Lumsali Commission. Records at the land management ministry show that around 46,000 bigha of land (30,820 hectares) have been distributed to some 150,000 families in the past three decades. However, tens of thousands of families are still landless. The irony is that the more ownership certificates are distributed, the number of squatters increases instead of decreasing.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2001
events.detail: 4 February: Maoists attack Chief Justice Keshab Prasad Upadhaya in Surkhet. 1 April: Maoists attack Rukumkot police post. 6 April: Maoists attack Naumule police post, Dolakha. 11 April: Integrated Security and Development Program (ISDP) launched in Maoist affected districts. 7 July: Maoists attack police posts in Taruka of Nuwakot, Bichaur of Lamjung and Bami of Gulmi.12 July: Holleri attack. 21 July: Sher Bahadur Deuba proposes peace talks. 22 July: The Maoists attack Pandusen police post in Bajura. 25 July: Government-Maoist ceasefire declared. 30 August: First round of talks held in Godavari. 13-14 September: Second round of talks held in Bardiya. 13 November: Third round of talks in Godavari. 21 November: Prachanda declares end of the ceasefire. 23 November: Maoists announce Central People's Government under Baburam Bhattarai. Simultaneous attacks on army in Dang, and district headquarters. 25 November: Attack on Salleri in Solukhumbu. 26 November: State of emergency declared, the Maoists labelled terrorists and the Royal Nepali Army is deployed.

events.title: NC Tenth General Convention
events.detail: Girija Prasad Koirala; Girija was re-elected from the Pokhara convention with the contest between Girija(936) Deuba(507) and Ramhari Joshi(10). Sushil Koirala was re-nominated General Secretary of the party.

events.title: Krishna Bahadur Gurung Killed
events.detail: NC Leader from Salyan, Kaski was killed by Maoists. He was 2-times Pradhan Pancha of Salyan VDC and Vice-president of NC Kaski district.

events.title: Royal Palace Massacre
events.detail: A mass shooting occured on Friday night royal family dinner resulting in the deaths of 9 members of the royal family, including King Birendra and Queen Aishwarya. A government-appointed inquiry team named Crown Prince Dipendra as the perpetrator of the massacre. Dipendra was declared king following the death of his parents but was comatose after shooting himself at the scene; he died in a hospital three days later without regaining consciousness. He was succeeded by Gyanendra, his paternal uncle and Birendra's younger brother.

events.title: Holleri Incident
events.detail: On July 12, 2001 the rebels then known as CPN (Maoist) had announced 'Nepal Banda'. To make it successful, they had planned to attack some of the posts of the security forces. Though they had decided to attack the camp of Armed Police Force in Bhaluwang of Dang after a careful study, the plot was exposed at the eleventh hour. The commanders were Nanda Kishor Pun along with Barshaman Pun. They then selected Holeri of Rolpa for the execution of the plan. The rebels had attacked police posts in Ropla even in the initial days of the armed conflict. The government had then added security force in Rolpa. But the rebels came to know that the police personnel would desert their camp at night in Holeri for fear of attack. This made them change the attack plan. The rebels then found out that the police would return to their camp early in the morning. Following this, the attack was planned for the morning. When police reached their post in the morning, they were taken by surprise when the rebels warned them by loud speaker to surrender. The police refused to surrender at first and opened fire. After a few hours of crossfire, the rebels took 72 police personal under control. A policeman had even lost his life. To contain the rebel force, the government decided to deploy army. This was the rebels' first encounter with the army. Three army helicopters had reached Nuwagaun of Rolpa the next day of the Holeri attack. One of the army helicopters made an emergency landing at Budhagaun of Rolpa after the rebels started attacking it. At Nuwagaun, Maoists then sent a letter to the army. “We do not have any plan to attack you right now. Why have you come here? If you have come to start war with us, we will be forced to take up the challenge. We have cordoned you off, so you cannot get out from here.” This was the detail of the letter. Later, the army said that it was there for training and not for any kind of attack. Following this, the two sides sat for talks. And it was agreed that the army would be given way out and it would leave peacefully, and kidnapped police and army personells would be freed. The 'failure' of the army was rejoiced by the rebels. This incident boosted self confidence, triggering historic changes in the political scenario. The army was deployed to Holeri but did not undertake the decisive rescue operation Koirala expected. Whether this represented deliberate insubordination, constitutional caution, or operational restraint remains contested.

events.title: PM Girija Resigned Over Pressure
events.detail: Holleri crisis, Royal Palace Massacre, corruption allegations over Lauda Air leasing and growing political pressure had weakened Koirala. PM Koirala subsequently resigned on 19 July, citing the army's non-cooperation in Holleri incident. After Koirala resigned, the Congress parliamentary party elected Deuba. Deuba therefore became both Congress parliamentary party leader and the party's candidate to head the government, after defeating Koirala's preferred candidate, Sushil Koirala by 32 votes (72-40).

events.title: Ghorahi Attack
events.detail: Soon after Deuba took over government and Maoists agreed to a ceasefire and began peace talks on 25 July, 2001. Three rounds of negotiations took place, but they failed. On 23 November, Maoists under Western Wing Commander Barshaman Pun “Ananta” launched coordinated attacks on army and police posts across the country, including the major attack on Ghorahi, Dang. Hundreds of fighters entered Ghorahi from Nepalgunj, Salyan, Rolpa and Pyuthan, using buses, trucks and minibuses to surround the town before attacking simultaneously at around 11 p.m. They targeted the District Administration Office, District Police Office, Army barracks, senior officials' residences, Traffic Police, banks and other government offices. The Maoists captured the Chief District Officer and his wife, the Superintendent of Police and numerous police and army personnel, looted large quantities of weapons, ammunition, money and communications equipment, destroyed government buildings and freed 37 prisoners. At the Army barracks, 14 soldiers, including commanding officer Major Naresh Uprety, were killed, while four policemen were killed and 14 injured; the Maoists also suffered casualties, though the source does not give a figure. After several hours of fighting, the Maoists withdrew in a convoy of roughly 20 buses, trucks and minibuses, taking prisoners and captured equipment toward Rolpa. The attack was especially significant because it demonstrated that the Maoists had moved beyond small guerrilla raids to large, coordinated attacks capable of temporarily overwhelming major government and military installations, and it directly triggered the government's decision to declare a nationwide state of emergency on 26 November 2001 and mobilize the Royal Nepal Army against the insurgency.

events.title: State of Emergency Declared
events.detail: Following the collapse of peace talks and the Maoists' nationwide attacks on 23 November, Deuba's government recommended a state of emergency for 3 months. Same day, King Gyanendra formally proclaimed the emergency, suspended several fundamental rights, declared the Maoists a terrorist organization, and authorized the nationwide mobilization of the Royal Nepal Army. On 27 November, parliament met and approved the emergency by a two-thirds majority, as required by the 1990 Constitution. The emergency was initially valid for three months, and Parliament later extended it for another three months.

events.title: Tek Bahadur Gurung Killed
events.detail: NC leader of Machhapuchhre VDC, Tek Bahadur Gurung was brutally killed by Maoists.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2002
events.detail: 21 February: Parliament endorses state of emergency. 23 April: Ransom on heads of Maoist leaders. 7 May: US President George W Bush backs government campaign against the Maoists and pledges support, Maoists attack army camp in Gam. 17 May: Parliament extends state of emergency. 22 May: Parliament dissolved on recommendation of Prime Minister, election date set for 3 November. 26 May 2002: Deuba expelled from Nepali Congress. 18 June: The Deuba faction expels party president Girija Prasad Koirala. 8 September: Maoists attack Sandhikharka in Arghakhachi, most government buildings destroyed. 3 October: Prime Minister Deuba recommends elections be postponed for a year. 4 October: King Gyanendra sacks Deuba and takes over executive powers. 11 October: Formation of a new cabinet under the premiership of Lokendra Bahadur Chand. 14 October: Maoists attack and destroy Jumla district headquarters. 26 January: Maoists assassinate Chief of Armed Police Krishna Mohan Shrestha, his wife Nudup Shrestha and bodyguard in Kathmandu. 28 January: Government decides to retract terrorist label, bounties and the red corner notice against the Maoists. 29 January: Government-Maoist ceasefire declared. 12 March: The Nepali Congress, the UML, People's Front and NMKP (Nepal Workers and Peasants Party) reach a consensus for a joint agitation against the October Fourth royal move. 28 March: Maoist negotiation team comes out in the open at a press conference. 8 April: Student leader killed in Butwal demonstration. 27 April: First round of government-Maoist peace talks at Shanker Hotel. 10 May: Second round of government-Maoist negotiations end with an agreement restricting army movement.

events.title: Rapti Highway Completed
events.detail: The 168 km Rapti Highway (Ameliya-Tulsipur-Salyan-Musikot Road) was built by the Government of Nepal with progressive track opening beginning around 1990s till 2002 and ongoing upgrading and blacktopping

events.title: Land Act (Fifth Amendment)
events.detail: Introduced mandatory strict two-year deadlines to force lagging land split between mohi and talshing; Ammended the land ceilings to represent the contemporaray socio-economic condition as follows: 133+13 ropani in Terai 25+5 roapni in Kathmandu Valley 70+5 ropani in Hill

events.title: Achham Incident
events.detail: About 2,500 Maoist guerillas, under Western Wing Commander Barshaman Pun “Ananta” perpetrated a massive attack against the Nepal army in Mangalsen and Sanphebagar in Achham district on 16 February 2002 killing 57 soldiers out of 59, 77 policemen and five civilians including the CDO. On midnight of 16 February 2002, the actual attack was made. First, the military barracks that had been located at the top spur of Mangalsen town were attacked. The rebels made five explosions and used automatic weapons and rockets. The first explosion was made at the top of the town, where the military barracks were located. The battle occurred for about half an hour. Police and soldiers fired back at the rebels, but the forces were outnumbered by the rebels. The Maoists looted 55 automatic weapons and five machine guns from the Mangalsen barrack. Next, the Maoists stormed Mangalsen town to attack government facilities, one of them was the Mangalsen Durbar which operated as the DIstrict Aministration Office. Another simultaneous attack was carried out at Sanphebagar 20 km north of Mangalsen a few hours later on the same day. The Maoists destroyed Sanphebagar Airport and killed 27 policemen. A hydropower plant at Kailash River was also destroyed. The incident is considered the single most damaging strike by the rebels during the Nepalese Civil War. After the incident, government troops from Kathmandu were sent by helicopter to surround the area and search for the rebels. PM Sher Bahadur Deuba, called an emergency cabinet meeting the following night to extend a state of emergency. The Parliament ratified the extension of the emergency by an additional three months. The Sanphebagar Airport reopened in 2018 after the repair started in 2006 marking the end of civil war. Achham Palace destroyed in the war was reconstructed in 2023.

events.title: State of Emergency Extended
events.detail: Parliament extended the emergency for another three months, as permitted by the 1990 Constitution, following continued Maoist attacks. It was due to expire in late May, but Parliament was dissolved on 22 May before a further extension could be considered.

events.title: India-Nepal Trade Treaty
events.detail: Stricter Rules of Origin: Required Nepali exporters to prove a minimum 30% local value addition and a change in tariff heading at the 4-digit Harmonized System (HS) level. Quantitative Restrictions: Set Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQs) on specific sensitive exports such as vegetable fats acrylic yarn and copper wire to protect domestic Indian industries. Primary Products Exception: Allowed duty-free and quota-free entry for agricultural goods without the 30% value-addition requirement provided they were produced in Nepal.

events.title: Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre–Masal i.e. मसाल) Formed
events.detail: This party was from the merger of Communist Party of Nepal (Unity Centre) and Communist Party of Nepal (Masal i.e. मसाल). General secretaries of the two parties, Ram Singh Shris of CPN (Masal) and Narayan Kaji Shrestha (Prakash) of CPN (UC) announced the merger publicly. The founding general secretary of the party was Mohan Bikram Singh. The two electoral mass fronts of the two parties, Samyukta Janamorcha Nepal and Rastriya Janamorcha, merged to form Janamorcha Nepal. The Janamorcha Nepal joined the Seven Party Alliance and took an active part in the 2006 People's Movement. After the end of the direct-rule by King Gyandendra in April 2006 the CPN (Unity Centre–Masal) was split into four. A minor faction broke away and formed the Communist Party of Nepal (2006), the party later merged into the CPN (Maoist). Mohan Bikram Singh broke away and formed a parallel CPN (Unity Centre–Masal), which later renamed itself to CPN (Masal). The party also formed a parallel Janamorcha Nepal, later Rastriya Janamorcha, led by Chitra Bahadur K.C. and took away with three members of the Interim Parliament from Janamorcha Nepal because of Singh's opposition towards joining the interim government. The other split emerged when Ram Singh Sris broke away with two members of the Interim Parliament from Janamorcha Nepal. The faction also had its own parallel Janamorcha Nepal led by Chitra Bahadur Ale. The faction later merged with other splinter groups of other communist parties and formed CPN (Unified).

events.title: House Dissolved, Fresh Elections Called, And Emergency Extended
events.detail: The state of emergency, declared in November 2001 after major Maoist attacks, was due to expire on 24 May 2002. PM Deuba wanted to extend it for another six months to continue the military campaign against the Maoists. But not only Opposition UML but also Girija Prasad Koirala and the NC leadership opposed the extension, meaning Deuba lacked the required two-thirds majority in Parliament. Meanwhile, the government registered a proposal to extend the emergency period by 6 months with the Parliament Secretariat on Jestha 3. After that, discord began within the party. On Jestha 7, Prime Minister Deuba was asked for a 24-hour explanation under the signature of General Secretary Sushil Koirala. Deuba responded on Jestha 20 by saying that he had not taken any decision by going beyond the party's decision. On Jestha 20, the Central Working Committee meeting directed the government to withdraw the proposal registered in Parliament. Deuba was also criticized in the parliamentary party meeting held on the same day. Deuba, who reached the royal palace that evening, and advised King Gyanendra to dissolve the House and call fresh elections for 13 November 2002. King Gyanendra accepted the recommendation and dissolved Parliament. With Parliament dissolved, the King issued an ordinance extending the emergency for another three months. An 11-member full bench, headed by Chief Justice Keshav Prasad Upadhyaya, upheld the dissolution unanimously. MPs of dissolved parliament, Hari Nepal (Nepali Congress) and Ganesh Pandit (UML), challenged Deuba's recommendation and sought reinstatement of Parliament.The Court held that the Prime Minister could recommend dissolution under Article 53(4) and did not have to obtain Cabinet approval first.

events.title: Tenth Five-Year Plan
events.detail: NPR 231.13 billion spent; ~98.7% spending rate due to scaled-back targets; Poverty Alleviation Fund (PAF) established; National Human Rights Commission institutionalized; Department of Money Laundering Investigation drafted; Middle Marsyangdi Hydroelectric project construction delayed; rural road networks expanded via local bodies; solar and micro-hydro expanded in off-grid districts; functioned as Nepal's official Poverty Reduction Strategy Paper (PRSP); targeted interventions for Dalit, indigenous (Adivasi/Janajati), and marginalized groups; poverty rate successfully dropped from 38% to 31%; social sector received 38.6%; transport and communication took 18.2%; agriculture and irrigation received 16.5%; ended amidst the 2006 Peace Accord and transition to a Republic; despite active conflict in early years, remittances began booming, keeping the economy afloat.

events.title: Sandhikharka Attack
events.detail: Sandhikharka, the headquarters of Arghakhanchi district, was attacked by roughly 4,000 Maoists under Top Bahadur Rayamajhi and Pampha Bhusal who had marched for days from their western strongholds. They simultaneously attacked the police, Armed Police and Royal Nepal Army positions and government offices in the town. The fighting lasted through the night, and the Maoists succeeded in overrunning the security positions and effectively taking control of the district headquarters. Government buildings were burned or destroyed, and a large number of security personnel were killed or captured. Government figures put the security-force deaths at 68, plus one civilian, while Maoist casualties were disputed. Nearly 100 government/security personnel were initially reported missing, many of whom were subsequently released. The importance of Sandhikharka was that it showed how powerful the Maoists had become after the 2001 escalation. They could mobilize thousands of fighters, surround an entire district headquarters and defeat multiple security positions simultaneously. It also came only days after the government had lifted the state of emergency on 29 August 2002, making the attack a dramatic demonstration that ending emergency rule had not ended the insurgency.

events.title: Nepali Congress (Prajatantrik) Founded
events.detail: Angered by Deuba's move of dissolving house, extending emergency, and calling elections, President Girija Prasad Koirala called on all party members in the Council of Ministers to resign within three days. Some resigned, while others stood by Deuba. Dr. Ram Sharan Mahat, Amod Prasad Upadhyaya, and Rajendra Kharel resigned. However a big chuck, Bijay Kumar Gachhadar, Bal Bahadur K.C., Chiranjivi Wagle, Jaya Prakash Prasad Gupta/Anand, Khum Bahadur Khadka, Govinda Raj Joshi, and Purna Bahadur Khadka remained. Meanwhile, the Central Disciplinary Committee on 26 May immediately expelled Prime Minister Deuba from being an ordinary member of the party and sent him a three-day explanation letter. Deuba responded to the Disciplinary Committee on June 12. However, on June 12, the disciplinary committee also expelled Deuba from the party for three years, stating that the explanation he presented was not reasonable and that the dissolution of the House of Representatives without informing the party was against the principles of the party system and a serious violation of the party's objectives, policies, code of conduct and statute. Deuba appealed to the Central Working Committee to withdraw the action. But there was no hearing. Meanwhile, Deuba called a meeting of his party's general convention representatives for 16-18 June. He turned the meeting called to put pressure on Koirala into a purported 10th General Convention. From the convention Koirala was removed from the presidency, and Sher Bahadur Deuba was elected as the president of the divided party. Thus, the Congress split. Later, the Koirala faction gained authority from Election Commission and Deuba's party became the Nepali Congress Democratic Party. When the split became formal, he took approximately 40 of the Congress's former House representatives and 37 Central Working Committee members with him.

events.title: Deuba Dismissed by King Gyanendra
events.detail: Deuba had dissolved Parliament in May 2002 and scheduled elections for November, partly because he could no longer secure parliamentary support to extend the emergency against the Maoists. Over the following months, the Maoist insurgency became much worse. The Maoists threatened to disrupt the elections, and the government concluded that it could not guarantee safe and credible voting. On 3 October 2002, Deuba's Cabinet therefore asked the King to postpone the election for one year. The next day, Gyanendra dismissed Deuba, saying he was "incompetent" and incapable of conducting the election, dissolved his Cabinet, postponed the election indefinitely and assumed executive authority. But there was also a constitutional and political calculation behind it. Parliament had already been dissolved, so there was no functioning elected legislature to constrain the King. Gyanendra used this vacuum and the Maoist crisis to argue that the political parties had failed and that the monarchy needed to take a more active role. He subsequently appointed the royalist Lokendra Bahadur Chand as Prime Minister on 11 October. Mainstream political parties condemned the move as undemocratic and unconstitutional and began protests demanding restoration of parliamentary democracy. The 4 October dismissal of Sher Bahadur Deuba was a crucial precursor and political litmus test for King Gyanendra's eventual full-fledged takeover. By dismissing an elected Prime Minister, cancelling elections, and assuming executive authority, the King demonstrated that he was willing to intervene directly in government when the political system appeared unable to function. This set the precedent for his progressively more assertive interventions, culminating in his direct takeover of executive power on 1 February 2005.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2003
events.detail: 29 January: Government and Maoists announce a nationwide ceasefire, beginning the second major peace process. 27 April: First round of government–Maoist peace talks begins. 9–10 May: Second round of peace talks takes place. 4 June: Surya Bahadur Thapa becomes Prime Minister after Lokendra Bahadur Chand resigns. 17 August: Third round of peace talks begins. 17 August: Doramba incident: security forces kill 19 Maoists and suspected Maoist supporters in Ramechhap. 27 August 2003: Maoists withdraw from negotiations and end the ceasefire; armed conflict resumes.

events.title: Second Maoist Ceasefire
events.detail: Soon after Lokendra Bahadur Chand came to power, the government and Maoists declared a ceasefire on 29 January 2003 and held peace talks. Meantime, on 17 August Nepali military and police forces kill 39 Maoist rebels in the Ramechhap district during an offensive launched jointly by the Army, Police, and Air Force of Nepal. 7 soldiers of the Nepali Army and 5 Constables of the Armed Police are also killed in the operation. The talks failed, and the Maoists ended the ceasefire on 27 August. Meanwhile, opposition parties continued protesting against royal rule.

events.title: CPN (UML)'s Seventh National Convention
events.detail: Oli’s democratization proposal rejected; Nepal resigns after elections; Madhav Kumar Nepal became General Secretary (At the congress K.P. Sharma Oli proposed the democratization of party life and Shankar Pokhrel presented a proposal on Constituent Assembly elections but neither was approved.

events.title: Lokendra Bahadur Chand Resigns Over Increasing Anti-monarchy Protests
events.detail: Five major parliamentary parties were jointly demanding restoration of Parliament and an all-party government, arguing that Chand's appointment by the King was unconstitutional. The protests had become increasingly large and confrontational. On 30 May, around 5,000 people demonstrated in Kathmandu, and police used batons and tear gas. Chand's government had also failed to obtain cooperation from the major parties, making it politically weak and increasingly difficult to govern. The ceasefire and peace talks with the Maoists did not solve the broader political crisis and were actually opposed by the mainstream parties, which boycotted the talks. Gyanendra concluded that replacing him might help defuse the crisis and bring the parties into a new government. The King was forced to retreat somewhat from the October 2002 arrangement, but instead of restoring Parliament, he tried another royal-appointed government, this time under Surya Bahadur Thapa.

events.title: Purna Bahadur (Bhujel) Thapa Killed
events.detail: Purna Bahadur (Bhujel) Thapa of Machhapuchhre VDC was brutally killed by Maoists.

events.title: Chandra Bahadur Ranabhat
events.detail: Chandra Bahadur Ranabhat of Budhibazar, Kaksi was killed by Maoists

events.title: Maoists Declared Specially Designated Global Terrorist by US
events.detail: United States designated the CPN (Maoist) as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist under Executive Order (SDGT) 13224, following its growing insurgency and attacks. When the U.S. designated the CPN (Maoist) on 31 October 2003, it did not formally classify it as an Foreign Terrorist Organization (FTO). Instead, it designated the organization as an SDGT. However, the practical effect was significant as U.S. persons were prohibited from providing funds or economic resources to the Maoists, and Maoist assets under U.S. jurisdiction could be blocked. The U.S. had already begun providing military assistance, training and weapons to Nepal's security forces in 2002. Congress had authorized roughly $12 million in assistance, and U.S. assistance included M16 rifles.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2004
events.detail: 5 February: An Army raid is carried out by the Bhairavnath Battalion on a village in Bhimad, Makwanpur district. Reports emerge that 14 suspected Maoist rebels and two civilians were executed after being captured. Amnesty International later wrote a letter to Prime Minister Surya Bahadur Thapa and Brigadier-General Nilendra Aryal, Head of the Royal Nepal Army (RNA) human rights cell, demanding an immediate inquiry. 10 February: Two central committee members of the CPN-M, Matrika Yadav and Suresh Paswan, are reported to have been handed over by India to Nepal. They were reportedly arrested in Lucknow after Nepal provided information. 13 February: Ganesh Chilwal leads an anti-Maoist protest on this day, the eighth anniversary of the commencement of the revolution. 15 February: Ganesh Chilwal is shot dead in his Kathmandu office by two suspected Maoists. 15 February: Fighting erupts at a Maoist jungle base in Kalikot District, 360 km west of Kathmandu. The base is said to hold 5000 Maoist troops. On 17 February, a security official says that a private helicopter flying troops to Kalikot was hit by Maoist fire but that it returned safely to Kathmandu. On 18 February, 65 Maoists are reported to have been killed, though this conflicts with other reported death tolls of 35 and 48. 15 and 16 February: State radio reports that 13 Maoist rebels were killed in seven separate small clashes with security forces across the country. 18 February: Lawmaker Khem Narayan Faujdar, a member of the parliament dissolved by King Gyanendra in 2002, is shot dead by two suspected Maoists riding a motorcycle in the Nawalparasi District, 200 km southwest of the capital, according to the police. 2 April: The largest rallies since 1990 begin in Kathmandu. They are variously labelled "pro-democracy" and "anti-monarchy." 4 April: "Hundreds of Maoist rebels" attack a Police outpost in Yadukuwa, Jadukhola. 13 policemen are killed, 7 wounded, and 35 are listed as missing. 8–9 Maoists are also killed. 24 June: The nephew of former Prime Minister Surya Bahadur Thapa is hacked to death by Maoist insurgents in Dhankuta district. 16 August: The Soaltee Hotel, a popular luxury hotel in Kathmandu, is bombed, after refusing a demand from the Maoists that the hotel be closed. 10 September: A bomb explodes at the United States Information Service office in Kathmandu. 11 November: Maoists kill NID Deputy Superintendent of Police Hemraj Regmi in front of his office residence in Butwal-6 in Rupandehi district. 15 December: Twenty government security personnel are killed in the western district of Arghakhanchi when the Maoists mount a surprise attack. 6 December: Sixteen Maoist rebels are killed in clashes with Nepali security forces in the western district of Dailekh. 23 December: Maoist forces launch blockade of Kathmandu.

events.title: Maoist's Beni Attack
events.detail: The 2004 Beni attack was one of the biggest attacks by the People's Liberation Army (PLA). Nanda Kishor Pun “Pasang” had overall operational command and coordinated the attack from the surrounding hills. The force was principally the Western Division under Barshaman Pun “Ananta.” Almost the entire Western Division of the PLA, numbering around 3,500, attacked government positions in Beni, on 20 March 2004 at around 10 pm. By 2003, the Maoist guerilla fighters were organised into a centralised military force, the People's Liberation Army, with battalion-level formations. It was divided into the Eastern Division and the Western Division, led by Nanda Kishor Pun (Pasang) and Barshaman Pun (Ananta), respectively. After the failure of the 2003 peace talks, the Maoists decided to start centralised attacks on government positions. Their first such attack, on positions in Dang and Banke, in October 2003, failed. By early 2004, the leadership started getting worried that the PLA cadre may get demoralised and frustrated, as the Nepalese Army (then Royal Nepalese Army (RNA)) claimed it had destroyed almost all of the PLA, while the PLA had not carried out successful large-scale attacks to disprove RNA's propaganda, in more than a year. The much smaller Eastern Division of the PLA carried out its attack on Bhojpur on 2 February 2004, resulting in 20 police and 12 military deaths. Around 3,500 PLA fighters, mainly from the Western Division, attacked Beni after weeks of preparation and a massive logistical mobilization involving roughly 1,700 civilian “volunteers,” many of whom were coerced or abducted. The Maoists surrounded the town, attacked the Royal Nepal Army barracks and police positions, destroyed government offices and freed prisoners from the district jail. They gained control of most of Beni but failed to capture the heavily defended army barracks, despite fighting for more than 12 hours. The Army eventually used helicopters to resupply and pursue them, forcing the Maoists to withdraw with around 40 hostages, including senior government and security officials. Casualty figures vary, but one widely cited reconstruction puts the deaths at about 140: 14 Army personnel, 17 police, 90 Maoist fighters and 19 civilians. The hostages were later taken to Thawang and released to the International Committee of the Red Cross on 6 April 2004. Strategically, Beni demonstrated the Maoists' ability to secretly mobilize thousands of fighters and temporarily overwhelm a district headquarters, but their failure to capture the Army barracks also demonstrated that they had not achieved military superiority over the state.

events.title: Anti-Monarchy Protest Intensified and Thapa Resigned
events.detail: 2 April saw the largest "pro-democracy" and "anti-monarchy" rallies since 1990. Protests became violent and thousands were arrested. Thapa had failed to bring the mainstream parties into his government or achieve the national consensus he had promised. Even factions within his own RPP were dissatisfied. Maoist war had resumed, making elections increasingly unrealistic. Donors were also pressing Nepal for democratic reforms and an end to the conflict. On 7 May 2004, Thapa resigned being unable to overcome opposition, political deadlock and growing pressure. Chand's resignation showed that the King could not govern indefinitely through a purely royalist government. Interestingly, the King then reappointed Sher Bahadur Deuba, giving him the task of holding elections and restoring political normality. But the major parties, including Girija's Nepali Congress, refused to join his government, and Parliament remained dissolved.

events.title: Ishwar Gurung and Dilman Gurung Killed by Maoists
events.detail: The Maoists accused Ishwar and Dilman of being informers for the security forces, allegedly because they operated a telephone in Ghandruk and supposedly passed information to the authorities. Around 9:30 p.m. on 10 April 2008, Maoists came to Ghandruk and took five people, including them to the Annapurna Conservation Area Project (ACAP) office, supposedly for a meeting. They were then taken through Landruk toward Lwang. The group reportedly consisted of hundreds of Maoist fighters. Maoists beat and tortured Ishwar and Dilman before shooting them dead in front of the other captives. The incident was particularly painful for the Congress because Ishwar was a Congress supporter, while Dilman supported the RPP. The 3 other captives were later released after 21 days, Dhurba Gurung was one of them, who is still active in NC politics.

Nepali Hostage Crisis in Iraq and Riots
events.detail: Iraq War was at peak. US had military camps in many locations of Iraq. It used to keep foreign laborers as cook in those camp as they were disciplined and cheap. An American company, Kellogg Brown & Root Dick, was given the responsibility to find those workers. At that time even US Vice President Chainey had investment in that company. The KBR, then outsourced the task to a Jordinian guy Dawat, who had agreement with a company called Morning Star. This company had connection with Nepal's Moonlight Manpower. The Moonlight Manpower published a vacancy for cooks in a five star hotel in Jordan. Without cross checking Kantipur newspaper publiched the vacancy. Channel Nepal and Spacetime Network also did the same. The workers were flown to Jordan from were the contractors from Morning Star picked them and were taken to a old house where there were already about 30-35 people coming in the same work. All were waiting to be transported to US military camps in Iraq. A very risky highway from Aman to Baghdad filled with enough hijackers had to be taken. On 19 August, some people in Iraqi military dress stop the vehicle carrying 12 Nepali workers at the midway of the highway. They told driver to keep the 12 workers in their checkpost from where American Army would take them. The drive naively left the workers in the checkpost and returned. And tragically the workers were kidnapped. The same day, the Terrorist group Ansa al-Sunnah, released the news in its website that 12 Nepalis have been taken hostage in Iraq. On 20 August, they released a video footage of the hostages, who pleaded for their lives and blamed an agent, Pralhad Giri of Moonlight Consultants, for their plight. All Nepali television channels air the footage. On 23 August, the government made an appeal through the Al Jazeera television for the release of the hostages. Nepali diplomats in Riyadh and Doha said that they were unable to establish contact with the kidnappers, nor ascertain what their demands were. On 26 August, the government wrote to the Iraqi government requesting it play a role in releasing the hostages. On 31 August, at 3 pm, international news agencies quoted a website announcement that the 12 hostages had been killed, news spread quickly through the Nepali media. At 8 pm, a group of 20 protestors turned up on the street at Maitidevi and moved on to other areas, pulling down and tearing off signs of manpower agencies. At Ghantaghar, they pelt stones at the Jame Masjid and continue back to Kupondole. By then the number of protestors is more than 150 and they started searching for the office of Moonlight Consultants. Some mistaked a private house for the office and started hurling stones. After midnight, protestors dispersed. Early morning at 6 am on September 1, protestors appeared in several clusters at intersections in Kathmandu and Patan burning tyres and obstructing vehicles. Some searched for offices of manpower agencies. Those located at central areas like Putali Sadak, Bag Bajar and Baneswor were the first to be ransacked. At 7:30 am some 100 protestors reached Ghantaghar chanting slogans against 'Islamic terrorists'. There they pelted stones at the mosque, some entered the premises, and even climbed to the roof. The mosque was damaged. Police appeared on the scene and took control of the situation. Protestors intensifed their search for manpower offices, took out all furniture and papers and set them on fire on the street. At 11 am, a group of protestors entered the Kantipur Publications, manhandled employees, pelted stones and got on a rampage for two hours. Police were nowhere to be seen. A dozen vehicles were set on fire. At 12 noon, the government announced a curfew within the Ring Road areas of Kathmandu and Patan from 2:00 pm. Regardless, at 1 am protesters advanced towards the Egyptian Embassy at Pulchok. Security personnel tried to stop them and finally opened fire. One protestor was killed and three injured. Protestors and security personnel also clashed near Ratna Park. One person was seriously injured and was rushed to the hospital, where he died. At least one dozen other protestors were injured. At 1;30 pm, demonstrators ransacked, looted and set fire to the Kathmandu office of Qatar Airways. The airline suspended its twice daily flights to Kathmandu. Other Middle East airline offices were also vandalised in Hatisar. At 1:45 pm, Spacetime Network was attacked. The news studio of Channel Nepal was destroyed and the company closed broadcasts. Officials charged the government with not providing security despite repeated requests. As cerfew went into effect starting 2 pm, the situation cooled down.

events.title: Multi-Fiber Arrangement Inport Quota Expired
events.detail: In 1974 GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade), which was the global trade organization before the WTO existed, signed a Multi-Fiber Arrangement (MFA) pushed by Wealthy countries like the US and EU to protect their own factories. Under the MFA strict, government-enforced quota was imposed on exact number of items a specific country could ship to a Western nation each year. It was done to protect their local garment workers and factories from being completely overwhelmed by sudden, cheap foreign competition. Big manufacturing countries like China and India filled their quotas very quickly. Once they hit their limit, Western stores had to buy clothes from smaller countries like Nepal. The US garment quota assigned for Nepal was estimated to be 2.38 pieces per capita, highest among South Asian countries. Many Indian garment industries hopped into Nepal setting up their settalite manufacturing unit where fabric was cut and stitched by local workers. Because the final shirt was assembled in Nepal, the factory legally obtained a Nepali Export Certificate. The 1971 MFA was conceived as a temporary tool but it received four extensions-in 1977, 1981,1986 and 1994-which increased its entrenchment and raised hope for a longer future. However, an agreement signed in Marrakech on 15 April, 1994, made the WTO effective from January 1, 1995. What this meant for MFA was that it was then replaced with the Agreement on Textiles and Clothing (ATC), which is committed to rid the international textile trade of any protection or regulation that is likely to undermine the free-market apparatus. A ten-member body under ATC planned out the abolition of MFA in four stages ending on January 1, 2005. Along with MFA abolition Nepal faced issues of load-shedding, civil war, and outdated machineries which finally put nail in the coffin of Nepali textile industry. An industry once made up of 1,200 firms now has only 50.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2005
events.detail: 2 January: Nepali media reports two children being killed in Dailekh district by a Maoist bomb. 4 January: Three government security personnel and between two and twenty-four Maoist rebels reported killed in fighting. 8 January: Maoists detain and later release 300 passengers from six buses that defy their blockade of Kathmandu. 15 January: Maoists allegedly detain 14 Indian Gurkhas from Chuha village in Kailali. 29 January: Government leader in the Lamjung district had been abducted and murdered with a gunshot to the head. 1 February: King Gyanendra dissolves the Deuba government and bans all news reports. The army begins arresting senior political leaders, journalists, trade unionists, human rights activists and civil society leaders. All telephone and internet connections are cut. 7 April: Maoists attack an army base in Khara, Rukum suffering 300 losses. 6 June: Badarmude bus explosion: Some 38 civilians are killed and over 70 injured after a packed passenger bus runs over a rebel landmine in Chitwan district. 9 August: Maoist rebels kill 40 security men in midwestern Nepal. 3 September: The Maoists declare a three-month unilateral ceasefire to woo opposition political parties. October: Chunbang Central Committee meeting in Rolpa decides to join hands with the political parties against the king 19 November: After negotiations, the Maoist rebels agree to work with opposition politicians in a common front against the rule of King Gyanendra.

events.title: Baburam Bhattarai Detained by Prachanda
events.detail: In 2004–05, a major strategic and leadership dispute developed between Prachanda and Baburam Bhattarai. Prachanda's camp explored the possibility of dealing with the monarchy and emphasized a military strategic offensive, while Bhattarai argued that the monarchy was the principal enemy and that cooperation with Nepal's parliamentary democratic forces should remain open. In August 2004, during a Maoist central committee meeting at Phuntibang, Rolpa, Prachanda proposed to centralise the party structure and the PLA to prepare for a counter-attack against state forces. Bhattarai disagreed and walked off from the meeting. Later, Bhattarai published an article in Kantipur titled "Princely Tendency and Democracy" without first obtaining the party leadership's approval. The article was highly critical of the monarchy and warned that King Gyanendra was moving toward direct authoritarian rule. Bhattarai argued that genuine democratic forces needed to recognize the danger posed by the king. From Bhattarai's perspective, he was making a legitimate political argument. From Prachanda's perspective, a senior Maoist leader was publicly airing an internal disagreement without authorization, potentially exposing the party's internal divisions. In January 2005, the Maoist leadership took disciplinary action against Bhattarai, removing from his leadership responsibilities and placing under armed detention. He, along with his wife Hisila Yami, was put under Maoist house arrest in Lawang, Rukum, guarded by armed Maoists. King Gyanendra's 1 February 2005 takeover changed the strategic environment which was rapidly moving in the direction Bhattarai had warned about. In early February Bhattarai was released from house arrest. The two leaders reconciled, and at Chunwang in October 2005 the Maoists adopted a strategy of cooperation with the Seven Party Alliance, leading to the 12-Point Agreement of 22 November 2005.

events.title: Ratan Singh Gurung Killed
events.detail: NC Leader Ratan Singh Gurung of Mijure Danda, Madi Gaupalika was killed by Maoists.

events.title: King Gyanendra Imposed Direct Rule
events.detail: On 1 February 2005, around 10:25 am King Gyanendra addressed the nation. He dismissed Deuba, assumed direct executive power, declared a state of emergency, detained political leaders, restricted civil liberties and imposed censorship. He also promised to restore democracy within three years. Immediately around the takeover fixed telephone lines were cut, mobile phone service was shut down, internet access was blocked, fax communications were disrupted, and international communication was severely restricted. The shutdown lasted roughly a week for many communications services, although some services were restored earlier or later depending on the location. The army's signals corps was specifically involved in shutting down satellite links. Armed soldiers were deployed to major newspapers, radio stations and television outlets. They monitored what was being published or broadcast and pre-screened news reports. Editors were summoned and warned about publishing material critical of the King or military. The censorship extended to FM radio, which was particularly important because radio reached much of rural Nepal. Private FM stations were prohibited from broadcasting news, effectively removing one of the country's most important independent sources of information. On 3 February, the government formally announced a six-month ban on articles, interviews, news, notices and opinions considered contrary to the royal proclamation. Political leaders were rounded up. Leaders like Girija Prasad Koirala, Sher Bahadur Deuba, and Madhav Kumar Nepal were kept under house arrest while other leaders like Krishna Prasad Bhattarai, Lokendra Bahadur Chand, Surya Bahadur Thapa, Pashupati Shamsher Rana, K.P. Sharma Oli, Bamdev Gautam, Bharat Mohan Adhikari, Amrit Kumar Bohara, Sahana Pradhan, etc. were detained.

events.title: Second Battle of Khara
events.detail: By 2005, the Royal Nepalese Army had learned from the losses of 2001–02 and had heavily fortified its bases. The Maoists therefore attempted something much more ambitious: a direct assault on a fortified Army position. On the night of 7 April 2005, thousands of PLA fighters attacked the Royal Nepal Army base at Khara. They used mortars, rocket launchers and infantry assaults and attempted to break through the defensive perimeter. The battle continued into 8 April, lasting roughly 15–18 hours. The Maoists managed to penetrate some outer obstacles but could not capture the main defensive position. Army forces used machine guns, mortars and helicopter support, and reinforcements eventually arrived. The PLA withdrew after suffering extremely heavy losses. The exact Maoist death toll is highly disputed. The Army initially reported 50, then 97, and subsequently claimed figures above 150; contemporary independent reporting could not independently verify the numbers. Three security personnel were officially reported killed. Khara exposed a fundamental military problem for the Maoists that they could defeat isolated police posts and sometimes overrun district headquarters, but they could not easily break a properly fortified Army position. The Maoists suffered another major defeat during the subsequent retreat, when fighting at Dalphing, Rukum, on 13 April 2005 reportedly killed around 60 Maoists, according to the Army. And this has a major political connection to the story you are studying: Khara helped convince the Maoist leadership that a purely military route to victory was extremely difficult. The Maoists subsequently reassessed their strategy, and the Chunwang meeting later in 2005 helped produce the political strategy that led to the 12-Point Understanding with the Seven Party Alliance in November 2005.

events.title: Ganesh Man Palikhe Killed
events.detail: NC Leader Ganesh Man Palikhe of Nagdhunga, Pokhara was killed by Maoists.

events.title: NC Eleventh General Convention
events.detail: Girija Prasad Koirala; Girija(1215 votes) got elected again for the president winning over Narhari Acharya(165 votes) in the Lalitpur convention. Ram Baran Yadav Ram Chandra Paudel Bimalendra Nidhi and Kul Bahadur Gurung were elected as the General Secretary. Girija died while he was president and Sushil Koirala was made the Acting President.

events.title: Chunbang Central Committee Meeting
events.detail: For almost ten years Maoists had been fighting to overthrow the monarchy and establish a revolutionary state. They had become a formidable insurgent force, but battles such as Khara in April 2005 demonstrated the fundamental limitation of their military strategy: they could attack and sometimes overwhelm government positions, but they could not defeat the Royal Nepal Army and seize the state militarily. The Chunwang meeting in Rukum concluded that the Maoists should join forces with the parliamentary parties against King Gyanendra. The Maoists also moved toward the objective of a democratic republic, rather than insisting that the immediate outcome had to be their earlier conception of a Maoist people's republic.

events.title: 12-Point Agreement Reached
events.detail: The Seven Party Alliance (SPA) was formed in May 2005, a few months after King Gyanendra's 1 February 2005 royal takeover. It brought together the major parliamentary parties to jointly oppose direct royal rule and demand restoration of democracy. Nepali Congress, UML, Nepali Congress (Democratic), Nepal Sadbhavana Party (Anandi Devi), Jana Morcha Nepal, Samyukta Baam Morcha, and Nepal Workers and Peasants Party were the seven parties. Importantly, the Maoists were not part of the SPA. They remained an armed underground movement. Negotiations gradually developed between SPA and Maoists during 2005, eventually producing the 12-Point Understanding of 22 November 2005 in Delhi. The Maoists made an extraordinary tactical concession. They agreed to: accept competitive multiparty democracy; respect fundamental rights, human rights and the rule of law; abandon the immediate objective of establishing a one-party communist state; eventually place their arms under international supervision; and participate in a political process leading toward a Constituent Assembly. The seven parties, meanwhile, agreed to pursue constitutional restructuring and a Constituent Assembly rather than simply restoring the old 1990 system unchanged. During much of the insurgency, India had supported Nepal's government and security forces against the Maoists. India was itself deeply concerned about Maoist insurgency because it had its own Naxalite/Maoist movements. But Gyanendra's takeover changed India's calculations. It eventually realized the need for sustained peace and democracy in Nepal and fascilitated to restore democratic politics, bring the Maoists into a political process, and prevent Nepal from descending into permanent war or authoritarian rule. India's tacit facilitation helped bring the two sides together in Delh, producing the 12-point agreement that became the political foundation of the 2006 democratic movement and ultimately the peace process.

events.title: Maoist Activities in 2006
events.detail: 2 January: Rebels decide not to extend a four-month ceasefire saying that the government had broken the ceasefire with numerous attacks on Maoist villages. 14 January: Maoists launch coordinated attacks on five military and paramilitary targets in the Kathmandu valley, the first demonstration of their ability to organize violence within the Valley, prompting curfews at night for the next several days. 14 March: Nepali rebels extend road blockade; nationwide strike called for 3 April. 5 April: General strike begins with Maoist forces promising to refrain from violence. 8 April: A curfew is imposed in Kathmandu from 10 pm to 9 am The king orders protesters violating the curfew to be "shot on sight." 26 April: The Maoists start to unblock streets and roads, but put forth some conditions. 27 April: Maoist insurgents, responding to a demand by the newly appointed prime minister Girija Prasad Koirala, announce a unilateral three-month truce after weeks of pro-democracy protests in Kathmandu, and encourage the formation of a new constituent assembly to rewrite the nation's constitution. 3 May: Nepal's new cabinet declares a ceasefire. This was not taken very seriously. The cabinet also announces that the Maoist rebels will no longer be considered a terrorist group. Rebels are also encouraged to open peace talks. 21 November: Peace talks end with the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Accord between Prime Minister Koirala and Maoist leader Prachanda. The deal allows the Maoists to take part in government, and places their weapons under UN monitoring.

events.title: 2062 Local Elections Amid Boycott
events.detail: Local elections were supposed to be held in 2059 after 2054. However, at that time, the Maoist armed struggle had reached its peak and its impact on power politics had also been felt. Issues such as the state of emergency and the dissolution of parliament threw the election into confusion. After the then King Gyanendra Shah took power on 19 Magh 2061, municipal elections were announced in 2062. Despite opposition and boycott by the Seven Party Alliance and Maoists, elections were held in 58 municipalities in 43 districts on 26 Magh 2062 for a total of 4,146 positions, including 58 mayors and deputy mayors, 806 ward chairmen, 2,418 ward members, and 806 women ward members. Gyanendra wanted these elections to demonstrate that political life could continue without the traditional parliamentary parties. At that time, all positions in 22 municipalities were elected unopposed as King's loyalists only gave the candidacy. Voting was held in 36 municipalities in 28 districts. However, the election couldn't be held in VDCs due to Maoist insurgency. The elections were widely regarded as a political failure because participation was very low and many candidates ran unopposed or with little meaningful competition. Because the terms of previously elected local officials had expired in 2002, the central government had simply handed total administrative control of the VDCs and DDCs over to centrally appointed civil servants, primarily VDC Secretaries and LDOs. The positions in municipalities also became vacant in 2006 after the success of Second People's Movement. Hence, the local bodies remained representative less for about 2 decades untill local election took place in 2017 under new constitution.

events.title: Second People’s Movement
events.detail: The SPA announced an indefinite nationwide general strike and mass movement beginning in early April. The principal date usually given for the beginning of Jana Andolan II is 6 April 2006, although mobilization and protest activity began on 5 April. On April 3 the Maoists announced a unilateral ceasefire inside Kathmandu Valley, reducing the immediate security threat as the SPA prepared for its nationwide movement. To block SPA from holding protests, the royal government banned demonstrations in Kathmandu and imposed a night curfew. About 100 political activists and leaders were detained ahead of the planned movement. Starting 6th April, the SPA's nationwide general strike began. At least 300 activists and journalists were arrested in Kathmandu, while demonstrations spread across the country. On April 7, Maoists attacked security installations in several districts while mass demonstrations continued. In the confrontation, 7 Maoists and 1 civilian were killed in Butwal, and 1 soldier, 2 policemen and 1 civilian in Taulihawa. On April 9, the SPA extended the strike indefinitely as demonstrations grew. Security forces fired on protesters, producing deaths and further anger against the government. On April 16, Gyanendra met foreign diplomats and signaled that he may be willing to make concessions, but gave no concrete proposal capable of satisfying the opposition. On April 19, Security forces killed additional protesters. Human Rights Watch (HRW) documented more than 2,000 injured and at least 9 dead by 20 April. The demonstrations had now become a sustained nationwide mass movement rather than merely a party-organized protest. With enormous crowds on the streets, on April 21, Gyanendra announced that he was prepared to return executive power to the people and asked the SPA to nominate a prime minister. The SPA rejected the offer because it did not restore Parliament or meet its broader political demands. On April 22, SPA crystallized its demands of restoring the dissolved House of Representatives, form an all-party/interim government, and holding Constituent Assembly elections. While on same day huge demonstrations defied curfew and moved toward the palace. On Arpil 23, Kathmandu was placed under an approximately 11-hour curfew, with authorities imposing a shoot-at-sight order. Meanwhile Maoists carried out attacks elsewhere: in Chautara, Sindhupalchowk, an OHCHR chronology recorded 4 Maoist combatants, 1 civilian and 1 Royal Nepal Army member killed. Despite this, the SPA announced an even larger demonstration for April 25. Late at night, on April 24, King Gyanendra announced that the House of Representatives dissolved in 2002 would be reinstated and called upon the SPA to form the government. The SPA accepted the proclamation and called off the nationwide strike. Second People's Movement had effectively succeeded. HRW later assessed that 18 people had been killed and around 4,000 injured by the security forces during the movement. On April 25, The SPA selected Girija Prasad Koirala to head the new government. Curfews were lifted, detainees are released and public celebrations spread across Nepal. The Maoists, however, rejected the King's proclamation as insufficient. On April 26, the Maoists declared a three-month unilateral ceasefire, signaling that they were prepared to shift from armed confrontation toward political negotiations.

events.title: Banks and Financial Institutions Act (BAFIA) Inacted
events.detail: BAFIA, 2063, this landmark legislation was introduced to unify and consolidate several older, fragmented banking laws—such as the Commercial Bank Act of 1974 and the Agricultural Development Bank Act of 1967. It served as the primary regulatory framework until it was entirely replaced by the current BAFIA, 2073. It divided institutions into Class A, B, C, and D based on size and services, granted Nepal Rastra Bank full authority over licenses, mergers, and enforcement, limited board sizes to 5–7 members, and restricted promoters from selling their shares for 10 years and set employee quotas among many others. The recent 2017 BAFIA amendment bill introduced critical reforms targeting corporate governance, digital financial shifts, and conflict-of-interest risks.

events.title: The Interim Constitution of Nepal 2007 Promulgated
events.detail: Following the Comprehensive Peace Agreement a committee representing the government and Maoists negotiated and prepared the Interim Constitution. The document was designed to replace the 1990 Constitution, which had become incompatible with the post-Jana Andolan political settlement. The restored House of Representatives met in the morning of January 15 and unanimously approved the Interim Constitution. At this point, the Maoists were not yet members of Parliament. Under the new Constitution, the existing House of Representatives was dissolved/replaced by the new Interim Legislature-Parliament. The Constitution itself specified that it was promulgated by the House of Representatives and would be approved by the Legislature-Parliament. Later, on the same day, The new Interim Legislature-Parliament was constituted, with 83 Maoist representatives joining the existing parliamentary parties. The legislature had roughly 330 seats. The newly constituted legislature held its first sitting, with the Maoist representatives now participating, and unanimously endorsed the Interim Constitution. It was therefore essentially a political/legislative act, not a royal proclamation. The Interim Constitution did not immediately abolish the monarchy. Instead, it stripped the King of virtually all constitutional authority. His powers were transferred to the Prime Minister.

events.title: Koshi River Embankment Breach
events.detail: The August 18, 2008 Koshi River embankment breach is considered one of the most catastrophic engineering and humanitarian disasters in the history of South Asia. Rather than being caused by an unusually high volume of water or extreme rainfall, the disaster was caused by structural neglect and the river's natural tendency to shift its path. Under the terms of the 1954/1966 Kosi Agreement, India was solely responsible for maintaining and repairing the embankments. However, routine maintenance, boulder reinforcement, and spur repairs had been critically neglected in the months leading up to the disaster. Crucially, the breach occurred at a water flow rate of roughly 144,000 cusecs. This was well below the barrage's designed maximum capacity of 950,000 cusecs, proving that poor maintenance, not an unprecedented flood volume, caused the structural failure. The rushing waters instantly inundated the Sunsari and Saptari districts, displacing over 70,000 Nepali citizens and destroying vital segments of the East-West Highway, which completely cut off eastern Nepal from the rest of the country. The water swept south into North Bihar, catching millions of people completely off guard. It submerged thousands of villages across districts like Supaul, Madhepura, Saharsa, and Araria. The disaster killed over 500 people(12-15 in Nepal), displaced more than 3.5 million people, and destroyed hundreds of thousands of acres of fertile agricultural cropland under thick layers of sand. the Koshi embankment reconstruction began in late 2008 and was successfully completed by early 2009, ahead of the next monsoon.

events.title: 7.8 Mag. Gorkha Earthquake
events.detail:
It struck on 25 April 2015 at 11:56 a.m., with a magnitude of about Mag. 7.8–7.9, along the Main Himalayan Thrust, at a shallow depth of about 8.2 km. Human loss: About 8,857 people died in Nepal and more than 22,000 were injured; nearly 3.5 million people were left homeless. Including deaths in India, China and Bangladesh, the total death toll was about 8,964. Cultural heritage: Numerous historic monuments and UNESCO World Heritage sites were destroyed or severely damaged, including parts of Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur Durbar Squares, Changu Narayan and major temples. Dharahara collapsed, killing at least 180 people. Immediate Response: The Nepal Army launched Operation Sankat Mochan. Around 90% of Nepal Army soldiers were mobilized for rescue and relief. Nepal Police and the Armed Police Force were also heavily deployed. According to PDNA, 65,059 Nepal Army personnel, 41,776 Nepal Police personnel, 24,775 Armed Police Force personnel, 22,500 civil servants, around 4,000 government and private health workers were involved in rescue and relief. International Response: A major assessment found that 34 countries physically sent personnel around 76 urban search-and-rescue team approximately 2,242 personnel, 135 search-and-rescue dogs, around 141 foreign medical teams, roughly 1,858 medical professionals and 18 foreign military teams participated in the emergency response. India's Operation Maitri involved the Indian Army, Indian Air Force and National Disaster Response Force. Indian aircraft began operating within hours sending its NDRF search-and-rescue teams. The Indian government subsequently reported 2,223 sorties, evacuation/rescue of approximately 11,200 people, transportation of around 1,700 tonnes of relief material, and medical assistance to 4,762 injured people. China, the United States, United Kingdom, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Japan, Israel, Australia, Canada, Spain, Singapore, Malaysia, Poland, Thailand and others contributed rescue personnel, medical teams, aircraft and supplies. The United States deployed military personnel and aircraft. One tragic episode occurred on May 12 when a US Marine Corps UH-1Y helicopter delivering relief supplies crashed near Charikot, killing six US Marines and two Nepali soldiers. Nepal's infrastructure could not easily absorb the sudden arrival of thousands of foreign personnel, aircraft and tonnes of relief material. Problems included congestion at Kathmandu airport, customs delays, insufficient helicopters, difficulty reaching remote areas, duplication of some forms of aid, inappropriate or unnecessary relief materials, concerns about distribution, coordination problems, political disputes over who controlled aid. There was also tension over whether international NGOs should route assistance through the government's official disaster-relief mechanisms or distribute it directly. Kathmandu airport itself became a bottleneck, and restrictions were placed on heavy aircraft after cracks appeared on the runway. PDNA and Aid: The Post-Disaster Needs Assessment estimated approximately $7 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs, while later estimates put total economic damage at around $10 billion. The housing problem was particularly enormous. On June 25, 2015, government organized an international donors' conference in Kathmandu. At the conference, international donors pledged approximately $4.4 billion ($2.2 billion in grants and $2.2 billions in loan) for Nepal's recovery and reconstruction covering 66% of the estimated $6.7 billion recovery and reconstruction requirement. The conference was therefore a diplomatic success for Nepal. However, actual agreement was reached for roughly $3.4 billion. Major pledges were: India ($250 million grant and $750 million soft loan); China (~$500 million grant); Japan (~$260 million grant); US ($130 million grant); EU ($100 million grant); and World Bank (~500 million loan). National Reconstruction Authority: After the earthquake, Nepal quickly realized that ordinary government ministries were not sufficient to handle reconstruction on this scale. There Sushi Koirala government passed an ordinance in June to establish National Reconstruction Authority (NRA) with mandate to lead and coordinate reconstruction with national and international partners. Dr. Govinda Raj Pokharel the then NPC vice-chair was chosen as the CEO. However, after Oli came to power the ordinance was failed resulting in dismissal of NRA. In December, approximately eight months after the earthquake, the Reconstruction Act was passed from the parliament and NRA was re-established under leadership of Sushil Gyewali. Housing Reconstruction: NRA determined the house reconstruction pipeline which involved survey of damaged houses, beneficiary verification, participation aggrement, first tranche of 50 thousands, construction begins, engineer inspection, second tranche of 1.5 lakhs, Roofing/ring beam level, third tranche of 1 lakhs, and completion certificate. World Bank spearheaded the Earthquake Housing Reconstruction Project (EHRP) program. Rather than launching distinct, competing projects, major Western donors—including the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Switzerland—pooled their financial assets directly into a Multi-Donor Trust Fund managed by the World Bank. Though India and Japan opted for separate financing NRA required both of them to strictly follow the EHRP project design and procedures. Hence all the houses whether funded by Multi-Donor Trust, Bilateral Aid, or Nepal Government all followed the same owner-driven house reconstruction model. World Bank constructed about ~310,000+ houses, Japan constructed ~95,000+ houses, India constructed ~50,000 houses, Multi-Donor Trust Fund constructed ~30,000 houses, and Nepal Government constructed ~310,000+ houses totaling ~730,000+ houses recieving third tranche. School and Health Facilities Reconstruction: The reconstruction of schools and health facilities were spearheaded by sector-specific implementation arms in respective ministries called Central Level Project Implementation Units (CLPIU). This structure allowed the NRA to remain a central coordinating authority, while sector specialists actually managed construction. The Education CLPIU, for example, explicitly operated under NRA policy, directives and resources while coordinating with donors, governments, NGOs and development partners. Different donors could finance particular schools. Under the program JICA built 274 schools, India built 70 schools,

These were sector-specific implementation arms

A major Rural Housing Reconstruction Program was established for earthquake-affected districts.

Damage was estimated at around US$10 billion, roughly half of Nepal’s GDP at the time. Reconstruction therefore became a major national economic challenge. Long-term social consequences: The disaster affected housing, migration, urbanization, debt, tourism, healthcare and social inequality. Vulnerable groups, particularly poor and marginalized communities, faced greater difficulty accessing relief and reconstruction assistance. International response: Nepal received massive international assistance. Around US$3 billion was pledged, with India launching Operation Maitri and numerous countries sending rescue teams, medical personnel, supplies and financial assistance.

events.title: BP Highway Completed
events.detail: The BP Highway (Banepa–Sindhuli–Bardibas Road) is a 158 km highway connecting Kathmandu Valley with the eastern Tarai Madhesh and Koshi Province. It is the shortest road link between Kathmandu and eastern Nepal. Construction began in 1996 with Japanese grant assistance and after repeated delays due to funding security and technical challenges was completed and handed over to Nepal in July 2015. The project cost approximately NPR 21.5 billion (¥26 billion). The highway introduced advanced engineering techniques to Nepal including shotcrete geotextiles and bioengineering for landslide control and slope stabilization alongside extensive environmental mitigation measures. It significantly reduced travel distance to eastern Nepal by about 200 km.

A person who obtains the citizenship of Nepal by descent may obtain a certificate of citizenship of Nepal with gender identity by the name of his or her mother or father. Honorary Citizenship: A special status that could be granted by the government to prominent foreign nationals who rendered exceptional contributions to Nepal and would be equal to naturalized citizenship. events.title: 2074 Local Election
events.detail: The 2017 Nepalese local elections were held in Nepal in three phases on 14 May, 28 June and 18 September in 6 metropolitan cities, 11 sub-metropolitan cities, 276 municipalities and 460 rural municipalities. It was the first local level election to be held since the promulgation of the 2015 constitution. Each local units elected one Mayor, and one Deputy Mayor among which one had to be female. And each wards elected one Ward Chairman and four Ward Members (one Dalit female, one female open, and two open). Overall, CPN UML came first, NC came second, and Maoist came third.

events.title: Forest Act 2019 Inacted
events.detail: The landmark case Shrestha v. Office of the Prime Minister et al. (decided in December 2018) served as the primary legal catalyst for Nepal's Forests Act of 2019. The Supreme Court of Nepal ruled in favor of Shrestha issuing a historic mandate ordering the government to immediately draft and enact comprehensive laws addressing climate mitigation and adaptation. Because the existing 1993 legal framework was completely unequipped to handle international climate mechanisms the federal parliament enacted the Forests Act of 2019 (alongside the Environment Protection Act of 2019) to institutionalize the court's order and align domestic laws with the Paris Agreement. Environmental Commodities: Legally defined natural forest resources—such as carbon storage emission reduction biodiversity and watershed protection—as distinct monetizable economic assets. Carbon Market Access: Transitioned forest management from local resource extraction (timber and fuel) to global climate trading establishing the domestic legal architecture required to sell certified carbon credits to international entities. Climate Finance Management: Established the Forest Development Fund (FDF) to house international revenue and legally mandates that these funds be spent exclusively on environmental recovery local adaptation and national conservation. Decentralized Management: Organized all national forests into six distinct regulatory categories—Government-managed Protection zones Community Partnership Lease-hold and Religious—to optimize ecological sustainability and socioeconomic prosperity. Forest Administration: Nepal's forest administration is divided into Government-Managed forests 57% Community forests 33% Collaborative forests 6% Protected Area system forests 3% and other minor leasehold religious or private categories 1%.

events.title: Upper Tamakoshi Hydroelectric Project Completed
events.detail: Nepal's largest operating project to date of capacity 456 MW. It was fully financed using national resources (pension funds insurance and public shares) and successfully transitioned Nepal into an electricity-surplus state during wet seasons. The majority share (51%) of the Company is held by four public entities namely Nepal Electricity Authority (NEA) Nepal Telecom (NTC) Citizen Investment Trust (CIT) and Rastriya Beema Sansthan (RBS). Rest 49% is owned by general public.

events.title: Karnali Highway Completed
events.detail: The 505 km Karnali Highway (Nepalgunj-Kohalpur-Birendranagar (prev. Ratna Highway)-Manma (Kalikot)-Khalanga(Jumla)-Nagma(Jumla)-Gamgadhi(Mugu)-Simikot(Humla)-Hilsa Road) was envisioned in 1992 with Girija Prasad Koirala laying stone. The Ratna Highway section was completed in late 1990s while the rest was completed in parts. The road track for Birendranagar-Khalanga was finally opened on April 2006 and the blacktopping was completed in 2015. The Nagma-Gamgadhi section was completed in 2012 while only 6 km of the road had been blacktopped. That too only in the Jumla section. Mugu does not yet have a blacktopped road. The responsibility of Gamgadhi-Simikot-Hilsa section of the highway was handed to Nepali Army in 2015 who completed the construction by 2019 and the final linkage via a Bailey bridge over the Chuwakhola River in 2025 after 26 years of intermittent development. Upgrades including blacktopping and widening have been prioritized lately but due to multiple contract failures it has been significantly delayed.
